Therefore, it is said:
no benefit is greater than simplicity,
no blessing is more enduring than peace.
If you were to give Jiàng Shí, a craftsman with a thousand years of life, a hook,
and have him follow compasses and squares,
and raise plumb lines and ink markers,
to correct Mount Tài;
and have Bēn and
Yù carry the Gānjiàng sword
to regulate the myriad people;
even if they exhausted their skill,
and reached the height of longevity,
Mount Tài would not be corrected,
and the people could not be regulated.
Therefore it is said:
Those who governed the world in ancient times
did not have Jiàng Shí exhaust his skill
to ruin the form of Mount Tài,
nor did they have Bēn and Yù exhaust their power
to harm the nature of the myriad people.
Relying on the Way and preserving the law,
the gentleman is happy and the great villain ceases.
Being indifferent, leisurely, and tranquil,
conforming to Heaven's mandate,
holding to the greater principle.
Therefore, he causes people to have no crime of departing from the law,
and fish to have no misfortune of losing water.
If it is like this,
then the world will have few impossibilities.
If the ruler does not emulate Heaven, he cannot universally cover (all things).
If the heart (of the ruler) does not emulate Earth, things will not necessarily be carried (by it).
Tài Shān does not establish likes and dislikes,
therefore it can achieve its height;
rivers and seas do not select small contributions,
therefore they can achieve their abundance.
Therefore, the great person entrusts their form to Heaven and Earth
and the myriad things are complete;
they apply their mind to mountains and seas
and the state is enriched.
Above there is no poison of anger,
below there is no hidden worry of resentment,
those above and those below interact with simplicity,
taking the Dao as their abode.
Therefore, long-term benefits accumulate,
great achievements are established,
fame is established in the front,
virtue is passed down to posterity,
this is the pinnacle of governance.
*Nèi Chǔ Shuō Shàng* Seven Techniques, Thirtieth.
These Seven Techniques are what the ruler uses,
and the Six Subtle Observations are what are examined.
The Seven Techniques:
First is comprehensively observing many clues;
Second, is the certain application of punishment to clarify authority;
third, is the reliable rewarding to exhaust ability;
fourth, is single-mindedly listening to place responsibility on subordinates;
fifth, is suspiciously issuing edicts and deceptively employing envoys;
sixth, is feigning knowledge and then questioning;
seventh, is inverting words and contradicting matters.
These seven are what the ruler employs.
First principle: comprehensive observation.
If observation and listening are not comprehensive,
then the truth will not be heard.
If listening has biased avenues,
then ministers will obstruct (the ruler).
The explanation lies in the dwarf's dream of seeing the stove,
and Āigōng's 哀公 statement, "Nothing is more confusing than a crowd."
Therefore, there is the Qí 齊 person's sighting of the Hé Bó 河伯,
and Huìzǐ's 惠子 saying about "losing half."
The problem lies in Shù Niú's 豎牛 starving Shū Sūn 叔孫,
and Jiāng Yǐ's 江乙 explaining the customs of Jīng 荊.
Sì Gōng 嗣公 wanted to govern but did not know how,
so he caused rivals.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler infers from a pile of iron,
and observes the troubles of a single market.
Second principle: certain punishment.
If love is excessive,
then the law will not be established.
When authority is weak and isolated,
inferiors will encroach upon their superiors.
Therefore, if punishments are not certain,
prohibitions will not be effective.
The explanation for this lies in Dǒngzǐ's administration of Shíyì,
and Zǐchǎn's instruction of Yóují.
Thus, Zhòngní spoke of fallen frost,
and the Yin dynasty law punished those who discarded ashes,
Yuèchí was about to be removed,
and Gōngsūn Yāng emphasized minor crimes.
Therefore, the gold of the Lì River cannot be guarded,
and the fire of the Jī Marsh cannot be rescued.
Chéng Huān weakened the state of Qí with excessive benevolence,
Bǔ Pí caused the King of Wèi to perish with kindness and generosity.
Guǎn Zhòng knew this,
therefore he executed dead people.
Sì Gōng knew this, therefore he bought convict laborers.
Third Canon: Rewards and Praise. 〓#
If rewards and praise are meager and insincere,
inferiors will not be useful.
If rewards and praise are generous and reliable,
inferiors will treat death lightly.
The explanation for this lies in Wénzǐ's saying
"like beasts and deer".
Thus, the King of Yuè burned his palaces,
Wú Qǐ leaned on the carriage shaft,
Lǐ Kuī judged lawsuits with archery,
Sòng Chóng died by destroying the gate.
Gōu Jiàn knew this,
therefore, he paid respect to an angry frog.
Zhāo Hóu knew this,
therefore, he hid his worn-out trousers.
Generous rewards cause people to act like Bēn and Zhū;
women pick up silkworms,
fishermen grasp sturgeon;
therefore, they emulate them.
Principle four: Unified Hearing. 〓#
Unified hearing prevents the wise and foolish from being confused;
assigning responsibility below prevents ministers from conspiring.
The explanation lies in searching for Zhèng and playing the yú.
The danger lies in Shēn Zǐ using Zhào Shào and Hán Tà for testing.
Therefore, Gōngzǐ Fàn proposed cutting off Hédōng,
and Yīng Hóu plotted to abandon Shàngdǎng.
Principle five: Deceptive Employment. 〓#
Frequent meetings and prolonged waiting without appointment will cause the treacherous to scatter like deer.
jiān zé lù sàn.
Employing someone to ask about others
prevents the selling of private favors.
Therefore, Páng Jìng returned the dukes and grandees,
and Dài Huān was ordered to inspect the warm carriages;
The ruler of Zhou lost a jade hairpin,
the Grand Minister of Shang discussed cow dung.
Chapter Six: Employing Wisdom. 〓#
By employing wisdom in questioning,
even the unwise become wise;
deeply understanding one thing,
all hidden things will change.
The explanation lies in how Marquis Zhao grasped one claw.
Therefore, one must pass through the south gate to gain the three districts.
The ruler of Zhou searched for a crooked staff, and his ministers were afraid;
Bǔ Pí used the commoners,
Xīmén Bào feigned losing a linchpin.
Chapter Seven: Inverted Speech. 〓#
Inverting words and reversing matters
to test what is suspected,
then treacherous intentions will be revealed.
Therefore, Yáng Shān deceived Jiū Shù,
Nào Chǐ served as an envoy for Qin,
A man of Qi wanted to cause trouble,
Zǐ [Shi] used white horses,
Zǐ Chǎn separated the litigants,
Sì Gōng passed through the border market.
Story One: 〓#
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Mí Zixia was favored,
He was dedicated to the state of Wèi.
A dwarf who was received in audience by the Duke said:
"My dream has come true."
The Duke said:
"What dream?"
He replied:
"I dreamed of a stove,
which is because I was going to see Your Lordship."
The Duke angrily said:
"I have heard that those who are to be received by a ruler dream of the sun.
Why do you dream of a stove when you are to be received by me?"
He replied:
"The sun illuminates the entire world,
and no single thing can block it.
The ruler illuminates the people of a country,
and no single person can conceal him.
Therefore, those who are to be received by a ruler dream of the sun.
As for the stove,
if one person obstructs it,
then those behind him cannot see it.
Now, perhaps there is someone obstructing Your Lordship?
Then, even if I dream of a stove,
is it not reasonable?"
Lǔ Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"A common saying goes:
"Do not be misled by the crowd."
Now, I, your subject, undertake affairs,
and deliberate with my ministers,
but the state becomes increasingly chaotic.
What is the reason for this?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 replied,
"When an enlightened ruler questions his ministers,
one person knows the answer,
and another does not know.
In such cases,
the enlightened ruler is above,
and the ministers offer straightforward advice below.
Now, all the ministers unanimously agree with Jìsūn 季孫,
and the entire state of Lǔ 魯 is transformed into one.
Even if you, my lord, were to ask the people within the borders,
you would still not escape chaos."
It is also said:
Yànzǐ 晏子 visited Lǔ 魯,
Āigōng 哀公 asked,
"The saying goes,
'Do not be misled by three people.'
Now, I, your subject, deliberate with the entire state,
yet Lǔ 魯 cannot escape chaos.
Why is this?"
Yànzǐ 晏子 said,
"The ancient saying 'None can be misled by three people'
means that if one person errs,
the other two will get it right.
Three people are sufficient to constitute a crowd,
hence the saying
'None can be misled by three people.'
Now, the assembled officials of the Lǔ (魯) state number in the hundreds and thousands.
Yet they speak only about the private affairs of the Jì (季) family.
The number of people is certainly not small,
but what they say is the opinion of only one person.
How can there be three?"
A Qí (齊) man said to the King of Qí (齊):
"Hé Bó (河伯),
the River God, is a great deity.
Why doesn't Your Majesty try to meet with him?
Your servant will arrange for Your Majesty to meet him."
So he built an altar on a large body of water,
and stood there with the King.
After a while,
a large fish moved,
and he then said:
"This is Hé Bó (河伯)."
Zhāng Yí (張儀) wanted to use the combined power of Qín (秦), Hán (韓), and Wèi (魏)
to attack Qí (齊) and Jīng (荊).
Huì Shī (惠施), on the other hand, wanted to stop the war between Qí (齊) and Jīng (荊).
The two men argued about it.
The assembled ministers and attendants all spoke in favor of Zhāng Zǐ's 張子 arguments,
advocating that attacking Qí 齊 and Jīng 荊 would be advantageous,
and no one spoke in favor of Huì Zǐ's 惠子 arguments.
The king indeed listened to Zhāng Zǐ,
and considered Huì Zǐ's words to be unacceptable.
The matter of attacking Qí and Jīng was settled,
and Huì Zǐ entered to see the king.
The king said:
"Sir, there is no need to speak!
Attacking Qí and Jīng is indeed advantageous,
the entire kingdom believes it to be so."
Thereupon Huì Zǐ argued:
"It is impossible not to investigate this!
If the matter of Qí and Jīng is truly advantageous,
and the entire kingdom believes it to be advantageous,
what a multitude of wise men there must be!
If the matter of attacking Qí and Jīng is truly not advantageous,
and the entire kingdom believes it to be advantageous,
what a multitude of fools there must be!
In all schemes,
there is doubt.
Doubt,
is true doubt:
half think it is possible,
Those who thought it could not be done were half.
Now, if the entire state thinks it can be done,
it is as if the king has lost half [of his power or influence].
To coerce the ruler
is indeed to lose that half."
Shū Sūn acted as the prime minister of Lǔ.
He was powerful, and he made the decisions.
The one he loved was called Shù Niú,
who also arbitrarily used Shū Sūn's orders.
Shū Sūn had a son named Rén.
Shù Niú was jealous and wanted to kill him.
Thus, he went with Rén to where the ruler of Lǔ was.
The ruler of Lǔ gifted him a jade ring.
Rén bowed and accepted it, but dared not wear it.
He sent Shù Niú to ask Shū Sūn about it.
Shù Niú deceived him, saying:
"I have already asked for you,
and he told you to wear it."
Rén thus wore it.
Shù Niú then said to Shū Sūn:
"Why don't you introduce Rén to the ruler?"
Shū Sūn said: "Why is such a young boy worth introducing?"
Shù Niú said:
"Rén has already met with the ruler several times.
The lord gifted him a jade ring,
Rén yǐ (壬已) wore it.
Shūsūn (叔孫) summoned Rén (壬) to see him,
and indeed he was wearing it.
Shūsūn (叔孫) was angered and killed Rén (壬).
Rén's (壬) elder brother was called Bǐng (丙).
Shù Niú (豎牛) was again jealous and wanted to kill him.
Shūsūn (叔孫) cast a bell for Bǐng (丙).
When the bell was completed,
Bǐng (丙) dared not strike it.
He sent Shù Niú (豎牛) to request permission from Shūsūn (叔孫).
Shù Niú (豎牛) did not request it for him,
and moreover deceived him, saying:
"I have already requested it for you,
and he told you to strike it."
Thereupon, Bǐng (丙) struck it.
Shūsūn (叔孫), upon hearing it, said:
"Bǐng (丙) did not ask permission and presumptuously struck the bell."
He was angered and banished him.
Bǐng (丙) fled to Qí (齊).
After living there for a year,
Shù Niú (豎牛) made amends to Shūsūn (叔孫) on his behalf.
Shūsūn (叔孫) instructed Shù Niú (豎牛) to summon him.
Again, he did not summon him but reported, saying:
"I have already summoned him,
Bing was very angry and
refused to come."
Shū-sūn was greatly angered and
sent someone to kill him.
After the two sons had died,
Shū-sūn fell ill,
so Shù Niú took sole care of him,
and removed his attendants,
not allowing anyone in,
saying:
"Shū-sūn does not want to hear human voices."
He did not feed him and starved him to death.
After Shū-sūn had died,
Shù Niú therefore did not announce the funeral,
but moved his storehouses' valuables
and emptied them before fleeing to Qi.
To listen to the words of those you trust
and have father and son be humiliated by others,
this is the disaster of not cross-examining.
Jiāng Yǐ, as the envoy of the King of Wei to Jing,
said to the King of Jing:
"I entered Your Majesty's territory,
and I heard that the customs of Your Majesty's country say:
'A gentleman does not obscure the merits of others,
nor speak of the evils of others.'
"Is there really such a thing?"
The king said,
"There is."
"Then, in the case of the rebellion of Bái Gōng (白公),
wouldn't it have been dangerous?
If I could truly do that,
then your servant would be spared the death penalty."
Wèi Sì Jūn (衛嗣君) valued Rú Ěr (如耳) greatly and
loved Shì Jī (世姬),
but feared that they would both use his love and esteem to obstruct him.
Therefore, he elevated Bó Yí (薄疑) to rival Rú Ěr (如耳),
and honored Wèi Jī (魏姬) to match Shì Jī (世姬),
saying,
"This is to have them check each other."
Sì Jūn (嗣君) knew that he wanted to avoid obstruction,
but hadn't found the right method.
If you don't let the lowly criticize the noble,
those below will surely sit upon (deceive) those above,
and if you must wait until the balance of power is equal
before they dare to criticize each other,
then you are only increasing the ministers who obstruct you.
Sì Jūn's (嗣君) obstruction has only just begun.
If arrows come from a known direction,
then accumulate iron to defend against that one direction.
If arrows come without aim,
then construct an iron room to be fully prepared for them.
If one is prepared, then the body will not be harmed.
Therefore, they use full preparation to avoid injury,
and we use thorough engagement to eliminate treachery.
Páng Gōng and the crown prince were sent as hostages to Hándān.
He said to the King of Wèi:
"Now, if one person says there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"I would not believe it."
"If two people say there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"I would not believe it."
"If three people say there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The king said,
"I would believe it."
Páng Gōng said,
"It is clear that there are no tigers in the market,
yet three people speaking make it a tiger.
Now, Hándān is farther from Wèi than the market,
and those who speak against me exceed three.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully."
Páng Gōng returned from Hándān,
but ultimately was not granted an audience.
*Shuō Èr*: 〓#
Dǒng Èyū was appointed as the governor of the upper lands of Zhào.
Traveling through the Shíyì mountains,
the ravines were deep,
precipitous like walls,
hundreds of *rèn* deep.
He then asked the surrounding villagers,
"Has anyone ever entered this place?"
They replied,
"No one has."
He asked,
"Have infants,
the deaf, dumb, or mentally deranged
ever entered this place?"
They replied,
"No one has."
"Have cattle, horses, dogs, or pigs
ever entered this place?"
They replied,
"No one has."
Dǒng Èyū sighed deeply and said,
"I can govern well.
If I govern without pardon,
It would be like entering a ravine knowing death is certain.
Then no one would dare to trespass.
Why wouldn't this lead to order?"
Zǐchǎn was the prime minister of Zhèng.
When he was sick and near death,
he said to Yóu Jí:
"After my death,
you will surely be used by Zhèng,
you must be strict in governing the people.
Fire has a strict form,
therefore people are rarely burned;
water has a weak form,
and people often drown.
You must make your form strict,
do not allow people to drown in your weakness."
Zǐchǎn died.
Yóu Jí was unwilling to be strict,
and the young men of Zhèng banded together to become thieves,
living in the marshlands,
and were about to become a disaster for Zhèng.
Yóu Jí led chariots and cavalry to fight them,
for one day and one night,
barely able to defeat them.
Yóu Jí sighed and said,
"Wú zǎo xíng fūzǐ zhī jiào,
bì bù huǐ zhì yú cǐ yǐ!"
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní, saying:
"The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records:
'In the twelfth month of winter, fallen frost did not kill the beans.'
Why was this recorded?"
Zhòngní replied, saying:
"This says that they could have been killed, but were not.
If what should be killed is not killed,
peach and plum trees will bear fruit in winter.
If Heaven loses its way,
even plants and trees will offend against it;
how much more so a ruler!"
In the laws of the Yīn dynasty,
throwing ashes in the street was punished.
Zǐgòng considered this severe,
and asked Zhòngní about it.
Zhòngní said:
"This is knowing the way to govern.
Throwing ashes in the street is sure to blind people,
blind people
will be angry,
if they are angry they will fight,
if they fight, three clans will surely destroy each other.
This is the way to exterminate three clans,
even to execute him would be permissible.
Moreover, heavy punishments
are what people detest;
but not discarding ashes,
is what people consider easy.
To cause people to do what is easy,
and not depart from what they detest,
this is the way to govern."
It is said:
The law of the Yīn dynasty
stipulated that whoever discarded ashes on a public road would have their hand cut off.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"The offense of discarding ashes is light,
the punishment of cutting off a hand is heavy,
why were the ancients so severe?"
It was said:
"Not discarding ashes
is what is easy;
cutting off a hand
is what is detested.
To do what is easy,
without encroaching on what is detested,
the ancients considered it easy,
therefore it was done."
The chancellor of Zhōngshān, Yuè Chí,
sent one hundred chariots to Zhào.
He selected from his retainers those who were intelligent
to act as leaders of the journey,
but midway, they became disorderly.
Yuè Chí said:
"I considered you to be intelligent
and appointed you to lead the journey,
but now you are disorderly midway,
why is that?"
The retainer then resigned and left,
saying:
"You do not understand governance.
One must have authority sufficient to subdue people,
and benefits sufficient to motivate them;
therefore, one can govern them.
Now I am,
merely one of your lesser retainers.
To follow the junior and correct the senior,
to govern the noble from a humble position,
without being able to control the power of reward and punishment
to manage them,
this is why there is disorder.
Try and let me:
The good among them I can make into ministers and chancellors,
"Those who are not good, I can cut off their heads,
why not govern this way!"
The laws of Gōngsūn Yāng emphasized punishing minor offenses severely.
Major offenses
are what people find difficult to commit;
while minor transgressions
are what people easily commit.
Make people abandon what is easy for them,
and not approach what is difficult,
this is the way to govern.
If minor transgressions do not arise,
major crimes will not occur,
then people will be without crime and disorder will not arise.
It is said:
Gōngsūn Yāng said:
"Apply punishment severely to minor offenses.
If minor offenses do not occur,
then major offenses will not come about,
this is called using punishment to eliminate punishment."
In the land of Jīng Nán,
in the Lì River, gold is produced,
and many people steal and mine the gold.
The prohibition against mining gold
is that if one is caught, they are immediately dismembered and displayed in the market.
There were very many;
they crowded the water;
and yet people stealing the gold did not stop.
Indeed, no crime is greater than being publicly displayed in pieces for punishment,
and yet those who don't stop,
is because they don't necessarily get caught.
Therefore, if there were now such a case,
saying:
"I will give you the world but kill you."
An ordinary person would not do it.
To possess the world
is a great benefit,
yet someone would not do it
knowing they will certainly die.
Therefore, if it is not necessarily obtainable,
then even with being publicly displayed in pieces,
stealing the gold would not stop;
knowing they will certainly die,
then possessing the world would not be done.
The people of Lǔ were burning a swamp.
The weather had a north wind,
the fire leaned south,
fearing it would burn the state.
Duke Āi was afraid
and personally led the crowd to save the fire.
With no one around,
everyone was chasing beasts
and no one rescued from the fire,
so he summoned and asked Zhòng Ní.
Zhòng Ní said:
"Those who chase beasts find pleasure
and face no punishment,
while those who rescue from the fire suffer
and receive no reward.
This is why no one rescues from the fire."
Āi Gōng said:
"Good."
Zhòng Ní said:
"The matter is urgent,
and there is no time for rewards.
If those who rescue from the fire are all rewarded,
then the state will not have enough to reward people.
Please, just implement punishments."
Āi Gōng said:
"Good."
Thereupon, Zhòng Ní issued an order, saying:
"Those who do not rescue from the fire
will be punished with the crime of surrendering to the enemy;
those who chase beasts
will be punished with the crime of entering the forbidden area."
Before the order was completely disseminated,
the fire was already extinguished.
Chéng Huān 成驩 said to the King of Qí 齊王:
"Your Majesty is too benevolent,
too unmerciful to people."
The King said:
"Is being too benevolent,
too unmerciful to people,
not a good reputation?"
He replied:
"This is the goodness of a subject,
not what a ruler should do.
A subject must be benevolent
before he can be consulted with,
and unmerciful to people
before he can be approached;
if he is not benevolent, he cannot be consulted with,
if he is merciless to people, he cannot be approached."
The King said:
"Then where am I too benevolent,
and where am I unmerciful to people?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty is too benevolent to Lord Xuē 薛公,
and too unmerciful to all the Tián 田.
Being too benevolent to Lord Xuē 薛公,
diminishes the weight of the great ministers;
being too unmerciful to all the Tián 田,
causes fathers and elder brothers to break the law.
When the great ministers lack weight,
the army becomes weak abroad;
if fathers and elder brothers break the law,
then the government will be chaotic internally.
If the military is weak externally,
and the government is chaotic internally,
this is the root of national destruction."
King Hùi of Wèi 魏惠王 said to Bǔ Pí 卜皮:
"What have you heard of my reputation?
What do you think of it?"
He replied:
"I have heard of Your Majesty's kindness and benevolence."
The king was happily pleased and said:
"In that case, to what end will my achievements arrive?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty's achievements will lead to ruin."
The king said:
"Kindness and benevolence
are virtuous actions.
If doing them leads to ruin,
why is that?"
Bǔ Pí replied,
"The compassionate are unfeeling,
and the generous like to give.
If one is unfeeling,
then one will not punish those who have transgressed;
if one likes to give,
then one will reward without waiting for merit.
If transgressions go unpunished,
and one receives rewards without merit,
even if one perishes,
wouldn't it be acceptable?"
In the state of Qí, the custom of lavish burials was prevalent,
with cloth and silk exhausted in clothing and shrouds,
and timber exhausted in coffins and outer coffins.
Duke Huán was troubled by this,
and told Guǎn Zhòng,
"If cloth and silk are exhausted, then there will be nothing to cover ourselves with;
if timber is exhausted, then there will be nothing to use for defense;
and if people do not cease their lavish burials,
what can be done to prohibit it?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied,
"All human actions
are either driven by fame,
or by profit."
Thereupon, he issued an order, saying:
"Those who excessively adorn coffins and outer coffins
shall have their corpses mutilated,
and the guilty shall be those responsible for the funeral."
To mutilate the dead
brings no fame,
and to punish those responsible for the funeral
brings no benefit.
Why, then, would anyone do it?
During the time of Wèi Sìjūn 衛嗣君,
there was a convict who escaped to Wèi 魏.
He then treated the illness of a consort of King Xiāng of Wèi 襄王.
Wèi Sìjūn 衛嗣君 heard of this
and sent someone to request to buy him for fifty gold pieces.
Five times he returned, but the King of Wèi 魏 did not grant it.
So, he exchanged him for Zuǒ Shì 左氏.
The assembled ministers and attendants remonstrated, saying,
"To buy a convict with an entire city,
is that permissible?"
The king said,
"This is not something you understand.
In governance, there is no such thing as a trivial thing that causes order,
and no such thing as a grand thing that causes disorder.
If the law is not established and punishment is not certain,
even having ten Zuǒ Shì 左氏 would be of no benefit.
If the law is established and punishment is certain,
even losing ten Zuǒ Shì 左氏 would be of no harm."
Wèi Wáng heard of it and said:
"The ruler desires to govern but is not listened to;
this is inauspicious."
Therefore, he loaded [him] up and went,
presenting him empty-handed.
*Shuō Sān*: 〓#
The King of Qí asked Wén Zǐ, saying:
"How should one govern a state?"
He replied:
"Reward and punishment as a principle [of governing]
are sharp weapons.
The ruler should firmly grasp them
and not show them to others.
Those like your servant
are like deer and other animals;
they only come where there is good grass."
The King of Yuè asked the grand master Wén Zhǒng, saying:
"I wish to attack Wú,
is it possible?"
He replied:
"It is possible.
My rewards are generous and trustworthy,
my punishments are strict and certain.
If your lord wishes to know,
why not try burning down the palace?"
Thereupon, they burned the palaces and houses,
and no one saved them.
So he issued an order saying:
"Those who try to put out the fire will die,
the reward will be the same as for dying in battle against the enemy;
those who put out the fire and do not die,
the reward will be the same as for defeating the enemy;
those who do not put out the fire,
the punishment will be the same as for surrendering to the enemy."
People smeared their bodies,
covered themselves with wet clothing and ran into the fire,
three thousand men on the left,
three thousand men on the right.
This shows a situation where victory is assured.
Wú Qǐ was appointed by Marquis Wǔ of Wèi as the governor of Xīhé.
Qín had a small outpost bordering the territory,
and Wú Qǐ wanted to attack it.
If they did not remove it,
it would greatly harm the farmers,
but removing it
would not be enough to mobilize the armored troops.
Therefore, he leaned a chariot axle outside the north gate
and ordered:
"Whoever can move this outside the south gate
will be rewarded with excellent fields and excellent houses."
No one would move it.
When someone finally moved it,
he was rewarded according to the order.
Soon after, he placed another shi (石) of red beans outside the east gate
and ordered, saying:
"Whoever can move this to outside the west gate
will be rewarded as before."
People competed to move it.
Then he issued an order, saying:
"Tomorrow we will attack the post (亭).
Whoever can be the first to ascend
will be appointed a senior minister of the state,
and be granted superior fields and residences."
People rushed to contend for it,
and so they attacked the post,
and captured it in a single morning.
Lǐ Kuī 李悝, serving as the guardian of the territory for Wèi Wénhóu 魏文侯,
and desiring the people to be good at archery,
then issued an order saying:
"For people who have doubtful lawsuits,
let them shoot at a target;
the one who hits it wins,
the one who misses loses."
Once the order was issued, people all diligently practiced archery,
Day and night without rest.
When he fought with the people of Qín,
he greatly defeated them,
because his men were good at fighting and archery.
In the alley of Chóngmén in Sòng, a man wore mourning clothes
and emaciated himself severely.
The ruler considered him to be kind and loving towards his parents
and appointed him as an official and teacher.
The next year,
the number of people who emaciated themselves to death
exceeded ten per year.
If wearing mourning for one's parents
is done out of love
and can still be rewarded and encouraged,
how much more so should the ruler treat the people!
King of Yuè, fearing an attack from Wú,
wanted the people to value death lightly.
He went out and saw an angry frog and bowed to it.
His attendants said:
"Why do you show respect to this?"
The king said:
"Because it has spirit."
The next year, those who requested to offer their heads to the king
exceeded ten per year.
From this, we can see that
praise is enough to kill people.
It is said:
King Gōujiàn of Yuè saw an angry frog and saluted it.
The charioteer said,
"Why do you salute it?"
The king said,
"The frog has such spirit,
how can I not salute it?"
When the scholars heard this, they said,
"The frog has spirit,
and the king still salutes it,
how much more so those scholars who are brave!"
That year,
there was a man who cut his own throat and presented his head.
Therefore, King Yuè was about to restore (his state and take revenge on) Wú,
and to test his teaching,
he burned a platform and drummed upon it,
and those who caused the people to rush into the fire
were rewarded for being in the fire.
He stood by the river and drummed upon it,
and those who caused the people to rush into the water
were rewarded for being in the water.
When facing battle, he would have men cut off heads
and disembowel themselves without hesitation,
and they would be rewarded for being in the army.
How much more effective is it to advance the worthy according to the law?
Its encouragement is very great.
Hán Zhāo Hóu 韓昭侯 ordered someone to hide worn-out trousers.
An attendant said:
"Your Lordship is also unkind;
you do not bestow the worn-out trousers upon your attendants
but hide them away."
Zhāo Hóu 昭侯 said:
"This is not something you understand.
I have heard that a wise ruler cherishes every frown and smile.
A frown is made for a purpose,
and a smile is made for a purpose.
Now, these trousers,
how are they different from a frown or smile?
Trousers are far more different from a frown or smile.
I must wait for someone with merit;
therefore, I store them away, not yet giving them to anyone."
The sturgeon resembles a snake,
the silkworm resembles a caterpillar.
People are startled when they see a snake,
and their hair stands on end when they see a caterpillar.
Yet women gather silkworms,
and fishermen grasp sturgeons.
Where profit lies,
they forget what they dislike,
and all become [like] Mèng Bēn 孟賁.
Discourses Four:
The King of Wèi said to the King of Zhèng:
"Originally, Zhèng and Liáng were one state,
but later separated.
Now, I wish to regain Zhèng and unite it with Liáng."
The King of Zhèng was troubled by this
and summoned his ministers
to discuss how to respond to Wèi.
A prince said to the King of Zhèng:
"This is very easy to answer.
Your Majesty should reply to Wèi:
'If Zhèng is considered as the old Wèi and can be merged,
then my humble state also wishes to obtain Liáng
and unite it with Zhèng.'"
The King of Wèi then desisted.
King Xuān of Qí employed men to play the *yú*,
invariably three hundred men.
A commoner named Nánguō offered to play the *yú* for the king.
King Xuān was pleased with him
and provided him with provisions as much as several hundred men received.
King Xuān died,
and King Mǐn ascended the throne,
who preferred to listen to each player individually.
The commoner fled.
First:
Hán Zhāo Hóu said:
"There are many *yú* players,
I have no way to know who is good."
Tián Yán replied:
"Listen to them one by one."
Zhào sent someone through Shēn Zǐ in Hán to request troops,
intending to attack Wèi.
Shēn Zǐ wanted to speak to the ruler,
but feared the ruler would suspect him of being involved in outside affairs,
otherwise he feared offending Zhào.
Therefore, he ordered Zhào Shào and Hán Tà
to probe the ruler's reactions
before speaking of it.
Internally, he would know Zhāo Hóu's intentions;
externally, he would gain merit with Zhào.
When the troops of the three states arrived at Hán,
the King of Qín said to Lóu Huǎn:
"The troops of the three states are deep within!
I, the lone man, want to cede Hédōng to make peace.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"To cede Hédōng
is a great expense;
to save the country from disaster
is a great achievement.
This is the responsibility of fathers and elder brothers.
Why doesn't Your Majesty summon Gōngzǐ Fàn
and ask him about it?"
The King summoned Gōngzǐ Fàn and informed him of the situation.
He replied,
"Making peace will also bring regret,
not making peace will also bring regret.
If Your Majesty now cedes Hédōng and makes peace,
and the three states return,
Your Majesty will surely say,
'The three states were already going to leave,
I merely used three cities to send them off.'
If you don't make peace,
and the three states also enter Hàn,
then the state will surely launch a major offensive,
and Your Majesty will greatly regret it.
Your Majesty will say,
'I didn't offer the three cities.'
Therefore, your servant said,
'Your Majesty making peace will also bring regret,
not making peace will also bring regret.'"
The King said,
"Doing what will bring regret for me,
I would rather lose three cities and regret it,
than be in danger and then regret it.
Guǎrén duàn jiǎng yǐ." [My sovereign has cut off the lectures.]
Yìng Hóu wèi Qín Wáng yuē: [The Marquis Yìng said to the King of Qín:]
"Wáng dé Wǎn, Yè, Lántián, Yángxià, [Your Majesty has obtained Wǎn, Yè, Lántián, and Yángxià,]
duàn Hénèi, [severed Hénèi,]
kùn Liáng, Zhèng, [besieged Liáng and Zhèng,]
suǒyǐ wèi wáng zhě, [the reason you have not become king,]
Zhào wèi fú yě. [is that Zhào has not submitted.]
Chí Shàngdǎng zài yī ér yǐ, [To relax control of Shàngdǎng is merely a matter of one thing,]
yǐ lín Dōngyáng, [in order to approach Dōngyáng,]
zé Hándān kǒu zhōng shī yě. [then Hándān is like a louse in the mouth.]
Wáng gǒng ér cháo tiānxià, [Your Majesty will arch your hands and receive the homage of the world,]
hòu zhě yǐ bīng zhōng zhī. [those who lag behind will be struck by arms.]
Rán Shàngdǎng zhī ānlè, [However, the peace and happiness of Shàngdǎng,]
qí chǔ shèn jù, [their situation is extremely critical,]
chén kǒng chí zhī ér bù tīng, [I fear that relaxing control will not be heeded,]
nài hé?" [what to do?"]
Wáng yuē: [The King said:]
"Bì chí yì zhī yǐ." [It will surely be easy to relax control."]
Shuō wǔ: [Speeches 5:] 〓
Páng Jìng, [Páng Jìng,]
xiànlìng yě. [was a magistrate.]
Qiǎn shì zhě xíng, [He sent merchants on their way,]
ér zhào gōng dàfū ér huán zhī. [and summoned dukes and grandees and brought them back.]
Lì yǒu jiàn, [After standing for a while,]
wú yǐ zhào zhī, [there was nothing with which to inform them,]
Finally, he sent them forth.
The market people thought that the magistrate and high officials had spoken words,
but were not to be trusted,
which led to the elimination of deceit.
Dài Huān,
the Grand Master of Sòng,
at night sent a man, saying:
"I have heard that for several nights there has been a covered carriage going to the gate of Lǐ Shǐ,
be sure to spy on it for me."
The sent man reported, saying:
"I did not see a covered carriage,
but I saw someone holding a box and speaking with Lǐ Shǐ,
after a while,
Lǐ Shǐ received the box."
The Lord of Zhōu lost a jade hairpin,
and ordered the officials to find it,
but they could not find it in three days.
The Lord of Zhōu had someone else search,
and they found it in the space between the walls of the family's house.
The Lord of Zhōu said:
"My officials do not attend to their duties.
Searching for a hairpin,
they could not find it in three days;
I had someone else search for it,
and they found it in less than a day."
Thereupon, the officials all became alarmed and fearful,
thinking the lord was divine and enlightened.
The grand steward of Shāng sent a junior subordinate to the market,
and deliberately after his return, asked him,
"What did you see in the market?"
He replied:
"I saw nothing."
The grand steward said:
"Even so,
what did you see?"
He replied:
"Outside the south gate of the market were very many oxcarts,
barely enough space to pass through."
The grand steward then cautioned the messenger:
"Do not dare tell anyone what I asked you."
He then summoned the market officer and reprimanded him, saying:
"Why is there so much cow dung outside the market gate?"
The market officer was very surprised that the grand steward knew it so quickly,
and was alarmed by his position.
Discourse six: 〓#
Hán Zhāohóu clenched his fist,
and pretended to have lost a fingernail,
searching for it very urgently,
so those nearby cut off their own fingernails and presented them to him.
Zhāohóu used this to observe whether those around him were loyal or not.
Hán Zhāohóu sent a cavalryman to the counties.
The messenger returned and
Zhāohóu asked,
"What did you see?"
He replied,
"I saw nothing."
Zhāohóu said,
"Even so,
what did you see?"
He said,
"Outside the south gate,
there was a yellow calf eating seedlings on the left side of the road."
Zhāohóu told the messenger,
"Do not dare reveal what I asked you."
Thereupon he issued an order, saying,
"During the seedling season,
there is already an existing order prohibiting cattle and horses from entering people's fields,
but the officials do not take it seriously,
and many cattle and horses enter people's fields.
Quickly report the number of them;
if you fail to do so,
their punishment will be increased."
Thereupon, the three districts investigated and reported them.
Zhāohóu said,
"It is not complete."
Again he went to investigate,
and then he found the yellow calf outside the South Gate.
The officials considered Marquis Zhāo (Zhāo Hóu) to be perceptive,
and they were all fearful of his scrutiny
and did not dare to do wrong.
The Lord of Zhōu (Zhōu zhǔ) issued an order to find a crooked staff,
and the officials searched for it for several days
but could not find it.
The Lord of Zhōu (Zhōu zhǔ) secretly sent someone to look for it,
and they found it within a day.
Thereupon he said to the officials:
"I know that the officials do not attend to their duties.
The crooked staff is very easy to find,
but the officials could not find it.
I ordered someone to look for it,
and they found it within a day.
How can you be considered loyal!"
The officials were all fearful of his scrutiny,
and regarded their lord as divine.
Bǔ Pí (Bǔ Pí) was made magistrate of the county.
His censor was corrupt and had a favorite concubine.
Bǔ Pí (Bǔ Pí) then sent a junior official to pretend to love her,
in order to find out the censor's secret affairs.
Xīmén Bào (Xīmén Bào) was made magistrate of Yè.
He feigned the loss of his carriage linchpin.
He ordered officials to search for it, but they could not find it.
He had someone search for it,
and they found it between the walls of a family's house.
Explanation 7:
Yángshān Jūn, while serving as chancellor in Wèi,
heard that the king suspected him.
So he falsely slandered Jiū Shù to find out if it was true.
Nào Chǐ, hearing that the King of Qí disliked him,
then falsely pretended to be an envoy from Qín to find out.
There was a man of Qí who wanted to create disorder,
fearing that the king would know of it.
He then falsely drove away someone he loved,
ordering that person to flee so the king would know.
Zǐ Zhī, serving as chancellor in Yān,
sat and pretended to say,
"What was that that ran out the door?
A white horse?"
The attendants all said they did not see it.
One person ran and chased after it,
and reported back, saying,
"Yes, there was."
Zǐ Zhī used this to know that his attendants were not honest and trustworthy.
Two people were in a lawsuit against each other.
Zǐchǎn separated them
and didn't allow them to fully express their arguments.
He reversed their words and used them to inform
himself, and thus understood the situation.
Duke Sì of Wèi sent someone to pose as a merchant passing through the border market.
The border market officials were strict and made things difficult for him.
So he bribed the border market officials with gold because of the situation,
and the border officials then released him.
Duke Sì then said to the border officials:
"At a certain time, there was a merchant passing through your post,
and he gave you gold,
and you then released him."
The border market officials were greatly terrified,
and considered Duke Sì to be extremely perceptive.
*Inner Storeroom of Sayings, Below, Six Minutiae, Thirty-first.*
*Six Minutiae*:
First: Authority is Lent to Subordinates.
Second: Profit is Diversely Lent Externally.
Third: Reliance on Apparent Similarities.
Fourth: Profit and Harm are Reversed.
Fifth: Internal Doubts and Disputes.
Sixth: The Abandonment of Enemy States.
These six things
are what the ruler should observe.
Classic One:
*Authority is Lent*.
Authority and power cannot be lent to others.
If the ruler loses one part of it,
the ministers will take it as a hundred.
Therefore, if a minister obtains a loan of
If they achieve their private gain,
they do not consider the country's troubles.
The explanation for this lies in the prayer of the man and wife of Wèi.
Therefore, Dài Xiē plotted with his younger brothers,
and the Three Huán attacked Duke Zhāo.
Gōngshū brought the Qí army inside,
and Dí Huáng summoned the Hàn soldiers.
Tài Zǎi Pǐ persuaded Daifu Zhǒng,
and Dàchéng Niú instructed Shēn Bùhài.
Sīmǎ Xǐ informed the Zhào king,
Lǚ Cāng planned with Qín and Chǔ.
Sòng Shí sent a letter to the ruler of Wèi,
Bái Guī taught violent reproof.
Classic Three: 〓#
Resemblance.
Matters of resemblance
are how rulers lose their punishments (due to misjudgment),
and how great ministers achieve their private gains.
Therefore, the gatekeeper discarded water, and Yí Shè was punished.
Jìyáng falsely accused himself, and two people were punished.
Sīmǎ Xǐ killed Yuán Qiān, and Jì Xīn was punished.
Zhèng Xiù spoke of a bad odor, and the new concubine had her nose cut off.
Fèi Wújì instructed Xiè Wǎn, and the chief minister was punished.
Chén Xū killed Zhāng Shòu, and Xī Shǒu fled.
Therefore, burning the hay storehouse leads to Zhongshan being punished,
while killing old scholars leads to Jìyáng being rewarded.
Classic Four: 〓#
Reversal.
If an incident arises and there is a benefit to be gained,
its corpse (blame) should be attributed to the ruler.
Gōngzǐ Gēn took Dōng Zhōu.
Wángzǐ Zhí was greatly favored,
and Shāng Chén indeed caused rebellion.
Yán Suì and Hán Wěi contended,
and Āi Hóu indeed met with assassins.
Tián Cháng, Kàn Zhǐ, Dài Huān, and Huáng Xǐ were enemies,
and the Song ruler and Jiǎn Gōng were killed.
The explanation lies in Hú Tū's naming of two favorites,
and Zhèng Zhāo's response of "not yet born."
Chapter Six:
Abandonment.
What the enemy strives for
is exhaustive investigation leading to ruin.
If the ruler is not discerning,
then the enemy will bring about abandonment.
Therefore, Wén Wáng employed Fèi Zhòng,
and the King of Qin worried about the Chu envoy.
Lí Qiě left Zhòng Ní,
and Gān Xiàng thwarted Gān Mào.
Therefore, Zǐ Xū declared his intentions, yet Zǐ Cháng was employed.
Accepting beautiful women led to the demise of Yú and Guó.
Feigning a lost letter led to Cháng Hóng's death.
Employing a rooster breeder led to the complete destruction of Kuài Jié.
Temple Attack.
Intervene in the matters of doubt and abandonment;
Míng zhǔ jué zhī yú nèi
and applies (measures) externally.
He supports the weak,
assists the feeble;
this is called "temple attack" (planning in the court).
Espionage having been put to use internally,
observation and listening also taking place externally,
then the enemy's false pretenses can be discovered.
The explanation lies in the Qin dwarf's advice to Lord Huìwén.
Therefore, Xiāng Cī spoke of attacking Yè,
and Sì Gōng granted him the mat of office.
Explanation One: 〓#
Authority and weight are
the ruler's deep pool;
ministers are
fish in that pool of authority and weight.
If the fish are lost from the pool,
they cannot be recovered;
if the ruler loses his authority and weight to his ministers,
he cannot recover it either.
The people of old found it difficult to speak directly,
so they entrusted their meaning to fish.
Rewards and punishments are
sharp weapons;
the ruler wields them to control his ministers,
Ministers obtain it to support their ruler.
Therefore, if the ruler first reveals what he will reward,
then the ministers will sell it to create favor for themselves;
if the ruler first reveals what he will punish,
then the ministers will sell it to create authority for themselves.
Therefore it is said:
"The sharp weapons of the state
cannot be shown to the people."
Lord Jìng Guō served as the prime minister of Qí,
and when he spoke for a long time with old acquaintances,
then the old acquaintances became rich;
when he favored those around him with patronage,
then those around him were held in high regard.
Prolonged conversation and lavish patronage
are small means,
yet they can still lead to wealth,
how much more so with the power of office?
In the time of Duke Lì of Jìn,
the six ministers were powerful,
Xū Tóng and Cháng Yú Jiǎo remonstrated, saying:
"When great ministers are powerful and weighty,
they rival the ruler in contending for affairs,
they establish factions outside in the marketplace,
they subvert the laws of the state below,
and above they threaten the ruler,
and that the state will not be endangered
(Such a thing) has never happened."
The Duke said:
"Good."
Thereupon he executed three ministers.
Xū Tóng and Chángyú Jiǎo further remonstrated, saying:
"Those who are equally guilty
are punished partially and not completely,
this is to harbor resentment and provide an opportunity for their animosity."
The Duke said:
"I eradicated three ministers in one morning,
I cannot bear to kill all of them."
Chángyú Jiǎo replied:
"If Your Grace cannot bear to (spare) them,
they will bear to (attack) Your Grace."
The Duke did not listen.
After three months,
the ministers stirred up trouble,
and subsequently killed Duke Lì and divided his territory.
The Marquis of Zhōu served as prime minister of Jīng,
was esteemed and made all the decisions.
The King of Jīng became suspicious of him,
and therefore asked those around him,
those around him replied,
"There is nothing wrong."
It was as if (the response) came from one mouth.
The people of Yàn were not easily fooled,
therefore they bathed in dog excrement.
A man of Yàn,
whose wife was having an affair with a scholar,
her husband returned early from outside,
the scholar just happened to be leaving,
the husband said:
"Who was that guest?"
His wife said:
"There was no guest."
He asked the servants,
and the servants all said, "There was no one,"
as if speaking with one voice.
His wife said:
"You are easily fooled."
Thereupon she bathed him with dog excrement.
Another story says:
Lǐ Jì of Yàn liked to travel far from home,
his wife was secretly having an affair with a scholar,
Jì suddenly returned,
the scholar was inside,
the wife was worried.
Her maid said:
"Tell the young master to go naked and let down his hair,
go straight out the door,
"We should pretend not to see."
Thereupon, the prince followed his plan
and quickly walked out the door.
Jì said,
"Who was that person?"
The family members all said,
"There was no one."
Jì said,
"Did I see a ghost?"
The woman said,
"Yes."
"What should be done about it?"
She said,
"Take arrows from five sacrificial animals and bathe with them."
Jì said,
"Agreed."
Then he bathed with arrows.
Another version says he bathed in orchid-infused water.
Tale Two: 〓
There was a couple in Wèi who were praying.
and the wife prayed, saying:
"Grant that I, without reason,
obtain a hundred bundles of cloth."
Her husband said,
"Why so little?"
She replied,
"If I get more,
you will use it to buy a concubine."
The King of Jīng wanted to send the princes to serve as eunuchs in the neighboring states.
Dài Xiē said:
"It is not permissible."
"Sending the young lords as eunuchs to the surrounding states
will surely make the surrounding states value them."
He said:
"If your sons, when sent out, are valued,
being valued
then they will certainly become partisans of the country that values them.
This is like educating your sons in a foreign marketplace,
which is not advantageous."
Mèngsūn (孟孫), Shūsūn (叔孫), and Jìsūn (季孫) of Lǔ (魯) joined forces to coerce Duke Zhāo (昭公),
thereby seizing his state and monopolizing its governance.
The Three Huán (桓) families of Lǔ (魯) oppressed the Duke.
Duke Zhāo (昭公) attacked the Jìsūn (季孫) clan,
and the Mèngsūn (孟孫) and Shūsūn (叔孫) clans conferred, saying:
"Shall we rescue him?"
The chariot driver of the Shūsūn (叔孫) clan said:
"I
am a household servant;
how would I know about the affairs of the ducal house?
"Between having the Jìsūn 季孫 clan and not having the Jìsūn 季孫 clan,
which is more advantageous to me?"
"Without the Jìsūn 季孫, there will surely be no Shūsūn 叔孫."
"In that case, rescue him."
They all said:
Thereupon, they charged through the northwest corner and entered.
Mèngsūn 孟孫 saw the flag of Shūsūn 叔孫 entering,
and also rescued him.
The Three Huán 三桓 became as one,
and Zhāo Gōng 昭公 could not defeat them.
He was driven out,
and died at Gānhóu 乾侯.
Gōngshū 公叔 was the chancellor of Hán 韓 and had attacked Qí 齊.
Gōngzhòng 公仲 was highly esteemed by the king.
Gōngshū 公叔 feared that the king would appoint Gōngzhòng 公仲 as chancellor,
so he had Qí 齊 and Hán 韓 make an alliance and attack Wèi 魏.
Gōngshū 公叔 then brought the Qí 齊 army into Zhèng 鄭
to threaten its ruler,
in order to secure his position,
and to ensure the fulfillment of the agreement between the two states.
Dí Huáng 翟璜,
was a minister of the King of Wèi 魏,
and was on good terms with Hán 韓.
He then summoned the Hán 韓 troops and ordered them to attack Wèi 魏,
then requested to reconcile them with the King of Wèi 魏
in order to value themselves.
The King of Yuè attacked the King of Wú.
The King of Wú apologized and offered to submit.
The King of Yuè wanted to agree.
Fàn Lǐ and Dàfū Zhǒng said,
"It is not permissible.
In the past, Heaven gave Wú to Yuè,
but Wú did not accept it.
Now, he rebels against Fūchāi,
it is also a disaster from Heaven.
Heaven is giving Wú to Yuè,
accept it with repeated bows,
it is not permissible to agree."
Tàizǎi Pǐ sent a letter to Dàfū Zhǒng, saying:
"When the cunning rabbit is exhausted, the good hound is cooked;
when the enemy state is destroyed, the resourceful minister dies.
Why does Dàfū not abandon Wú and worry about Yuè instead?"
Dàfū Zhǒng received the letter and read it,
sighing deeply and lamenting:
"Kill him.
Yuè and Wú share the same fate."
Dàchéng Niú, from Zhào, said to Shēn Bùhài in Hán,
"Use Hán to increase my importance in Zhào,
and I will use Zhào to increase your importance in Hán.

Three Explanations: 〓 #
A senior official from Qí, named Yí Yè,
was drinking with the king.
He got extremely drunk and exited,
leaning against the Lang Gate.
The gatekeeper, who was a eunuch, knelt and asked:
"Would you unintentionally bestow upon me some of your leftover drink?"
Yí Yè scolded him, saying:
"Get away!
You castrated remnant,
how dare you beg for drink from your elders!"
The eunuch retreated.
After Yí Yè left,
the eunuch then poured water under the eaves of the Lang Gate,
making it resemble someone drowning.
The next day,
the king came out and questioned him,
He asked,
"Who drowned here?"
Yuè, a man who had lost a foot, knelt and replied,
"Your servant did not see it.
However, yesterday the Senior Grand Master Yí Shè stood here."
Consequently, the king executed Yí Shè.
Loss of roots.
To follow principle without seeing empty achievements,
to gauge sentiment by devious and treacherous means,
then how can the two not both be lost?
Therefore, empty scholars establish a reputation internally,
while rhetoricians consider strategies externally,
hence foolishness, timidity, bravery, and wisdom are linked together,
and empty doctrines are connected to customs
and accommodated to the world.
Therefore, their laws are not implemented,
and punishments are not applied to those deserving of disgrace.
If this is the case,
then how can punishment and reward not tolerate the two?
Reality is therefore what one arrives at,
while principle loses its measure;
the loss of measure
is not caused by law,
but by the establishment of law and entrusting it to wisdom.
To abandon law and entrust it to wisdom
then how can those who receive tasks obtain their duties?
If duty does not accord with the task,
then how can the law not be lost,
and how can punishment not be burdensome?
Therefore, rewards and punishments are disturbed and disordered,
and the way of the state is erroneous,
because distinctions between rewards and punishments are not made clear.

also delighted in and loved her,

you must cover your mouth."

During the time of Duke Wén (Wén Gōng),

that is my second offense.

this is my first offense deserving death.
The charcoal from the mulberry tree roasts the meat;
the meat turns red and white, but the hair does not singe;
this is my second offense deserving death.
When the roasting is complete,
I further examine it with double eyelashes (i.e., careful scrutiny);
yet with hair wrapped around the roast, my eyes do not see it;
this is my third offense deserving death.

Outer Store of Sayings, Left, Section One, Thirty-Second
Classic One: 〓#
The way of the enlightened ruler is,
like the response of Rú Yǒu (如有) to Mì Zǐ (密子).
When a ruler listens to words,
he admires eloquence;
when he observes conduct,
he praises those who are distant (from worldly affairs).
Therefore, the words of the officials and common people are
circuitous and expansive,
and their personal conduct
is detached from the world.
The explanation for this lies in Tián Jiū's (田鳩) response to the King of Jīng (荊王).
Thus, Mò Zǐ (墨子) made a wooden kite,
and Ǒu Guǐ (謳癸) built the Wǔ Palace (武宮).
Medicines, wine, and loyal advice,
are what enlightened rulers and sagacious masters rely on for their unique insight.
Section Two: 〓#
When a ruler listens to words,
if he does not take practical use as the target,
then those who speak
will mostly present sophistries like "thorns" and "white horses";
if he does not use the proper standard as the barrier,
then all archers will seem like Yì (羿).
When rulers listen to speeches,
they are all like the King of Yān (燕王) learning the Dao;
and those who engage in lengthy discourses,
are all like the people of Zhèng (鄭) arguing about age.
Therefore, discourses that are meticulous and probe into subtle difficulties
are not practical matters.
Thus, Jì (季), Huì (惠), Sòng (宋), and Mò (墨) were all mere strategists.
Arguments that are roundabout, profound, vast, and grand
are not for practical use.
Thus, Wèi (魏), Cháng (長), Zhān (瞻), Chén (陳), and Zhuāng (莊) were all like ghosts and demons.
Conduct that is contrary to difficulties and stubbornly firm
is not meritorious.
Thus, Wù (務), Biàn (卞), Bào (鮑), Jiè (介), and Tián Zhòng (田仲) were all like hard gourds (i.e., useless).
Moreover, Yú Qìng (虞慶) surpassed the craftsman, yet the house collapsed;
Fàn Qiě (范且) exhausted the artisan's skill, yet the bow broke.
Therefore, to seek for their sincerity,
it is impossible without providing a return offering.

if one works for oneself, things will be done.

those who are hired to work advance delicious soup.

but the meaning to the world was great;
some had intentions that were great
but the meaning to the world was small;
it is impossible to know for sure.
The explanation lies in the Song people interpreting the "Book [of Documents]"
and the Liang people reading the "Record[s]".
Therefore, the former kings had Yǐng writings,
while later generations had many Yān interpretations.
Those who do not fit the affairs of the state but deliberate about the former kings,
All are those who seek to obtain standards.
Classic Four: 〓#
Where profit lies, the people flock to it;
where fame is displayed, the scholars die for it.
Therefore, if merit lies outside the law and rewards are added to it,
then the ruler will be unable to obtain what he profits from below;
if fame lies outside the law and praise is added to it,
then the scholars will be encouraged by fame and not accumulate it for the ruler.
Therefore, when Zhōng Zhāng and Xū Jǐ became officials,
half of the people of Zhōngmù abandoned their fields and gardens to follow literary scholars in the towns;
when Píng Gōng suffered from pain and numbness in his feet and
dared not break his posture,
the number of officials resigning and entrusting (their duties to others) in the state of Jìn was the weight of the state.
These three scholars,
if their words followed the law,
then they were merely registered in the government offices;
if their actions were within the affairs of the state,
then they were like the people who followed orders;
the two rulers' courtesy was too excessive.
If their words departed from the law and their actions accomplished distant merits,
then they were people outside the bounds of the law;
why would the two rulers again show courtesy to them?
The courtesy should be abolished.
Moreover, scholars who reside in learning,
when the state has no affairs, they do not exert effort,
In times of trouble, they do not wear armor.
If they are treated with propriety,
then they will become lazy in cultivating the achievements of agriculture and war;
if they are not treated with propriety,
then they will harm the laws of the ruler.
When the state is secure, they are honored and prominent;
when it is in danger, they diminish the ruler's authority.
What can a ruler gain from scholars who stay at home studying?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler would discuss Lǐ Cī's view of Zhōngshān.
Chapter Five:
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"If you are not diligent and intimate,
the common people will not trust you."
Teach them using the saying,
"Do not wear purple without permission,"
and support it with the examples of Zhèng Jiǎn and Sòng Xiāng;
and hold them accountable by honoring and emphasizing agriculture and war.
If distinctions are not made clear,
and honesty is not demanded,
but instead, you personally attend to the duties of subordinates,
and even walk, sleep, and lie down as a servant,
along with concealing flaws and wearing humble clothing,
Kǒng Qiū did not understand this,
so he praised Yú;
The ruler of Zōu did not understand this,
so he brought disgrace upon himself first.
The Way of an enlightened ruler,
is like Shū Xiàng's 叔向 hunting ode,
and Zhāo Hóu's 昭侯 listening to his servants.
The first principle of governance: 〓#
Small acts of trustworthiness lead to
the establishment of great trust.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler accumulates trust.
If rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
then prohibitions and orders will not be enforced.
This is illustrated by Wén Gōng's 文公 attack on Yuán 原,
and Jī Zhèng's 箕鄭 saving the starving.
Therefore, Wú Qǐ 吴起 waited for an old friend to eat,
and Wén Hóu 文侯 met with the forester before hunting.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler demonstrates trustworthiness,
like Zēng Zǐ's 曾子 killing the pig.
The danger lies in Lì Wáng's 厲王 sounding the alarm drums without cause,
and Lǐ Kuí's 李悝 deceiving the two arbitrators.
First explanation: 〓#
Mì Zǐjiàn 宓子賤 governed Dānfù 單父.
Yǒu Ruò 有若 saw him and said,
"Why are you so thin?"
Mì Zǐjiàn 宓子賤 said,
"My lord does not know of my unworthiness,
and made me govern Dānfù 單父.
Official matters are pressing,
"My heart is troubled by it,
therefore I am emaciated."
Yǒu Ruò said:
"In the past, Shùn played the five-stringed lute,
sang the poem 'Nán Fēng',
and the world was well-governed.
Now, even governing the small place of Dānfù causes you worry,
if you were to govern the world, what would you do?
Governing the world would be extremely difficult!
Therefore, if you have the method to govern,
even if you sit in the temple halls
with the complexion of a maiden,
it will not hinder governance;
but without the method to govern,
even if your body is worn and emaciated,
it will still be of no benefit."
The King of Chǔ said to Tián Jiū:
"Mòzǐ is
a prominent school of thought.
His personal conduct is acceptable,
but his words are numerous and not well-argued,
why is that?"
Tián Jiū replied:
"In the past, the Earl of Qín married his daughter to the Duke of Jìn,
ordering Jìn to provide elaborate decorations for her,
Following her, there were seventy attendants dressed in embroidered garments.
When she arrived in Jìn,
the people of Jìn loved her concubine but despised the duke's daughter.
This can be said to be good at marrying off a concubine,
but cannot be said to be good at marrying off a daughter.
A man of Chǔ was selling his pearls in Zhèng.
He made a casket of magnolia wood,
perfumed it with cinnamon and pepper,
adorned it with pearls and jade,
decorated it with roses,
and lined it with jadeite.
The people of Zhèng bought the casket and returned the pearls.
This can be said to be good at selling the casket,
but cannot be said to be good at selling the pearls.
The discussions in the present age
all concern the words of eloquent speeches and literary compositions.
The ruler examines their literary style and forgets their usefulness.
The teachings of Mòzǐ,
transmit the Way of the former kings,
discuss the words of the sages
to proclaim to the people.
If one argues about the wording,
then I fear that people will cherish the literary style
and forget its directness,
and use the literary style to harm its usefulness.
This is the same as the man of Chǔ 楚 who sold pearls
and the Lord of Qín 秦 who married off his daughter;
therefore, his words are often illogical."
Mòzǐ 墨子 made a wooden kite,
which took three years to complete,
but it flew for only one day before it broke.
His disciples said,
"Master's skill
is so great that he can make a wooden kite fly."
Mòzǐ 墨子 said,
"I am not as skillful as the one who makes the linchpin for a cart.
Using wood of only a few inches,
without spending even a morning's work,
it can pull a load of thirty *shí* 石,
reach far and exert much strength,
and last for many years.
Now, I made a kite,
which took three years to complete,
but it flew for only one day before it broke."
Huìzi 惠子 heard of this and said,
"Mòzǐ 墨子 is greatly skilled;
he is skilled at making linchpins
and clumsy at making kites."
The King of Sòng 宋 was at odds with Qí 齊 and
The Wǔ Palace was being built.
Ōu Guǐ sang songs,
Travelers stopped to listen,
The builders did not tire.
The king heard of this,
Summoned him and bestowed gifts upon him.
He replied,
"My teacher, Shè Jī's ōu
is even better than Guǐ's."
The king summoned Shè Jī and ordered him to sing.
Travelers did not stop,
The builders knew weariness.
The king said,
"Travelers do not stop,
The builders know weariness,
His ōu is not as beautiful as Guǐ's,
Why is this?"
He replied,
"Your Majesty, try measuring their work."
Guǐ four *bǎn*,
Shè Jī eight *bǎn*;
Test its firmness,
Guǐ five *cùn*,
Shè Jī two *cùn*.
Good medicine is bitter to the taste,
Wise men advise others to drink alcohol moderately,
knowing that excessive indulgence leads to illness.
Honest advice grates on the ear,
but enlightened rulers heed it,
knowing it can lead to the achievement of merit.
Tale Two: 〓#
A man from Sòng
requested to carve a female monkey on the tip of a thorn for the King of Yān,
requiring a three-month fast
before it could be viewed.
The King of Yān therefore supported him with the revenue of three carriages (of taxpayers).
A right-hand royal metalworker then said to the king:
"I have heard that a ruler should not abstain from feasting for more than ten days.
Now I know that the king cannot fast for long
to view a useless trinket,
hence the three-month period.
In general, those who carve and whittle
must use tools smaller than what they carve.
Now, I am a metalworker,
and I have no tools small enough to carve such a thing.
This is an impossible object,
your majesty must investigate."
The king then imprisoned and interrogated the man.
It was indeed a lie,
so he killed him.
A smith said to the king:
"Plans are without measure,
and the words of the debaters are full of thorny arguments."
One story says: 〓#
The King of Yān was fond of minute craftsmanship.
A man of Wèi said:
"I can carve a monkey on the tip of a thorn."
The King of Yān was pleased with him
and supported him with the stipend of five chariots.
The king said:
"I will try to watch
the guest carve the monkey on the thorn."
The guest said:
"If the ruler wants to see it,
he must not enter the palace for half a year,
nor drink wine or eat meat.
After the rain clears and the sun comes out,
observe it in the hazy dimness,
and then the monkey on the thorn will be visible."
The King of Yān therefore supported the man of Wèi,
but could not see his monkey.
A smith below the terrace in Zhèng
said to the King of Yān:
"Your servant
is a carver.
All minute objects must be carved with a knife,
and the knife used to carve must be larger than the object being carved.
Now, the tip of a thorn is too small to accommodate the edge of a knife,
making it difficult to work on the tip of a thorn.
Your Majesty, please observe the craftsman's carving;
it will then be clear whether it is possible or not."
The king said,
"Good."
He said to a man from Wèi:
"The craftsman claims to be carving a monkey on a thorn tip;
how does he do it?"
The man said,
"With a knife."
The king said,
"I wish to see it."
The craftsman said,
"Your servant will go home to fetch it."
Thereupon, he fled.
Ér Yuè,
a man from Sòng,
was a skilled debater,
and holding
the proposition "A white horse is not a horse,"
he subdued the debaters of Jìxià in Qí.
When riding a white horse through a pass,
Then, consider the "White Horse" rhapsody.
Therefore, empty words
can conquer a state.
Examining reality and judging by form,
cannot deceive even one person.
Now, newly sharpening a whetstone to kill arrows,
drawing a crossbow to shoot,
even if blindly firing,
its tip will invariably hit an autumn hair.
However, one cannot find its exact place again.
It cannot be called good archery,
because there is no constant target.
Setting up a five-inch target,
drawing back ten steps away,
only Yì and Páng Méng can surely hit it completely,
because there is a constant target.
Having a standard is difficult,
while not having a standard is easy.
With a constant target,
Yì and Féng Méng are skillful at hitting the five-inch target;
without a constant target,
hitting an autumn hair with a random shot
is clumsy.
Therefore, responding without a standard
leads to verbose arguments from debaters;
If standards are set and adhered to,
even those who are knowledgeable will still fear making mistakes,
and dare not speak recklessly.
Now, rulers listen to speeches,
but do not respond to them with standards, instead praising their eloquence;
they do not measure things by merit,
praising actions that do not enter the border passes.
This is how rulers are constantly deceived,
and how speakers are constantly nurtured.
There was a guest who taught the King of Yàn how to achieve immortality.
The king sent someone to learn it.
Before the person sent to learn could learn it,
the guest died.
The king was furious
and executed him.
The king did not realize that the guest had deceived him,
but punished the learner for being slow.
To believe in things that are not so
and execute innocent ministers
is the calamity of not observing carefully.
Moreover, what people are most concerned about
is nothing more than their own bodies;
if they cannot make themselves immortal,
how can they make the king live forever?
There were men of Zhèng arguing about their ages.
A person said,
"I was born in the same year as Yáo."
Another person said,
"I was born in the same year as the elder brother of Huángdì."
They argued about this without resolution,
and whoever gives up the argument last will be the victor.
A guest painted a chopstick for the ruler of Zhōu,
and it took three years to complete.
The ruler examined it,
and it looked the same as a plain lacquered chopstick.
The ruler of Zhōu was greatly angered.
The painter said,
"Build a wall ten *bǎn* thick,
and cut an eight-foot window,
and when the sun first comes out,
place the chopstick above it and look at it."
The ruler of Zhōu did as he was told,
and when he looked at its shape,
it completely formed dragons, snakes, birds, beasts, chariots, and horses.
The shapes of all things were fully present.
The ruler of Zhōu was greatly pleased.
The accomplishment of this chopstick was not insignificant or easy,
but its use was the same as a plain lacquered chopstick.
A guest was painting for the king of Qí.
The king of Qí asked,
"What is the most difficult thing to paint?"
He said:
"Dogs and horses are difficult."
"What is the easiest?"
He replied:
"Ghosts and demons are the easiest."
As for dogs and horses,
people know them,
they are completely presented before us from morning till night,
they cannot be misrepresented,
therefore they are difficult.
Ghosts and demons,
are formless,
they are not completely presented before us,
therefore they are easy to paint.
In Qi, there was a recluse named Tián Zhòng,
a man from Song named Qū Gǔ met him,
and said:
"I, Gǔ, have heard of your principles, sir,
of not relying on others for food,
now I, Gǔ, have a giant gourd,
as hard as stone,
thick and without openings,
I offer it to you."
Zhòng said:
“Now, what is valued in a gourd is
that it can be used for holding things.
But if it is thick and without an opening,
then it cannot be cut open to hold things;
and if it bears weight like a hard rock,
then it cannot be cut open to ladle with.
I have no use for such a gourd.”
He said:
“Indeed,
Gǔ will discard it.”
Now, Tián Zhòng 田仲 does not rely on others to eat,
nor does he benefit the state of others,
he is also like a hard gourd.
Yú Qìng 虞慶 was building a house,
and said to the craftsman:
“The house is too high.”
The craftsman replied:
“This is a new house,
the plaster is wet and the rafters are green.”
Yú Qìng 虞慶 said:
“That is not so.
If the wet plaster is heavy and the green rafters bend,
using bent rafters to bear heavy plaster,
it should be lower.”
As time passes,
then the plaster is dry and the rafters are arid.
When the plaster is dry, then it is light,
when the rafters are arid, then they are straight,
using straight rafters to bear light plaster,
this is increasingly esteemed.
The artisan was overruled,
he made it and the house collapsed.
One says: 〓#
Yú Qìng was about to build a house,
the artisan said:
"The wood is green and the plaster is wet,
now if the wood is green, then it is pliable,
if the plaster is wet, then it is heavy,
using pliable materials to bear heavy weight,
even if it is completed now,
it will inevitably collapse in the long run."
Yú Qìng said:
"If the wood is dry, then it is straight,
if the plaster is dry, then it is light.
If we can truly obtain dry materials now,
it will become lighter and straighter day by day,
even if it lasts for a long time,
it will definitely not collapse."
The artisan was overruled,
he made it and it was completed,
after a while, the house indeed collapsed.
Fàn Qiě said:
"The breaking of a bow,
necessarily occurs at its limit,
not at its beginning.
Now, when a craftsman strings a bow,
he keeps it in a press for thirty days and then steps on the string.
If he activates the release mechanism in one day,
this is moderating its beginning
and rushing its end,
how can it not break?
But stringing a bow is not like that.
Pressing it for one day and stepping on the string,
and activating the release mechanism in thirty days,
this is rushing its beginning
and moderating its end."
The craftsman is at his wit's end,
doing it this way,
and the bow breaks.
The words of Fàn Qiě and Yú Qìng,
are all elegant and rhetorically superior,
but they contradict the reality of the matter.
If the ruler is pleased and does not restrain them,
this is the reason for failure.
Not planning for the merit of governing and strengthening the state,
but being enamored with eloquent arguments
The sound of ornate language,
is precisely that of scholars skilled
in taking on ruined houses and broken bows.
Therefore, the ruler's management of state affairs
generally does not reach the level of artisans'
constructing houses and stringing bows.
However, scholars like Fàn Qiě 范且 and Yú Qìng 虞慶, are driven to poverty,
because empty rhetoric,
being useless, prevails;
while practical matters,
being straightforward, lead to their downfall.
Rulers often favor useless arguments,
and seldom hear straightforward advice,
this is the cause of disorder.
Now, the world is full of those acting like Fàn Qiě 范且 and Yú Qìng 虞慶, tirelessly,
and rulers find endless pleasure in them,
this is valuing the type of failure and breakage,
and treating knowledgeable people as mere artisans.
When artisans are not allowed to apply their skills,
houses collapse and bows break;
when knowledgeable people are not allowed to implement their methods,
the state becomes disordered and the ruler is endangered.
When infants play together,
they use dust as rice,
mud as soup,
Making meat from wood,
yet invariably returning home for supper by the end of the day,
mud pies and dirt soup are suitable for play
but not for eating.
Those who cite the praises of high antiquity,
arguing without sincerity,
who speak of the benevolence and righteousness of former kings
but cannot rectify the state,
this is also suitable for play
but not suitable for governing.
Those who admire benevolence and righteousness but become weak and disordered are
the Three Jìn (Sān Jìn) states.
Those who do not admire them but become well-governed and strong are
Qín.
However, the reason they have not become emperors
is that their governing is not yet complete.
The "Explanation of Three": 〓 #
When a person is an infant,
if the parents raise them carelessly,
the child will resent them when they grow up.
When the child matures into an adult,
if their support for the parents is meager,
the parents will become angry and scold them.
Child and parent
Even among the closest of relatives,
those who scold or resent each other
all harbor mutual expectations
without fully considering their own interests.
Now, when employing laborers for plowing,
the master spends household funds and provides delicious food,
and assesses cloth to seek easy cash,
it is not out of love for the hired hands,
but he says:
"If it is like this,
the plowing will be deep,
and the weeding will be thoroughly done."
The hired hands devote their strength
and diligently plow and weed,
exhaust their skills to straighten the field paths,
it is not out of love for the master,
but they say:
"If it is like this, the broth will be delicious,
and the cloth will be easily exchanged for money."
This nourishment of effort
resembles the kindness between father and son,
but the mind is attuned to utility,
all harbor selfish intentions.
Therefore, when people act and give,
with benefit as the guiding principle,
even people of Yuè (越) are easily harmonized;
When one harbors intentions to harm,
father and son will be estranged and resentful.
When Duke Wén of Jìn (晉文公, Jìn Wén Gōng) attacked Sòng (宋),
he first declared:
"I have heard that the ruler of Sòng is without principle,
disrespecting the elders,
unfairly distributing wealth,
and whose commands are not trustworthy.
I have come to execute him on behalf of the people."
When Yùe (越) attacked Wú (吳),
they first declared:
"I have heard that the King of Wú is building the Terrace of Rú Huáng (如皇之臺),
digging deep ponds,
exhausting the people with labor,
wasting wealth and resources,
and exhausting the strength of the people.
I have come to execute him on behalf of the people."
A woman of Cài (蔡) became the wife of Duke Huán (桓公, Huán Gōng).
Duke Huán rode in a boat with her.
The lady rocked the boat.
Duke Huán was greatly afraid.
He forbade her but she did not stop.
He became angry and dismissed her.
Then he was about to recall her,
but she had already remarried.
Huán Gōng was greatly angered and
prepared to attack Cài.
Zhòng Fù advised,
"A game played on a bed
is not sufficient reason to attack another's country.
Success cannot be hoped for.
Please do not let this be a hindrance."
Huán Gōng did not listen.
Zhòng Fù said,
"If it must be done,
the Chǔ state has not sent its jīng máo (貢菁茅) to the Son of Heaven
for three years.
Your Lordship might as well raise troops to attack Chǔ on behalf of the Son of Heaven.
Once Chǔ submits,
then turn back and attack Cài,
saying,
'I am attacking Chǔ on behalf of the Son of Heaven,
but Cài did not obey with its troops.'
And so, destroy it.
This is righteous in name
and beneficial in reality,
thus there will certainly be the name of punishing them on behalf of the Son of Heaven,
and the reality of avenging a grudge."
Wú Qǐ was a general of Wèi and attacked Zhōngshān.
A soldier had a carbuncle.
Wú Qǐ 吳起 knelt and personally sucked out the pus.
The wounded man’s mother stood weeping.
Someone asked,
"The general treats your son like this,
why are you still weeping?"
She replied,
"Wú Qǐ 吳起 sucked the wound of his father, and his father died.
Now this son is also going to die.
This is why I am weeping."
Zhào Zhǔfù 趙主父 ordered craftsmen to install hooked ladders
and climb Bòwú 播吾 (a mountain),
carving sparse footprints on it,
three feet wide,
five feet long,
and inscribed it with the words:
"Zhǔfù 主父 often strolled here."
King Zhāo of Qín 秦昭王 ordered craftsmen to install hooked ladders
and ascend Mount Huà 華山,
using the heartwood of pine and cypress as game pieces,
arrows eight feet long,
chess pieces eight inches long,
and inscribed it with the words:
"King Zhāo 昭王 once played chess with the celestial gods here."
When Duke Wén 文公 returned to his state,
Arriving at the Hé River,
he ordered that the biān dòu vessels be discarded,
that the mats and cushions be discarded,
and that those with calloused hands and feet and a dark, grimy face
be placed at the back.
Jiù Fàn heard this and wept in the night.
The Duke said,
"I have been in exile for twenty years,
and now I am able to return to my state.
Jiù Fàn hears this and does not rejoice but weeps,
does he perhaps not wish me to return to my state?"
Fàn replied,
"The biān dòu
are for eating from,
the mats and cushions are for sleeping on,
yet you discard them.
Those with calloused hands and feet,
with dark, grimy faces,
are those who have labored and have merit,
yet you place them at the back.
Now I, your servant, am among those placed at the back,
and my heart cannot bear the sorrow,
therefore I weep.
Moreover, I have committed many acts of deceit and falsehood to help you return to your state.
I still despise myself for it,
Ér kuàng yú jūn?"
He bowed twice and took his leave.
Wén Gōng stopped him and said:
"A proverb says:
'He who builds the altar,
haphazardly plants the pillar,
but with solemn ceremony sacrifices to it.'
Now you helped me take it,
but you do not help me govern it;
you helped me establish it,
but you do not help me worship it,
how can that be?"
He unharnessed the left trace horse
and made a covenant by the river.
A man from Zhèng County, Bǔ Zǐ, had his wife make trousers for him.
His wife asked, "How should these trousers be?"
The husband said, "Like my old trousers."
Thereupon the wife destroyed the new trousers,
making them like the old ones.
