A man from Zhèng County found a yoke
but did not know its name.
He asked someone, "What kind of thing is this?"
He replied:
Soon, he found another one.
He asked someone:
"What kind of thing is this?"
He replied:
"This is a yoke."
The questioner became very angry and said:
"Earlier you said it was a yoke,
now you again say it is a yoke,
what is the meaning of this abundance?
This woman is deceiving me!"
Thereupon, he fought with her.
There was a man from Wèi 衛 who assisted in hunting with arrows.
When a bird arrived,
he first waved his sleeve at it,
startling the bird away without shooting it.
The wife of Bǔ Zǐ 卜子, a man from Zhèng 鄭 county, went to the market
and bought a turtle to take home.
When they passed the Yǐng 潁 River,
thinking it was thirsty,
she let it go so it could drink,
and thus lost her turtle.
When a junior serves a senior in drinking,
The elder drinks,
and he also drinks himself.
One story says:
There was a man in Lǔ who thought highly of himself.
He saw an old man drinking wine but unable to finish it,
so he spat at him.
He also imitated the spitting.
Another story says:
There was a young man in Sòng who also wanted to imitate good behavior.
Seeing an elder drink without leaving any wine,
even though he couldn't handle alcohol, he wanted to finish it all.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Gird it with a sash, bind it tightly."
There was a man in Sòng who governed,
and he added weight to his sash, girding it tightly himself.
People asked:
"What is this?"
He replied:
"The book says so,
it is naturally like this."
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Having been carved and polished,
return to its original simplicity."
There was a man in Liáng who governed.
To act and speak based on learning,
to base actions on texts,
saying:
"It's difficult."
Consequently, they lose the actual meaning.
Someone asks:
"What is this?"
The reply is:
"The book says so;
it must be so."
A person from Yǐng sent a letter to the prime minister of Yān.
Writing at night,
the fire was not bright,
so he said to the candle holder:
"Raise the candle."
But in the process, he mistakenly wrote "raise the candle"
"Raise the candle,"
was not the meaning of the letter.
The prime minister of Yān received the letter and was pleased with it,
saying: "To 'raise the candle'
means to value brightness;
to value brightness
means to promote the worthy and appoint them."
The prime minister of Yān reported this to the king,
and the king was greatly pleased,
and the country was well-governed as a result.
It is well-governed,
but it is not the meaning of the book.
Scholars in the present age are mostly like this.
There was a man from Zhèng 鄭 who was about to buy shoes.
He first measured his foot and placed the measurement on his seat.
When he went to the market, he forgot to take it with him.
Having obtained the shoes,
he then said,
"I forgot to bring the measurement."
He returned home to get it.
By the time he returned,
the market was over,
and he could not get the shoes.
Someone said,
"Why not try them on with your feet?"
He said,
"I would rather trust the measurement
than trust myself."
*Shuō Sì*: 說四
Wáng Dēng 王登 became the magistrate of Zhōngmù 中牟.
He reported to the lord of Xiāng 襄, saying,
"In Zhōngmù 中牟, there are scholars named Zhōng Zhāng 中章 and Xū Jǐ 胥己.
They cultivate themselves greatly,
and their learning is very broad.
Why doesn't Your Lordship promote them?"
The lord said,
"If you see him,
I will make him a senior minister."
The chancellor advised,
"A senior minister is a high rank in Jìn.
To receive it now without merit
is not what the Jìn ministers intend.
Has your lord merely heard of him, and not yet seen him?"
Lord Xiāng said,
"I have taken on Dēng,
and have already heard of and seen him;
what Dēng has taken,
I have also heard of and seen;
thus, the use of ears and eyes for personnel selection can never end."
Wáng Dēng in one day had an audience with two senior ministers,
and gave them fields and houses.
The people of Zhōng Mù abandoned their cultivated fields,
sold their houses and gardens to follow scholars,
half the town did so.
Shū Xiàng was seated in attendance,
Duke Píng requested an audience,
the duke's calves ached and his feet were numb and cramped,
yet he dared not shift his position.
When the state of Jìn heard of this, they all said,
"Shū Xiàng is a worthy man,
Píng Gōng treated him with courtesy,
(but he) suffered a cramp and dared not break his sitting posture."
Those in the Jìn Guó who resigned from office on the pretext of admiring Shū Xiàng
were the weights of the state.
In Zhèng Xiàn, there was a man named Qū Gōng,
upon hearing of the enemy,
was afraid,
and consequently died;
once the fear had passed,
he consequently lived.
Zhào Zhǔ Fù sent Lǐ Cī to inspect
whether Zhōngshān was attackable.
Returning, he reported,
"Zhōngshān is attackable.
If Your Lordship does not attack quickly,
it will be overtaken by Qí and Yān."
Zhǔ Fù said,
"Why is it attackable?"
Lǐ Cī replied,
"Their ruler shows favor to scholars of caves and grottos,
and makes efforts, stopping his chariot to meet
scholars in poor villages and narrow lanes
by the tens,
and treats commoners with courtesy
by the hundreds."
The ruler said,
"According to your description,
he is a virtuous ruler.
How can we attack him?"
Cī (疵) said, "That is not so.
If one favors reclusive scholars
and brings them into the court,
then the warriors will be lax in battle formations.
If the ruler honors scholars
and the lower gentry occupy positions in the court,
then the farmers will become lazy in the fields.
If the warriors are lax in battle formations,
then the military will be weak.
If the farmers are lazy in the fields,
then the state will be poor.
A military that is weak against its enemies
and a state that is poor internally
will inevitably perish.
I have never seen a case where they did not perish.
Is it not advisable to attack him?"
Zhǔfù (主父) said,
"Good."
He raised an army and attacked Zhōngshān (中山),
and consequently annihilated it.
Persuasion 5: 〓#
Qí Huán Gōng liked to wear purple,
and the entire country wore purple.
At that time,
five bolts of plain silk could not be exchanged for one bolt of purple.
Huán Gōng worried about this
and said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"I like to wear purple,
and purple is extremely expensive.
The people of the entire country like to wear purple and won't stop.
What should I do?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"If you wish to stop it,
why not try not wearing purple yourself?"
He said to his attendants:
"I greatly dislike the smell of purple."
Consequently, if an attendant happened to be wearing purple and approached,
the duke would inevitably say:
"Step back a little.
I dislike the smell of purple."
The duke said:
"Alright."
On that day,
none of the courtiers wore purple.
The next day,
no one in the capital wore purple.
After three days,
Within the borders, no one wore purple clothing.
It is said:
Qí Wáng (齊王), the King of Qi, liked to wear purple clothing,
so the people of Qi all liked it too.
In the Qi kingdom, five bolts of plain fabric could not be exchanged for one bolt of purple.
Qí Wáng (齊王) worried about the high price of purple,
and Fù Yuè (傅說) said to the king:
"The *Shī* (詩, Book of Odes) says:
'If you do not do it yourself, if you are not personally involved,
the common people will not believe you.'
Now, if the king wishes the people not to wear purple clothing,
Your Majesty, please remove your purple robe and attend court.
If any of your ministers come to court wearing purple,
say to them:
'Stay away!
I abhor the smell.'"
On that day,
none of the gentlemen wore purple;
in that month,
no one in the country wore purple;
in that year,
within the borders, no one wore purple.
Zhèng Jiǎn Gōng (鄭簡公), Duke Jian of Zheng, said to Zǐ Chǎn (子產):
"Our state is small,
hemmed in between Jing and Jin.
Now the city walls are not complete,
and the armor and weapons are not prepared,
we cannot prepare for the unexpected."
Zǐchǎn 子產 said:
"I have already closed off its exterior far away,
and secured its interior firmly.
Although the state is small,
it still cannot be endangered.
Your Majesty, please do not worry."
Therefore, until the death of Duke Jiǎn 簡公, he had no worries.
It is said:
Zǐchǎn 子產 was the prime minister of Zhèng 鄭.
Duke Jiǎn 簡公 said to Zǐchǎn 子產:
"Drinking wine is not joyful.
The sacrificial vessels are not large,
the bells, drums, yú 竽, and sè 瑟 do not sound,
my affairs are not consistent;
the state is not stable,
the people are not well-governed,
plowing and warfare are not harmonious,
it is also your fault.
You have your duty,
and I also have my duty,
let each of us guard our duty."
Zǐchǎn 子產 retired and governed for five years,
The state had no robbers or thieves;
on the roads, no one picked up lost items;
even peaches and dates shading the streets, no one would pluck them.
A needle or knife lost on the road could be recovered after three days.
If this did not change for three years,
the people would have no hunger.
Sòng Xiānggōng 宋襄公 fought with the people of Chǔ 楚
above Zhuōgǔ 涿谷.
The Sòng 宋 people had already formed their ranks,
but the Chǔ 楚 people had not yet finished crossing [the river].
The Right Sīmǎ 司馬, Gòu Qiáng 購強, rushed forward and advised, saying:
"The Chǔ 楚 people are numerous, while the Sòng 宋 people are few.
Please allow the Chǔ 楚 people to cross halfway, and before they have fully formed their ranks, attack them;
we will certainly defeat them."
Xiānggōng 宋襄公 said:
"I have heard that a gentleman says:
'Do not inflict multiple wounds,
do not capture the gray-haired,
do not push people into danger,
do not press people into straits,
do not drum [to attack] those not yet formed in ranks.'
Now, to attack the Chǔ 楚 before they have crossed [the river]
would be harmful to righteousness.
Please allow the Chǔ 楚 people to finish crossing and form their battle lines,
and then we will drum and advance our soldiers."
The Right Sīmǎ said:
"Your lord does not love the people of Sòng,
and your inner circle is incomplete.
You are acting merely out of righteousness."
The Duke said:
"Do not return to your ranks, I will enforce the law."
The Right Sīmǎ returned to his ranks.
The Chǔ people had already formed ranks and arrayed their troops.
The Duke then beat the drums to attack.
The Sòng people were utterly defeated.
The Duke was wounded in the thigh.
He died three days later.
This is a calamity brought about by admiring and personally pursuing benevolence and righteousness.
To insist that only when the ruler personally does everything
will the people listen and obey,
that would be to make the ruler
till the fields for food
and dress in battle gear to fight, moving in orderly formation.
Only then would the people be willing to farm and fight.
Wouldn't the ruler then be in great danger?
And wouldn't the ministers then be too secure?
Duke Jǐng of Qí was touring Shǎohǎi.
An express messenger came from within to report, saying:
"Yīng is seriously ill,
and near death.
I fear you will be too late."
Jǐng Gōng hurriedly got up,
and another messenger on horseback arrived.
Jǐng Gōng said,
"Quickly prepare the carriage with Fánqiě's horses,
and have Zōu Zi and Hán Shū drive it."
After traveling several hundred steps,
thinking Zōu Zi was not fast enough,
he seized the reins and took over the driving;
after another several hundred steps,
thinking the horses were not advancing quickly enough,
he completely abandoned the carriage and ran.
Even with the excellence of Fánqiě's horses
and the skill of Zōu Zi and Hán Shū,
he thought it was not as good as running himself.
Wèi Zhāo Wáng wanted
to share official duties,
and said to Mèngcháng Jūn,
"I want to share official duties."
Mèngcháng Jūn said,
"If Your Majesty wants to share official duties,
then why not try practicing reading the laws?"
Zhāo Wáng read more than ten bamboo slips of the laws and then fell asleep.
The king said,
"I cannot read these laws."
If one does not personally grasp the power and authority,
Ér yù wéi rén chén suǒ yí wéi zhě yě, And desiring to do what a subject ought to do,
shuì bù yì yí hū? is sleeping not appropriate?
Confucius said:
"Wèi rén jūn zhě, "He who is a ruler of men,
yóu yú yě; is like a vessel;
mín the people
yóu shuǐ yě. are like water.
Yú fāng shuǐ fāng, If the vessel is square, the water is square;
yú huán shuǐ huán." if the vessel is round, the water is round."
The ruler of Zōu liked to wear long tassels,
and those around him all wore long tassels,
so the tassels became very expensive.
The ruler of Zōu was troubled by this,
and asked those around him,
and those around him said:
"The ruler likes to wear them,
and the common people also wear them a lot,
therefore they are expensive."
So the ruler first cut off his own tassel and went out,
and in the country, everyone stopped wearing long tassels.
The ruler could not issue an order
to set a standard for the common people's clothing and prohibit it,
but cut off the tassel to show an example to the people first,
which is like first punishing oneself to govern the people.
Shū Xiàng
those with great merit received much,
those with little merit received little.
Hán Zhāo Hóu said to Shēn Zǐ,
"Legal codes and standards are very difficult to implement."
Shēn Zǐ said,
"Law is
to bestow rewards based on demonstrated merit,
and to assign office based on ability.
Now, if Your Lordship establishes legal codes and standards
but listens to the requests of those around you,
this is why it is difficult to implement."
Zhāo Hóu said,
"From this day forward, I know how to implement the law.
What should I listen to?"
One day,
Shēn Zǐ requested to appoint his elder cousin to an official position.
Zhāo Hóu said,
"This is not what I learned from you.
If I listen to your request,
would I be ruining your doctrine?
Or perhaps destroying the reason I employed you?"
Shēn Zǐ withdrew and begged forgiveness.
Explanation six:
Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Yuán,
They packed ten days' worth of provisions,
and then he agreed with the officer to a ten-day deadline.
When they arrived at Yuán and after ten days Yuán still had not surrendered,
he sounded the gong to retreat,
and withdrew the troops.
A soldier came out from within Yuán and
said, "Yuán will surrender in three days."
The assembled officials and attendants advised,
"Yuán's food is exhausted and its strength depleted,
Your Lordship should wait for it."
The Duke said,
"I agreed with the officers on a ten-day deadline.
If I do not leave,
I will lose my credibility.
To gain Yuán but lose credibility,
I will not do it."
Thereupon he withdrew the troops and left.
The people of Yuán heard of this and said,
"Having a ruler so trustworthy,
how can we not submit?"
And so they surrendered to the Duke.
The people of Wèi heard of this and said,
"Having a ruler so trustworthy,
how can we not follow him?"
And so they submitted to the Duke.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and recorded it, saying,
"That one who attacked Yuán and obtained Wèi did so through trustworthiness."
Duke Wén asked Jī Zhèng, saying:
"What can be done to relieve famine?"
He replied, saying:
"Trustworthiness."
The Duke said:
"Wherein lies trustworthiness?"
He said:
"Trustworthiness in names, trustworthiness in affairs, trustworthiness in righteousness.
Trustworthiness in names
then the assembled officials will guard their offices,
good and evil will not exceed their bounds,
and all undertakings will not be neglected;
trustworthiness in affairs
then one will not lose the opportune time,
and the people will not transgress;
trustworthiness in righteousness
then close relatives will exhort and encourage each other,
and those far away will return to him."
Wú Qǐ went out,
encountered an old friend and stopped him to eat.
The old friend said:
"Yes,
I will now return and prepare."
Master Wú said:
"Waiting for him to eat."
Therefore, when the friend didn't come by dusk,
he got up and didn't eat, waiting for him.
The next morning,
he sent someone to look for the friend.
The friend came,
and then he ate with him.
Wèi Wénhóu 魏文侯 made an appointment to hunt with his forester.
The next day,
they encountered a strong wind.
His attendants stopped Wénhóu 魏文侯,
but he didn't listen,
saying:
"I cannot. To break my promise because of the wind
would be untrustworthy,
I will not do it."
So he drove his own chariot and went,
braved the wind and dismissed the forester.
Zēngzǐ's 曾子 wife went to the market,
her son followed her, crying.
His mother said:
"Go back,
and when I return, I will kill a pig for you."
When she came back from the market,
Zēngzǐ 曾子 wanted to catch the pig and kill it.
His wife tried to stop him, saying:
"It's just playing with the baby."
Zēngzǐ said:
"Playing with a baby is not the same as mere jesting.
A baby is not yet knowledgeable,
and depends on parents to learn,
listening to the parents' instruction.
Now, if you deceive him,
you are teaching your son to deceive.
If a mother deceives her son,
the son will not trust his mother,
and that is not a way to establish proper teaching."
So, he cooked the pig.
King Lì of Chǔ, Chǔ Lì Wáng, had a situation requiring alert,
so he had a drum made
to alert the people for defense.
He got drunk from drinking wine,
and accidentally beat the drum,
which greatly alarmed the people.
He sent someone to stop them, saying:
He said:
"I was drunk and playing with my attendants,
and accidentally beat the drum."
The people all dispersed.
After a few months,
When there was an alarm,
the drums were beaten, but the people did not come.
Then, a clearer signal was ordered
and the people believed it.
Lǐ Kuí 李悝 warned his two hé 和 (a military unit),
saying:
"Be vigilant against the enemy;
they will arrive morning and evening and attack you."
This happened two or three times, but the enemy did not arrive.
The two hé 和 became lax
and did not trust Lǐ Kuí 李悝.
After several months,
the people of Qín 秦 came to attack them,
nearly seizing their army.
This is the trouble of not being believed.
Another story says:
Lǐ Kuí 李悝 was fighting with the people of Qín 秦.
He said to the left hé 和:
"Hurry up!
The right hé 和 has already advanced."
Then he rode to the right hé 和 and said:
"The left hé 和 has already advanced."
Both the left and right hé 和 said,
"They have advanced!"
Thereupon, they all fought to advance.
The following year,
he fought with the people of Qín.
The people of Qín ambushed him,
almost seizing his army.
This was the disaster of lack of trust.
〓# There were people who were suing each other.
Zǐchǎn separated them and did not allow them to communicate their arguments directly.
He would take their words and relay them, thus understanding the situation.
Duke Sì of Wèi sent a man to impersonate someone passing through the market checkpoint.
The checkpoint officer interrogated and challenged him.
Taking the opportunity, the man bribed the checkpoint officer with gold.
The checkpoint officer then let him pass.
Duke Sì said to the checkpoint officer:
"At a certain time, a guest passed through and gave you gold,
and I will therefore reprimand you."
The checkpoint officer was greatly afraid,
considering Duke Sì to be discerning and insightful.
"Outer Collection of Sayings, Left Below," Thirty-Third
Chapter One: 〓#
If one is punished for a crime,
the people will not resent their superiors,
as demonstrated by Yuè Wēi and Zǐ Gāo sitting in a dangerous situation.
If one is rewarded for merit,
the subjects will not be grateful to the ruler,
Zhái Huáng held the right tally and rode in a carriage.
King Xiāng didn't understand,
therefore Zhāo Mǎo rode in five carriages while wearing straw sandals.
If superiors don't over-delegate,
and subordinates don't falsely claim ability,
then I, your servant, will become the Zhou of Fū Shǎoshì.
*Jīng* Two: 〓#
Relying on power and not relying on trust,
therefore Dōngguō Yá criticized Guǎn Zhòng.
Relying on tactics and not relying on trust,
therefore Hún Xuān spoke ill of Duke Wén.
Therefore, a ruler with tactics
uses trustworthy rewards to fully utilize talent,
and uses certain punishments to prohibit evil.
Even if there is conflicting behavior,
he will surely obtain what he wants.
When Jiǎn Zhǔ made Yáng Hǔ his minister,
Duke Āi asked about "one foot."
*Jīng* Three: 〓#
If the principles of the relationship between ruler and subject are lost,
then King Wén will personally tread and boast.
If the location of morning and leisure gatherings is not changed,
then Jì Sūn will be solemn his entire life and meet a bandit.
Chapter Four:
Where profit is prohibited,
where prohibition is profitable,
even a god cannot succeed.
Where praise is punished,
where slander is rewarded,
even Yáo cannot govern.
To make a door but not allow entry,
to entrust benefit but not allow advancement,
is how chaos arises.
If the Marquis of Qí does not listen to his attendants,
if the Lord of Wèi does not listen to those who praise,
but clearly observes and illuminates all his officials,
then what is great will not waste gold coins,
and what is weak will not need jade.
Xīmén Bào's request to govern Yè again,
is enough to know this.
It is like a thief taking a fur coat from a baby,
and giving ornamented clothes to a lame and precarious child.
If Zǐ Chuò's attendants are always scheming,
chasing away ants and driving away flies,
how can there not be Huán Gōng's worry of asking for an official post
and Xuān Zhǔ's concern about skinny horses?
Chapter Five:
If a subject takes humility and frugality as his conduct,
If reward is not used with discretion, it will be insufficient to inspire admiration;
if favor and glory are without restraint,
then subordinates will encroach.
The explanation lies in Miáo Bēn-huáng's criticism of Xiàn Bó,
and Kǒng Zǐ's discussion of Yàn Yīng.
Therefore, Zhòng Ní commented on Guǎn Zhòng and Sūn Shū-áo.
If demeanor in coming and going changes,
Yáng Hǔ's words reveal his subservience.
But Jiǎn Zhǔ's response to his ministers reveals his failure to understand the art of rulership.
If factions harmonize with each other,
and ministers get what they desire,
then the ruler becomes isolated;
if the assembled ministers publicly recommend,
and inferiors do not harmonize with each other,
then the ruler is enlightened.
Yáng Hǔ intended to follow the virtue of Zhào Wǔ,
and the impartiality of Jiě Hú,
but Jiǎn Zhǔ considered them brambles,
not the way to instruct the state.
Principle Six: 〓#
If the ducal house is debased,
then honest words are resented;
if private conduct prevails,
then public achievements are few.
The explanation lies in Wén Zǐ's straightforward speech,
Wǔzǐ used a staff;
Zǐchǎn loyally remonstrated;
Zǐguó scolded in anger;
Liáng Chē enforced the law;
and Chénghóu surrendered his seal;
Guǎn Zhòng acted in the public interest;
yet the people slandered and resented him.
Explanation 1: 〓 #
When Kǒngzǐ was prime minister of Wèi,
his disciple Zǐgāo was a prison official,
and he had a man's foot cut off.
The man whose foot was cut off became a gatekeeper.
Someone spoke ill of Kǒngzǐ to the ruler of Wèi,
saying:
"Ní intends to rebel."
The ruler of Wèi wanted to arrest Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ fled,
his disciples all scattered,
Zǐgāo came out the gate,
and the amputee pulled him
and hid him under the gate in a room,
so the officers pursuing him could not find him.
At midnight,
Zǐgāo asked the amputee:
"I could not violate the lord's laws
You caressed the feet of Yuè (crippled) son.
This was the time for your son to take revenge.
Why then did you choose to flee from me?
How did I ever deserve this from you?"
Yuè Wēi said:
"My feet were cut off.
Indeed, it was right that I was punished;
there was nothing to be done.
However, when Fāng Gōng was trying my case in prison,
you leaned towards the law,
using words to try to acquit me,
you greatly desired for me to be freed,
and I knew it.
When the trial concluded and the sentence was decided,
you appeared anxious and displeased,
showing it in your expression,
and I saw and knew it.
This wasn't just because of me;
it's that human nature is inherently benevolent,
that the heart is naturally so.
This is why I am pleased
and grateful to you."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Those who are good at acting for profit
Planting virtue,
if it cannot be for benefit,
plants resentment.
The leveler
is the one who measures fairly;
the official
is the one who executes the law fairly;
the one who governs the state
must not lose fairness."
Tián Zǐfāng was traveling from Qí to Wèi.
He saw Dí Huáng riding in a curtained carriage, with a horse-drawn carriage going out.
Fāng thought it was Marquis Wén,
so he moved his carriage, changed his route, and avoided it,
but it was only Dí Huáng.
Fāng asked,
"Why are you riding in this carriage?"
He replied,
"The ruler planned to attack Zhōngshān,
and I recommended Dí Jiǎo,
and the plan succeeded;
and when attacking it,
I recommended Yuè Yáng, and Zhōngshān was conquered;
having obtained Zhōngshān,
worried about governing it,
I recommended Lǐ Kè, and Zhōngshān was governed:
therefore, the ruler bestowed this carriage."
Fāng said:
"The reward for your achievement is still meager."
When Qín and Hán attacked Wèi,
Zhāo Mǎo persuaded them from the west, and Qín and Hán withdrew;
when Qí and Jīng attacked Wèi,
Mǎo persuaded them from the east, and Qí and Jīng withdrew.
King Xiāng of Wèi supported him with five chariots.
Mǎo said:
"Bó Yí was buried as a general at the foot of Mount Shǒuyáng,
and the world said:
'Given Bó Yí's virtue
and his reputation for benevolence,
to bury him as a general
is like leaving his hands and feet uncovered.'
Now, I have stopped the armies of four states,
and the king rewards me with only five chariots.
The reward for this achievement
is like Yíng Shèng winning and wearing straw sandals."
"Shàoshì Zhōu was
an upright, honest, clean, and sincere man of ancient times,
and was a powerful warrior for Lord Xiāng of Zhào.
He wrestled with Xú Zǐ of Zhōngmóu,
and was not as strong,
so he told Lord Xiāng
Taking him as a replacement for oneself.
Xiāng Zhǔ said:
"Your position
is what people desire,
why do you speak of Xú Zi as a replacement for yourself?"
He replied:
"Your subject serves you with strength.
Now Xú Zi has more strength than your subject,
if your subject does not offer him as a replacement,
I fear others will speak of it
and I will be blamed."
Another account:
Shào Shì Zhōu was Xiāng Zhǔ's charioteer.
Arriving at Jìnyáng,
there was a strongman, Niú Zi Gēng,
with whom he wrestled but did not win.
Zhōu said to the lord:
"The reason Your Lordship employs your subject as charioteer
is because your subject is strong.
Now there is one stronger than your subject,
I wish to recommend him."
Explanation Two: 〓#
Qí Huán Gōng was about to establish Guǎn Zhòng.
He ordered his ministers:
"I am going to establish Guǎn Zhòng as my second father (仲父, zhòngfù).
"The virtuous enter to the left,
the unvirtuous enter to the right."
Dōngguō Yá stood at the central gate.
The Duke said,
"I have appointed Guǎn Zhòng as my second father [仲父, zhòngfǔ],
and the order is:
'The virtuous to the left,
the unvirtuous to the right.'
Why do you now stand at the central gate?"
Yá said,
"With Guǎn Zhòng's wisdom,
can he devise plans for the whole world?"
The Duke said,
"He can."
"With his decisiveness,
will he dare to undertake great affairs?"
The Duke said,
"He will dare."
Yá said,
"If he knows how to devise plans for the whole world
and dares to undertake great affairs,
you are therefore entrusting him with the power of the state entirely.
With Guǎn Zhòng's abilities,
taking advantage of your position to govern the state of Qí,
how can there be no danger?"
The Duke said,
"Good."
Thereupon, he ordered Xí Péng to manage internal affairs
and Guǎn Zhòng to manage external affairs, so they could complement each other.
When Duke Wén of Jìn fled into exile,
Jī Zhèng carried a pot of food
and followed him.
Becoming lost and losing their way,
he was separated from the Duke.
Hungry, he wept on the road,
suffering hunger but daring not to eat.
When Duke Wén returned to his state,
he raised troops to attack Yuán,
conquering and capturing it.
Duke Wén said,
"To lightly endure the hardship of hunger
and insist on keeping the pot of food intact,
this person will certainly not betray me with Yuán."
Thereupon, he appointed him as the governor of Yuán.
The senior official Hún Xuān heard of this and criticized it,
saying,
"Because of not moving the pot of food,
to rely on him not betraying with Yuán,
is that not inept?"
Therefore, an enlightened ruler
Do not rely on them not betraying me;
rely on my being unbetrayable.
Do not rely on them not deceiving me;
rely on my being undeceivable.
Yáng Hǔ deliberated and said:
"If the ruler is wise and discerning,
then serve him with all your heart;
if he is unworthy,
then adorn deceit and test him."
He was banished from Lǔ,
suspected in Qí,
and fled to Zhào.
Lord Jiǎn of Zhào welcomed him and made him his minister.
Those around him said:
"Hǔ is good at stealing the government of other states,
why make him minister?"
Lord Jiǎn said:
"Yáng Hǔ is bent on seizing,
I am bent on guarding."
Thereupon, he adhered to his principles and controlled him.
Yáng Hǔ did not dare to do wrong,
and served Lord Jiǎn well,
enhancing the lord's strength,
almost to the point of hegemony.
Lord Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ,
"I have heard that in ancient times there was Kuí with one foot.
Is it really true that he had one foot?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"No,
Kuí was not one-footed.
Kuí was resentful and malicious,
and many people did not like or rejoice in him.
However,
the reason he was able to avoid being harmed by others
was because of his trustworthiness.
People all said,
'This single quality
is enough.'
Kuí was not one-footed,
but one [quality] was sufficient."
Āigōng said,
"If it is truly so,
then indeed it is sufficient."
Another account says:
Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ,
"I have heard that Kuí had one foot.
Is it true?"
He said: #
"Kuí
was a man.
Why would he have one foot?
In that, there was nothing particularly unusual,
except that he was singularly skilled in music.
Yáo said:
"Kuí alone is sufficient."
He appointed him as Director of Music.
Therefore, the wise man said:
"Kuí had one
foot,
but it was not literally one foot."
Explanation Three:
Wén Wáng attacked Chóng,
reaching the Phoenix Yellow Mound,
his sock tie came undone,
so he tied it himself.
Tài Gōng Wàng said:
"Why do you do this?"
The King said:
"Those above
in relationship to the ruler are all his teachers;
those in the middle
are all his friends;
those below
are all his servants.
Now, they are all the former ruler's ministers,
gù wú kě shǐ yě."
One instance:
Jìn Wéngōng 晋文公 fought with Chǔ 楚.
When they reached the tomb of Huángfèng 黄凤,
the string of his shoe came undone.
So he tied it himself.
His attendants said,
"Could you not have had someone do it for you?"
The duke said,
"I have heard that:
for a superior
ruler, those who reside with him
are all those who fear him;
for a middling
ruler, those who reside with him
are all those whom he loves;
for an inferior
ruler, those who reside with him
are all those whom he insults.
Although I am unworthy,
the people of my late ruler are all still present,
and that is why I find it difficult (to make them do such things)."
Jìsūn 季孙 loved scholars,
and was solemn throughout his life.
His dwelling and clothing were always as if he were at court.
However, Jì Sūn occasionally became lax,
had faults and errors,
and could not maintain it for long.
Therefore, his retainers thought he disdained them and treated them lightly,
and they resented him together,
and then killed Jì Sūn.
Therefore, the wise person avoids excess and extremism.
It is said:
Nángōng Jìngzǐ asked Yán Zhuōjù:
"Jì Sūn supported the disciples of Kǒngzǐ,
those who wore court robes and sat with him numbered in the tens,
yet he met with treachery.
Why is that?"
He said:
"In the past, King Chéng of Zhōu
kept jesters and dwarfs close
to indulge his desires,
but consulted with wise men on matters of state,
thus he was able to accomplish his desires throughout the land.
Now, Jì Sūn supports the disciples of Kǒngzǐ,
those who wear court robes and sit with him number in the tens,
but consults with jesters and dwarfs on matters of state,
therefore he met with treachery.
Thus it is said:
It's not about who you associate with,
"That's what to consult with."
Kǒngzǐ was sitting in the presence of Lǔ Āigōng,
Āigōng bestowed upon him peaches and millet.
Āigōng said:
"Please partake."
Zhòngní first ate the millet and then savored the peach,
those around him all covered their mouths and laughed.
Āigōng said:
"The millet,
it is not for eating,
but to cleanse the peach."
Zhòngní replied:
"I understand it.
Millet,
is the chief of the five grains,
and is considered a superior offering when sacrificing to former kings.
Among the six fruits,
the peach is the lowest,
and is not allowed into the temple when sacrificing to former kings.
As I have heard,
a gentleman uses the inferior to cleanse the superior,
but I have not heard of using the superior to cleanse the inferior.
Now, to use the chief of the five grains
to cleanse the lowest of fruits,
is to use the superior to cleanse the inferior.
Qiū thought it would hinder righteousness,
therefore he did not dare to put it before
the splendor of the ancestral temple."
Jiǎn Zhǔ said to his attendants:
"The carriage mat is too beautiful.
Though a hat is cheap,
the head must wear it;
though shoes are expensive,
the feet must tread on them.
Now this carriage mat is so
beautiful,
what shall I use as shoes to tread on it?
To beautify the bottom while diminishing the top
is the root of hindering righteousness."
Fèi Zhòng persuaded Zhòu, saying:
"Xībó Chāng is virtuous,
the people are pleased with him,
the feudal lords are attached to him,
he must be executed;
if he is not executed,
he will surely become a disaster for Yīn."
Zhòu said:
"What you say is righteous,
why should he be executed?"
Fèi Zhòng said:
"Although the hat is worn and tattered,
it must be worn on the head;
although the shoes are brightly colored,
they must be trod upon the ground.
Now, Xī Bó Chāng,
is a subject,
yet he cultivates righteousness and people turn to him,
ultimately becoming a trouble for the realm.
Will he not surely flourish?
A subject who does not use his wisdom for his lord,
is surely someone who must be punished.
Moreover, for the lord to punish a subject,
where is the fault?"
Zhòu said:
"These things, benevolence and righteousness,
are what those above use to encourage those below.
Now Chāng loves benevolence and righteousness,
to punish him is not permissible."
He did not heed his advisors three times,
therefore he perished.
King Xuān of Qí asked Kuāng Qiàn,
"Are scholars gamblers?"
He said,
"No, they are not."
The king said,
"Why?"
Kuāng Qiàn answered,
"In gambling, the xiāo (owl) is held in high regard.
The winner must kill the xiāo.
To kill the xiāo
is to kill what is valued.
The Ru scholars consider this harmful to righteousness,
therefore they do not gamble."
He asked again,
"Do Ru scholars use the yì (arrow attached with a string) to shoot birds?"
He replied,
"No.
Using the yì,
is to harm those above from below,
it is to injure the ruler from below.
The Ru scholars consider this harmful to righteousness,
therefore they do not use the yì."
He asked again:
"Do Ru scholars play the sè zither?"
He replied: "No.
The sè zither uses small strings to produce loud sounds,
and large strings to produce soft sounds.
This is to change the order of large and small,
and reverse the positions of noble and lowly.
therefore they do not play the sè."
King Xuān (Xuān Wáng) said,
"Good."
Zhòng Ní said,
"Rather than have the people flatter those below them,
it is better to have them flatter those above them."
Persuasion Four: 〓#
Jù,
was a recluse of Qí;
Chán,
was a recluse of Wèi.
The rulers of Qí and Wèi were not enlightened
and were unable to personally oversee their territories,
but listened to the words of those around them.
Therefore, these two men spent gold and jade
in order to seek entry into officialdom.
Xīmén Bào, as magistrate of Yè,
was upright, frugal, pure, and sincere,
not taking even the slightest personal benefit.
And he greatly simplified the people around him.
Those around him therefore formed cliques with each other
and disliked him.
After a year,
at the time of the year-end report,
the ruler took back his seal.
Bào himself requested,
"Your subject formerly did not know how to govern Yè,
now your subject understands.
Your subject wishes to request the seal
again to govern Yè.
If it is not proper,
your subject requests to submit to the punishment of axe and block."
Wén Hóu could not bear it
and returned it to him.
Bào then heavily taxed the common people,
urgently serving those around him.
After a year,
when the accounts were submitted,
Wén Hóu greeted him and bowed.
Bào replied,
"Last year, your subject governed Yè for you,
and you took your subject's seal;
now your subject governs Yè for those around you,
and you bow to your subject.
Your subject cannot govern anymore."
He then presented the seal and left.
Wén Hóu did not accept it,
saying,
"I formerly did not understand you,
now I understand.
I wish you would strive to govern it for me."
He ultimately did not accept it.
In Qí, there was a son of a dog thief
playing and boasting with a crippled man whose feet had been cut off (yuè wēi zi).
The thief's son said:
"My father's fur coat is unique in that it has a tail."
The crippled man said:
"My father is unique in that he never loses his trousers in winter."
Zǐ Chuò said:
"No one can draw a square with the left hand
and a circle with the right hand at the same time.
Using meat to get rid of ants,
the ants only increase;
using fish to drive away flies,
the flies only flock more."
Duke Huán of Qí said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"Offices are few, but those who request them are many;
I am worried about this."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Do not listen to the requests of those around you;
assign salaries based on ability,
and grant offices based on merit.
Then, no one will dare to request an office;
what do you have to worry about?"
Hán Xuānzǐ said:
"My horses have plenty of beans and grain,
"Why are they so thin?"
"What is the reason?
I am troubled by this,"
Zhōu Shì 周市 replied,
"Even if you ordered the grooms to feed them all the grain,
they still would not be fat;
that is impossible.
If you claim to give them a lot in name,
but in reality give them little,
they also will not be thin;
that is also impossible.
If the ruler does not examine the true facts of the situation,
and just sits and worries about it,
then the horses will still not be fat."
Duke Huán 桓公 asked about placing officials to Guǎn Zhòng 管仲,
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 said,
"In discerning words [and arguments],
in being clean in matters of wealth,
and in being familiar with human emotions,
Yí Wú 夷吾 is not as good as Xián Shāng 絃商;
I request to establish him as the Grand Judge.
In ascending and descending, being respectful and yielding,
in order to make clear propriety when treating guests,
I am not as good as Xí Péng 隰朋;
I request to establish him as the Grand Herald.
Clearing the grass to establish a village,
reclaiming land to produce grain,
I, your servant, am not as good as Níng Qī,
please let him be in charge of agriculture.
Forming the three armies into battle array,
making the soldiers regard death as returning home,
I, your servant, am not as good as Gōngzǐ Chéngfǔ,
please let him be the Grand Commander.
To remonstrate boldly and frankly,
I, your servant, am not as good as Dōngguō Yá,
please establish him as a Remonstrating Minister.
To govern Qí,
these five men are sufficient;
if you wish to become a Hegemon,
then Ǒu Yí is here."
Saying Five: 〓#
When Mèng Xiànbó was minister of Jìn,
goosefoot and lamb's quarters grew beneath the hall,
thorns and brambles grew outside the gate,
he did not eat two kinds of flavor,
he did not sit on layered mats,
Jìn had no concubines dressed in silk,
he did not feed horses millet in his residence,
he did not go out in a carriage.
Shū Xiàng heard of this,
and told Miáo Bēn Huáng.
Biàn Huáng (賁皇) criticized this, saying:
"This is using the prince's rank and emolument
to ingratiate himself with his subordinates."
It is said that:
When Mèng Xiànbó (孟獻伯) was appointed to be Senior Minister (上卿),
Shū Xiàng (叔向) went to congratulate him.
At the gate there was a groom,
but the horses did not eat grain.
Xiàng (向) asked:
"You do not have two horses or two carriages,
why is that?"
Xiànbó (獻伯) said:
"I observe that the people of the state
still have a hungry look on their faces,
therefore I do not feed my horses;
many with white hair are walking on foot,
so I do not have two carriages."
Xiàng (向) said:
"I initially congratulated you on your appointment as minister,
now I congratulate you on your frugality."
Xiàng (向) went out,
and said to Miáo Biàn Huáng (苗賁皇):
"Help me congratulate Xiànbó (獻伯) on his frugality."
Master Miáo (苗子) said:
"What is there to congratulate
? For titles and stipends, flags and insignia,
are the means to differentiate meritorious service
and distinguish the worthy from the unworthy.
Therefore, in the laws of the state of Jìn,
the highest grand masters have two carriages and two teams of horses,
the middle grand masters have two carriages and one team of horses,
and the lowest grand masters have a single team of horses for their exclusive use.
This clarifies the hierarchy.
Furthermore, a minister must be involved in military affairs;
therefore, they maintain chariots and horses,
and equip soldiers and chariots
to prepare for war.
In times of crisis,
they are prepared for the unexpected;
in times of peace,
they are available for court affairs.
Now, to disrupt the government of the state of Jìn,
to neglect preparation for the unexpected,
to fulfill one's ambition,
to purify one's personal reputation,
is Xiàn Bó's thrift acceptable?
What is there to congratulate?"
Guǎn Zhòng was the minister of Qí,
and said,
"Your servant is of high rank,
yet your subject is poor."
Duke Huán said,
"I will give you a family estate with three residences."
He said,
"Your subject is rich,
yet your servant is lowly."
Duke Huán had him stand above Gāo and Guó.
He said,
"Your servant is honored,
yet your servant is estranged."
Then he was established as Zhòngfǔ (second father).
Confucius heard of this and criticized it, saying,
"He is excessively extravagant and presses upon his superior."
It is said that
when Guǎn Zhòngfǔ went out,
he had a vermillion parasol and wore blue garments,
he set up drums to announce his return,
his courtyard had displayed cauldrons,
and his household had the means to support three families.
Confucius said,
"He is a good senior official,
but his extravagance presses upon his superior."
Sūn Shū'áo, serving as prime minister of Chǔ,
had a cart with a mare,
Coarse rice congee with vegetable broth,
a meal of dried fish,
a lambskin coat in winter,
a linen garment in summer;
if his face has a look of hunger,
then he is a good grand master,
and his frugality presses upon his subordinates.
Yáng Hǔ left Qí and fled to Zhào.
Jiǎn Zhǔ asked him, saying,
"I have heard that you are good at cultivating men."
Hǔ said,
"When I lived in Lǔ,
I cultivated three men,
and all became magistrates;
when I committed offenses in Lǔ,
all searched for me.
When I lived in Qí,
I recommended three men;
one got close to the king,
one became a county magistrate,
and one became a border patrol officer;
when I committed offenses,
the one close to the king did not see me,
the county magistrate welcomed me and bound me,
the border patrol officer chased me to the border,
stopping when he couldn't catch me.
"Tigers are not good at planting trees."
The ruler lowered his head and smiled, saying:
"Those who plant orange and grapefruit trees,
when eaten, are sweet,
and when smelled, are fragrant.
Those who plant tribulus and jujube trees,
when grown, prick people.
Therefore, a gentleman is careful in what he plants."
Zhōngmóu lacked a magistrate.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Zhào Wǔ, saying:
"Zhōngmóu,
is the limb and pillar of our state,
the shoulder and thigh of Hándān.
I desire to obtain a good magistrate for it.
Who can be sent?"
Wǔ said:
"Xíng Bózǐ is suitable."
The Duke said:
"Isn't he your enemy?"
Wǔ replied:
"Private enmity does not enter the public gate."
The Duke further asked, saying:
"For the magistrate of the Central Treasury,
who can be sent?"
Wǔ said:
"A subject can do it."
Therefore, it is said:
"In external appointments, do not avoid enemies;
in internal appointments, do not avoid one's own son."
Zhào Wǔ 赵武 recommended forty-six people,
and when Wǔ 武 died,
each took their proper position as guests (of the state).
His lack of private considerations was like this.
Duke Píng 平公 asked Shū Xiàng 叔向, saying:
"Among the ministers, who is virtuous?"
He replied: "Zhào Wǔ 赵武."
The duke said:
"You are partial to your teacher."
Xiàng 向 said:
"Wǔ 武 stands as if unable to support his own clothes,
speaks as if reluctant to open his mouth,
yet the men he has recommended number several dozen,
all of them attaining their aims,
and the ducal house relies heavily upon them.
And when Wǔzi 武子 was alive,
he did not benefit his family,
and in death, he did not entrust his orphans to anyone.
I dare to consider him virtuous."
Jiě Hú 解狐 recommended his enemy to Lord Jiǎn 简 as prime minister.
His enemy thought that he would fortunately be released,
and so went to pay his respects and express his gratitude.
Hú (狐) then drew his bow to greet him and shot him,
saying:
"That I recommended you
was a public matter,
because you were capable of holding the position.
That I am your enemy
is my personal grudge,
and I would not, because of my personal grudge against you,
keep you from my lord."
Therefore, personal grudges do not enter the public gate.
Another version says:
Xiè Hú (解狐) recommended Xíng Bólǐu (邢伯柳) to be the governor of Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Liǔ (柳) went to thank him, saying:
"You released me from my offense,
how dare I not bow to you twice?"
Xiè Hú (解狐) said: "Recommending you
was a public matter;
resenting you
is a private matter.
You may go,
my resentment towards you will be as it was from the beginning."
A man from Zhèng (鄭) County was selling piglets.
Someone asked him the price.
He said:
"The road is long and the day is late,
how can I have time to talk to you?"
Explanation Six: 〓
Fàn Wénzǐ liked direct speech.
Wǔzǐ struck him with a staff:
"Those who speak frankly,
are not tolerated by others.
Being not tolerated,
then endanger themselves.
Not only endanger themselves,
but will also endanger their father."
Zǐchǎn was the son of Zǐ Guó.
Zǐchǎn was loyal to the ruler of Zhèng.
Zǐ Guó angrily scolded him, saying:
"To be markedly different from other ministers
and singularly loyal to the lord.
If the lord is virtuous and wise,
he will listen to you;
if he is not wise,
he will not listen to you.
Whether he listens or not is not yet certain,
but you have already alienated yourself from the other ministers.
Being alienated from the other ministers,
Then it will surely endanger your own life.
It's not just endangering yourself,
but also endangering your father."
Liáng Chē, newly appointed as magistrate of Yè,
had his elder sister come to visit him.
It was late in the evening,
and the city gate was closed.
So she climbed over the outer wall to enter.
Chē then had her feet cut off.
Zhào Chénghóu considered this unkind,
took away his official seal, and dismissed him from his post as magistrate.
Guǎn Zhòng, in shackles,
was being transported from Lǔ to Qí.
On the way, hungry and thirsty,
he passed the border warden of Qǐwū and begged for food.
The warden of Qǐwū knelt down and fed him,
showing great respect.
The warden then secretly said to Zhòng:
"If, by chance,
you reach Qí without dying and are employed by Qí,
how will you repay me?"
Zhòng said:
"According to your words,
I will employ the worthy,
use the capable,
A discussion on labor.
"How shall I repay you?"
The border official resented him.
Outer Storage of Discourses, Right, Part One, Thirty-fourth
There are three ways a ruler governs his subjects.
Principle One:
If power is insufficient to transform (them), then eliminate them.
Shī Kuàng's reply,
Yàn Zǐ's explanation,
both involved abandoning the easy path of power
and pursuing the difficult path of moral guidance,
which is like chasing a running beast,
without knowing how to eliminate the trouble.
Troubles can be eliminated,
as in Zǐ Xià's interpretation of the "Spring and Autumn Annals":
"One who is good at wielding power nips evil in the bud."
Therefore, Jì Sūn yielded to Zhòng Ní when it came to meeting power,
let alone entrusting it to a ruler?
Thus, Tài Gōng Wàng killed Kuáng Yù,
and a slave does not ride a great steed.
Sì Gōng knew this,
therefore he did not drive a deer.
Xuē Gōng knew this,
therefore he gambled with the Two Luán.
These all understand the reversal of sameness and difference.
Therefore, the way a wise ruler manages his ministers
lies in the method of raising crows.
Chapter Two: 〓#
The ruler of men
is like the axel of profit and harm.
Because there are many shooters,
the ruler is exhausted.
Therefore, if likes and dislikes are revealed,
subordinates will have something to exploit,
and the ruler will be confused.
If speech and words are easily understood,
ministers will find it difficult to speak frankly,
and the ruler will lose his divine insight.
The explanation lies in Shēn Zǐ's 申子 words about the "Six Precautions,"
and Táng Yì's 唐易 words about falconry.
The trouble lies in Guó Yáng's 國羊 request to change the law,
and Xuān Wáng's 宣王 sighs.
Clarify it with Jìng Guō Shì's 靖郭氏 presentation of ten earrings,
and Xī Shǒu's 犀首
and Gān Mào's 甘茂 method of digging a hole to hear secrets.
Táng Xī Gōng 堂谿公 understood strategy,
therefore he asked about the jade cup;
Zhāo Hóu 昭侯 was skilled in strategy,
therefore he used sleeping alone to listen.
The way of an enlightened ruler,
lies in heeding Shēn Zǐ's advice to make decisions alone.
Chapter Three: 〓#
The failure of methods
has a reason.
If you don't kill the dog,
then the wine will turn sour.
The state also has its "dogs,"
and moreover, those around the ruler are all "rats of the shrine."
The ruler should not repeat Yáo's second attempt at execution,
nor Zhuāng Wáng's response to the crown prince,
but should rather follow Báo ǎo's decision regarding Cài ǒu.
If someone knows what is valued, but is unable,
one should first measure them by the method of teaching songs.
Wú Qǐ driving out his beloved wife,
and Duke Wén beheading Diān Xié,
were both actions that went against their feelings.
Therefore, those who can get others to lance boils,
must be those who can endure the pain themselves.
Exposition One: 〓#
If rewards and praise do not encourage,
and punishments and denigration do not inspire fear,
and even if all four are applied, there is no change,
then they should be removed.
When Duke Jǐng of Qí
followed Duke Píng to a drinking gathering,
Shī Kuàng was in attendance.
Duke Jǐng asked Shī Kuàng about governance, saying,
"Grand Master, what will you teach me?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"Your Lordship must simply benefit the people."
In the middle of the gathering,
with the wine flowing freely,
as he was about to leave,
he again asked Shī Kuàng about governance, saying,
"Grand Master, what will you teach me?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"Your Lordship must simply benefit the people, that's all."
Duke Jǐng exited the lodging,
and Shī Kuàng saw him off.
Again, he asked Shī Kuàng about governance.
Shī Kuàng said,
"Your Lordship must simply benefit the people, that's all."
Duke Jǐng returned,
pondering,
still not fully sober,
and understood what Shī Kuàng meant:
Gōngzǐ Wěi and Gōngzǐ Xià,
Duke Jǐng's two younger brothers,
were very popular among the people of Qí,
If a family is wealthy and the people speak well of them,
comparing them to the ducal house,
this endangers my position.
Now, those who say I am benevolent to the people,
are they trying to make me compete with my two younger brothers for the people?
Thereupon, he returned to the state,
opened the granaries and distributed grain to the poor,
and dispersed the remaining wealth in the treasury to bestow upon orphans and widows.
The granaries were empty of old grain,
and the treasury had no surplus wealth.
Palace women who were not favored were allowed to marry.
Those seventy years and older received stipends of rice.
He was selling virtue and bestowing kindness upon the people,
already competing with his two younger brothers.
After two years,
the two younger brothers fled;
Gōngzǐ Xià fled to Chǔ,
and Gōngzǐ Wěi fled to Jìn.
Jǐng Gōng was touring Shǎo Hǎi with Yànzi,
ascending the Bǎiqǐn Terrace and looking back at his state,
saying,
"How beautiful!
How vast,
how magnificent!
Who in later generations will possess this?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"Will it belong to the Tián Chéng family!"
Jǐng Gōng said,
"I possess this state,
yet you say the Tián Chéng family possesses it,
why is that?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"The Tián Chéng family greatly wins over the people of Qí.
In their dealings with the people,
they request ranks and stipends from above to distribute among the great ministers;
below, they privately use large dòu and hú measures, and qū and fǔ vessels
to lend out,
and small dòu and hú measures, and qū and fǔ vessels to collect in return.
When slaughtering an ox,
they take only a dòu of meat,
and the rest they use to feed the retainers.
Throughout the year,
they take two sets of cloth and silk,
and the rest they use to clothe the retainers.
Therefore, the price of timber in the market
is no more expensive than in the mountains;
the fish, salt, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, snails, and clams from the marshes
are no more expensive than in the sea.
Your Lordship heavily levies taxes,
while the Tián Chéng family generously bestows.
In Qí 齊, there was once a great famine.
The number of people starving to death by the roadside was countless.
Yet one never heard of fathers and sons leading each other to go to Tián Chéngshì 田成氏.
Therefore, the people of Qín 秦 and Zhōu 周 together sang,
"Oh,
is it over!
How abundant,
will we go and return to Tián Chéngzǐ 田成子!"
The *Shī* 詩 (Book of Songs) says:
"Even if he has no virtue to give you,
we will sing and dance."
Now, because of Tián Chéngshì's 田成氏 virtue, the people sing and dance.
The people's virtue is returning to him.
Therefore it is said:
"It's probably Tián Chéngshì 田成氏!"
The duke, with tears welling up, said:
"Isn't this sad!
I have the state,
but Tián Chéngshì 田成氏 possesses it.
What can be done about this?"
Yànzǐ 晏子 replied:
"What worries do you have?
If you want to take it back,
then draw near to the virtuous and keep the unworthy at a distance,
govern its disorders,
Relax punishments,
assist the poor and care for the orphaned and widowed,
practice kindness and provide for those in need,
and the people will return to you,
then even if there were ten Tián Chéngsǐs,
what could they do to you?"
Someone said:
Jǐng Gōng didn't know how to use power,
and Shī Kuàng and Àn Zǐ
didn't know how to eliminate trouble.
Now, a hunter,
relying on the comfort of a carriage,
using the strength of six horses,
and having Wáng Liáng assist with the reins,
can easily catch swift animals without tiring himself.
Now, if one were to abandon the advantages of the carriage,
discard the strength of the six horses
and the guidance of Wáng Liáng,
and instead chase after animals on foot,
then even with the feet of Lóu Jì, one would never catch an animal.
Relying on good horses and a sturdy carriage,
even a slave could succeed.
The state
is the ruler's carriage;
power
It is about the ruler's horses.
If one does not use their position of power
to prohibit and punish ministers who act arbitrarily and enjoy excessive favor,
but instead relies on the accumulation of virtue
to act in accordance with the world and compete for the people,
these are all like those who do not ride the ruler's chariot,
do not make use of the horse's advantage,
and abandon the chariot to walk on foot.
Therefore, it is said:
"Jǐng Gōng 景公 did not know how to use the power of his position,
and Shī Kuàng 師曠 and
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 did not know how to eliminate ministers who were a source of trouble."
Zǐ Xià 子夏 said:
"The *Chūn Qiū 春秋* records instances of ministers killing their rulers
and sons killing their fathers
numbering in the dozens.
These were not accumulated in a single day,
but gradually developed until they reached that point."
Generally speaking, those who are treacherous
act for a long time and accumulate power,
and with accumulated power, their strength increases,
and with increased strength, they are able to kill.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler eliminates them early.
Now, the rebellion of Tián Cháng 田常
The signs of trouble were gradually becoming apparent,
yet the ruler did not punish [the offenders].
Yàn Zǐ did not make his ruler forbid ministers who encroached and insulted [others],
but made his lord practice benevolence,
therefore Duke Jiǎn received his misfortune.
Therefore Zǐ Xià said:
"Those who are good at maintaining power
nip the sprouts of evil in the bud."
Jìsūn was the chief minister of Lǔ,
Zǐ Lù was the magistrate of Hóu.
Lǔ, in the fifth month, mobilized the people to dig a long canal.
When this was being done,
Zǐ Lù used the grain from his private official stipend to make porridge and rice,
inviting those digging the canal to eat at the Five Fathers' Intersection
and feed them.
Confucius heard of this
and sent Zǐ Gòng to overturn their rice,
smashing their utensils,
saying:
"The ruler of Lǔ has the people,
why do you feed them?"
Zǐ Lù was angrily displeased,
rolled up his sleeves, and went in,
requesting [to speak], saying:
"Does the Master dislike Yóu's practice of benevolence and righteousness?
What we learn from our master
is benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness
means sharing one's possessions with the world and sharing its benefits equally.
Now, using Yóu's salary and grain to feed the people,
what's wrong with that?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu is indeed rustic!
I thought you understood this principle,
but you haven't grasped it after all.
No wonder you are so ignorant of ritual!
You are feeding them
because you love them.
Now, according to ritual,
the Son of Heaven loves the entire world,
the feudal lords love their own territories,
the high officials love their positions,
and the gentlemen love their families.
To go beyond what one is supposed to love is called encroachment.
Now, the ruler of Lǔ owns the people,
and you presume to love them on your own.
This is encroachment,
is it not a falsehood!"
Before he had finished speaking,
an envoy from the Jì Sūn family arrived,
rebuking him, saying:
"If Féi 吔 rises up the people and uses them,
and you, sir, order your disciples to command the servants
and feed them,
are you going to seize the people of Féi?"
Confucius harnessed his carriage and left Lǔ.
With the virtue of Confucius,
and Jìsūn was not the lord of Lǔ,
with the resources of a minister,
he employed the methods of a ruler.
He prohibited things early, before they took shape,
and Zǐlù was unable to carry out his private favors,
and harm could not arise.
How much more so a ruler!
If Duke Jǐng of Qí had used his power to prohibit Tián Cháng's encroachments,
then there certainly would have been no calamity of being coerced and murdered.
When Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in the east at Qí,
on the eastern seaboard of Qí there were two recluse brothers named Kuáng Yù and Huá Shì,
who declared:
"We will not be ministers to the Son of Heaven,
nor friends with the feudal lords.
We till the land and eat from it,
we dig wells and drink from them.
We have no requests of others.
No highest name,
no salary from a lord,
we do not serve officials but devote ourselves to our own strength."
Tàigōng Wàng arrived at Yíngqiū,
and ordered the officials to seize and kill them
as the first to be punished.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn heard of this from Lǔ,
sent an urgent message and asked, saying:
"Those two men
were virtuous.
Today, while enjoying the state, you kill virtuous men,
why is that?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"These two brothers made an agreement saying:
'We will not be ministers to the Son of Heaven,
nor friends with the feudal lords,
we will till the land and eat from it,
dig wells and drink from them,
we will have no needs from others.
We seek no superior reputation,
nor the emoluments of a ruler,
we will not pursue officialdom, but rely on our own strength.'
Since they will not be ministers to the Son of Heaven,
it means I, Wàng, cannot make them my ministers;
since they will not be friends with the feudal lords,
it means I, Wàng, cannot employ them;
since they till the land and eat from it,
dig wells and drink from them,
One who seeks nothing from others,
cannot be induced with rewards and punishments, or encouraged and restrained.
Furthermore, lacking a desire for high reputation,
even if knowing,
they will not act in the hope of being employed.
Not relying on the lord's emoluments,
even if wise,
they will not act in the hope of gaining merit.
If not serving,
then not governing;
if not entrusted,
then not loyal.
Moreover, the means by which the former kings governed their subjects
were nothing other than titles and emoluments, or punishments.
Now, if these four things are insufficient to make them serve,
then for whom should one act as a lord?
To become prominent without bearing arms,
to gain fame without personally engaging in farming,
is also not the way to instruct the country.
Now, suppose there is a horse here,
resembling the form of a Jì horse,
the finest of horses in the world.
Yet, if urging it forward does not make it advance,
and stopping it does not make it halt,
turning it left does not make it go left,
and turning it right does not make it go right,
Then even a lowly slave
would not entrust his feet to it.
The reason a slave wishes to entrust his feet to a jì (fine horse)
is because a jì can pursue benefits and avoid harms.
Now, if it is not used by people,
even a lowly slave
would not entrust his feet to it.
If someone considers himself a worthy gentleman of the world
but is not employed by the ruler,
exhibiting extreme virtue but not being used by the prince,
this is not someone a wise ruler would employ as a minister.
It is like a jì that cannot be controlled,
and therefore he is executed."
It is also said:
Tài Gōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí in the east.
There was a worthy man by the sea named Kuáng Yù.
Tài Gōng Wàng heard of him and went to invite him,
he turned his horse away three times at the gate,
but Kuáng Yù did not respond and refused to meet him.
So Tài Gōng Wàng executed him.
At that time,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was in Lǔ,
and he rushed to stop it;
by the time he arrived,
he had already been executed.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Kuáng Yù,
is a worthy man in the world.
Why did you, Master, execute him?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Kuáng Yù was plotting not to be a subject of the Son of Heaven,
and not to befriend the feudal lords.
I feared that he would disrupt the law and change the teachings,
therefore, I made him the first to be punished.
Now there is a horse here,
its appearance resembles a fine steed,
but when driven, it does not go,
when pulled, it does not advance,
even a slave would not place his feet upon its crossbar."
Rú Ěr persuaded Duke Sì of Wèi,
Duke Sì of Wèi was pleased but sighed.
His attendants said:
"Why doesn't Your Grace appoint him as prime minister?"
The Duke said:
"A horse that resembles a deer
is valued at a thousand gold pieces.
However, there are horses worth a thousand gold pieces
but no deer worth a thousand gold pieces,
because horses are used by people,
while deer are not used by people.
"It is like this now.
He is the minister of a state of ten thousand chariots.
Outwardly, he is concerned with the intentions of the great powers.
His heart is not in Wèi.
Even if he is discerning and wise,
he will not work for my benefit.
This is why I will not make him my minister."
When Xūe Gōng was minister to Marquis Zhāo of Wèi,
among his attendants were Luan Zi,
namely Yáng Hú and Pān Qí.
They were greatly valued by the king,
but they did not work for Xūe Gōng.
Xūe Gōng was troubled by this.
Thereupon, he summoned them to play bó with him.
He gave each of them a hundred jīn,
and ordered their brothers to play bó.
Soon after, he added two hundred jīn to each of them.
While they were playing bó with great interest,
the attendant announced that the son of Zhāng Jì was at the gate.
The duke became furious,
grasped his weapon, and instructed the attendant:
"Kill him!
I have heard that Jì does not approve of wén."
After a moment,
Jì Yǔ, who was at his side,
said:
「不然。
I secretly heard that Jì was very devoted to the public,
but I haven't heard of his virtue being hidden."
So he stopped the killing of the guest,
treated him with great courtesy,
and said:
"Formerly, I heard that Jì did not act virtuously,
so I wanted to kill him;
now he truly acts virtuously,
how could I forget Jì!"
He informed the granary to present a thousand *shí* of grain,
informed the treasury to present five hundred *jīn*,
informed the stable managers to present two carriages of fine horses from his private stables,
and consequently ordered the eunuch to present twenty beautiful concubines from among the palace women to be given to Jì as well.
Luán Zǐ consequently said to each other:
"Those who work for the public will certainly benefit,
those who do not work for the public will certainly suffer,
what do we hesitate to do for the public?"
Consequently, they privately competed and encouraged
each other and then acted in that way.
Xuē Gōng, with the power of a subject,
pretended to use the methods of a ruler,
and harm could not arise;
how much more so with a true ruler!
Now, those who train birds cut off their lower feathers.
By cutting off their lower feathers,
they are forced to rely on people for food.
How could they not be tame?
Now, the way an enlightened ruler keeps his ministers is also like this.
He makes the ministers have no choice but to profit from the ruler's emoluments,
and have no choice but to submit to the reputation of their superior.
Now, if they profit from the ruler's emoluments,
and submit to the reputation of their superior,
how could they not be obedient?
Discourse 2: 〓#
Shēn Zǐ said:
"If the ruler's discernment is apparent,
people will be on guard against him;
If his discernment is not apparent,
people will deceive him.
If his wisdom is apparent,
people will embellish for him;
If his ignorance is apparent,
people will conceal it from him.
If it is apparent that he has no desires,
people will control him;
If it is apparent that he has desires,
people will bait him.
Therefore, it is said:
'I have no way of knowing him,'
Only non-action (wúwéi) can be used to set the standard."
One said:
Shēn Zǐ said:
"If you are cautious in your speech,
people will know you;
if you are cautious in your actions,
people will follow you.
If you have knowledge and perception,
people will hide from you;
if you have no knowledge and perception,
people will guess your intentions.
If you have knowledge,
people will store you away (value your knowledge);
if you have no knowledge,
people will use you.
Therefore, it is said:
Only non-action (wúwéi) can be used to set the standard."
Tián Zǐfāng asked Táng Yìjū, saying:
"What should a hunter be cautious of?"
He replied, saying:
"Birds watch you with hundreds of eyes,
and you control them with two eyes;
you should be careful of Zhōu Zǐlǐn."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"Good.
If the son adds to his hunt,
I shall add to my state."
The elder of Zhèng heard this and said:
"Tián Zǐfāng knows that he wants to build a granary,
but he has not grasped how to build a granary.
Those who are empty and have no appearance,
that is the granary."
One version says:
King Xuān of Qí asked Táng Yìzǐ about hunting, saying:
"What is valuable about hunting?"
Táng Yìzǐ said:
"It lies in being careful of the granary."
The king said:
"What do you mean by 'being careful of the granary'?"
He replied:
"A bird uses dozens of eyes to watch people,
and people use two eyes to watch birds.
How can one not be careful of the granary? 〓#
Therefore, it is said 〓#
'It lies in being careful of the granary.'"
The king said:
"If that is the case, then for the world,
how does one make this granary?
Now the ruler uses two eyes to watch a state,
and a state uses ten thousand eyes to watch the ruler.
What shall I rely on to provide for myself?"
He replied,
"A certain Elder Zheng said,
'Truly, emptiness and tranquility, non-action and non-appearance.'
Can these be used to provide for myself?"
Guó Yáng was valued more highly than the ruler of Zheng.
Hearing that the ruler disliked him,
he attended a banquet,
and then first said to the ruler,
"If I, your servant, have the misfortune of having faults,
I hope that you, my ruler, will be kind enough to tell me.
I ask to reform myself,
then I will be spared the death penalty."
A guest persuaded King Xuān of Hán.
King Xuān was pleased and sighed.
Those around him recounted the king's delight
to first tell the guest, thinking it would be a good deed.
When Lord Jìng Guō was Prime Minister of Qi,
the queen died,
and it was not known who would be appointed in her place.
He then presented jade earrings to find out.
One account says:
When Lord Xuē was Prime Minister of Qi,
the wife of King Wēi of Qí died.
There were ten young favorites in the court, all dear to the king.
Lord Xuē wished to know whom the king intended to establish as queen,
and requested to place one person as a consort.
If the king listened to him,
then his advice would be heeded by the king,
and be weightier than placing a consort;
if the king did not listen,
then his advice would not be heeded,
and be lighter than placing a consort.
Wishing to first know whom the king desired to place
in order to urge the king to place her,
therefore he made ten jade earrings,
beautified one of them,
and presented them.
The king distributed them to the ten young favorites.
The next day, at court,
he observed where the beautiful earring was located
and urged the king to make her the queen.
Gān Mào served as the prime minister to King Huì of Qín.
King Huì loved Gōngsūn Yǎn,
and spoke something with him in private,
saying:
"I intend to appoint you as prime minister."
A clerk of Gān Mào secretly heard this,
and told Gān Mào.
Gān Mào entered to see the king and
said,
"If Your Majesty obtains a worthy minister,
I dare to bow twice to congratulate you."
The king said,
"I have entrusted the state to you,
how could I obtain another worthy minister?"
He replied,
"It will be Xī Shǒu as minister."
The king said,
"How did you hear of this?"
He replied,
"Xī Shǒu told me."
The king was angered by Xī Shǒu's leak,
and thus banished him.
It is said:
Xī Shǒu was the best general in the world,
a subject of the King of Liáng.
The King of Qín wanted to obtain him to govern the world together,
but Xī Shǒu said,
"Yǎn is a man who is a subject,
and dare not leave his lord's state."
After a year,
Xī Shǒu was convicted of a crime by the King of Liáng,
and fled to Qín,
where the King of Qín treated him very well.
Chūlǐ Jí, a general of Qín,
fearing that Xī Shǒu would replace him as general,
dug a hole in the place where the king often spoke in private.
Soon after, the king indeed discussed matters with Xī Shǒu,
saying:
"I want to attack Hán,
what do you think?"
Xīshǒu said:
"Autumn would be a good time."
The king said:
"I want to entrust the country to you,
you must not reveal this."
Xīshǒu stepped back, bowed twice, and said:
"I accept the command."
Thereupon, Chūlǐ Jí listened through the hole.
The attendants all said:
"The army will rise in autumn to attack Hán,
and Xīshǒu will be the general."
On that very day,
all the attendants knew it;
in that very month,
everyone within the borders knew it.
The king summoned Chūlǐ Jí and said:
"What is all this commotion,
where did it come from?"
Chūlǐ Jí said,
"He resembles Xīshǒu."
The King said,
"I have nothing to say to Xīshǒu,
what about this Xīshǒu?"
Chūlǐ Jí said,
"Xīshǒu is a sojourner,
newly convicted,
his heart is isolated,
this means he intends to attach himself to many others."
The King said,
"Indeed."
He sent someone to summon Xīshǒu,
but he had already fled to another state.
Tángxī Gōng said to Zhāo Hóu,
"Now there is a jade cup worth a thousand gold pieces,
open but without a bottom,
can it hold water?"
Zhāo Hóu said,
"It cannot."
"If there is a clay pot that does not leak,
can it hold wine?"
Zhāo Hóu said,
"It can."
He replied,
"Now, earthenware vessels,
are of the lowest value,
but if they do not leak,
they can hold wine.
Although there might be a jade cup worth a thousand gold pieces,
supremely valuable but without a bottom,
leaking,
and unable to hold water,
who would pour even thin gruel into it?
Now, to be the master of men
and leak the words of one's ministers,
is like a bottomless jade cup.
Though one possesses sagely wisdom,
none will exhaust their skills for you,
because you leak."
Zhāo Hóu said:
"Indeed."
Zhāo Hóu, hearing the words of Táng Xī Gōng,
from that time on,
whenever he wished to enact a major event concerning the world,
he would always sleep alone,
fearing that he might speak in his dreams
and cause others to know his plans.
Another account says:
Táng Xī Gōng saw Zhāo Hóu and said:
"Now, suppose there is a white jade cup without a handle,
and there is a clay cup with a handle.
If you are thirsty,
which would you use to drink?"
The ruler said:
"I would use the clay cup."
Táng Xī Gōng said:
"The white jade cup is beautiful,
but you do not use it to drink,
because it has no handle?"
The ruler said:
"That is so."
Táng Xī Gōng said:
"For a ruler
to leak the words of his ministers,
is like a jade cup without a handle."
Every time Táng Xī Gōng visited and left,
Zhāo Hóu would sleep alone,
fearing that words spoken in dreams
would be leaked to his wives and concubines.
Shēn Zǐ said:
"He who sees alone is called discerning,
he who hears alone is called perceptive.
He who can decide alone,
therefore can be the ruler of the world."
Saying Three: 〓#
There was a man from Sòng 宋 who sold wine.
His measures were very fair,
he treated customers very respectfully,
the wine he made was very good,
and the sign hanging in front of his shop was very tall and conspicuous.
Yet, it didn't sell,
and the wine turned sour.
He wondered about the reason for this.
He asked someone he knew,
and inquired of the elder Yáng Qiàn 楊倩.
Yáng Qiàn 楊倩 said,
"Is your dog fierce?"
The man said,
"It is fierce,
but what does the dog have to do with the wine not selling?"
Yáng Qiàn 楊倩 said,
"People are afraid of it.
If someone sends a child
carrying money and holding a jug or jar to buy wine,
the dog will rush out and bite them.
This is why the wine turns sour and doesn't sell."
A state also has "dogs."
A man of principle, possessing his skill,
desires to enlighten the ruler of ten thousand chariots.
Dàchén who act like fierce dogs meet [troublemakers] and bite them.
This is why the ruler is obstructed and threatened,
and why men of principle are not employed.
Therefore, Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What is the greatest worry in governing a state?"
He replied:
"The greatest worry is the shrine rats."
The Duke said:
"Why worry about shrine rats?"
He replied:
"Has your lord ever seen those who build shrines?
They plant trees and plaster them [with mud].
Rats burrow between them,
digging holes and dwelling within.
If you smoke them out, you fear burning the trees;
if you flood them, you fear the plaster will collapse.
This is why the shrine rats cannot be eradicated.
Now, those around the ruler,
when they go out, they wield great power
and extract profits from the people;
when they come in, they collude and conceal evil from the ruler.
They secretly communicate the ruler's feelings to the outside,
creating a powerful connection between inside and outside,
which all the officials and hundred officers consider wealth.
If the officials are not punished, they will disrupt the law;
if they are punished, the ruler will be uneasy.
To occupy and possess them,
this is also a temple rat of the state."
Therefore, ministers of state who hold power and arbitrarily enforce prohibitions,
clearly benefit those who are for them,
and surely harm those who are not for them,
these are also fierce dogs.
If great ministers act as fierce dogs
and bite virtuous scholars,
and those around the ruler also act as temple rats and sow discord in the ruler's feelings,
the ruler does not realize it.
If this is the case,
how can the ruler not be obstructed,
and how can the state not perish?
It is said: 〓#
In the state of Sòng, there was a wine seller named Master Zhuāng,
whose wine was always good.
Someone sent a servant to buy Master Zhuāng's wine,
but his dog bit the person,
so the messenger did not dare to go,
and instead bought wine from another family.
He was asked:
"Why did you not buy Master Zhuāng's wine?"
He replied: "Today Master Zhuāng's wine is sour."
Therefore it is said: "If you do not kill his dog, then the wine will be sour."
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng,
"What is the greatest worry in governing a state?"
The answer was:
"The most troubling are the shrine rats.
For a shrine
is wood covered with plaster,
and the rats rely on it for shelter.
If you smoke them out, the wood will burn;
if you flood them out, the plaster will crumble.
This is why shrine rats are so troublesome.
Now, those around the ruler of men,
when they go out, they abuse their power to collect profit from the people;
when they come in, they form cliques, deceive, insult, and conceal evil
to trick the ruler.
If they are not punished, they will disrupt the law;
if they are punished, the ruler will be in danger.
Holding onto and possessing such people,
these are also shrine rats."
Therefore, when ministers hold power and monopolize prohibitions,
those who obviously benefit them will surely gain,
and those who do not benefit them will surely suffer harm;
these are like fierce dogs.
Therefore, if those around the ruler are shrine rats,
and those in power are fierce dogs,
then strategies will not be implemented.
When Yáo was about to abdicate the throne to Shùn,
Gǔn remonstrated, saying:
"This is inauspicious!
Who would use the world to pass it on to a commoner?"
Yáo did not listen,
and raised troops to execute Gǔn on the outskirts of Yǔshān.
Gònggōng again remonstrated, saying:
"Who would use the world to pass it on to a commoner?"
Yáo did not listen,
and again raised troops
to execute Gònggōng in the capital of Yōuzhōu.
Thereupon, no one in the world dared to speak against
not passing the world on to Shùn.
Zhòng Ní heard of this and said:
"Yáo knowing that Shùn was virtuous
was not the difficult part.
The fact that he even executed remonstrators, yet still insisted on passing it on to Shùn,
that was the difficult part."
It is said:
"Not allowing what one doubts to ruin what one has discerned
is difficult."
