Outer Compendium of Persuasions, Right, Section Three, Thirty-fifth.
*Jīng* One:
If rewards and punishments are shared,
then prohibitions and orders will not be enforced.
How is this made clear?
It is made clear by Zào Fù and Yú Qī.
Zǐ Hǎn made offerings of pigs,
Tián Héng made pleasure gardens and ponds,
therefore the rulers of Sòng and Jiǎn were murdered.
The danger lies in Wáng Liáng and Zào Fù sharing a chariot,
and Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào sharing a zither.
*Jīng* Two:
Order and strength arise from law,
Weakness and chaos arise from favoritism and indulgence.
If the ruler is enlightened about this,
then he will correctly administer rewards and punishments,
and not be benevolent to his inferiors.
Rank and emolument arise from merit,
execution and punishment arise from crime.
If the minister is enlightened about this,
then he will expend his utmost strength,
and not be loyal to the ruler.
If the ruler understands the principle of seeming unbenevolence,
and the minister understands the principle of seeming disloyalty,
then it is possible to achieve kingship.
Zhāo Xiāng (昭襄) understood the ruler's true feelings and therefore did not open up the five parks;
Tián Wěi (田鮪) understood the minister's true feelings, so he instructed Tián Zhāng (田章),
and Gōngyí (公儀) declined the fish.
Three principles: 〓#
An enlightened ruler
observes outwardly,
and outward affairs cannot but be accomplished,
therefore Sū Dài (蘇代) criticized the King of Qí (齊).
If the ruler observes those above him,
then those who dwell (in positions) will be neither suitable nor obvious,
therefore Pān Shòu (潘壽) spoke of Yǔ's (禹) true feelings.
If the ruler has no awareness,
then I alone will understand it,
therefore I fear those who wear the same clothes and are of the same clan,
How much less can one rely on power!
Wú Zhāng knew this,
therefore he persuaded with pretense,
how much less can one rely on sincerity!
The King of Zhào disliked people with tiger-like eyes and blocked them.
The way of an enlightened ruler
is like the Zhou messenger who rebuffed the Marquis of Wèi.
Chapter Four:
The ruler of men
establishes merit by upholding the law and demanding results.
It is heard that there may be officials who cause chaos,
yet there are subjects who are individually virtuous,
but it is not heard that there are chaotic subjects
and yet there are officials who govern alone;
therefore an enlightened ruler governs officials, not the people.
The explanation lies in shaking the root of the tree
and pulling the rope of the net.
Therefore, the stingy man who loses a fire
cannot go unpunished.
Those who extinguish fires,
if the official carries a pot and runs to the fire,
then it is the effort of one man.
To use a whip to command men
is to enslave ten thousand.
Therefore, encountering those with skill
is like Zàofù encountering a startled horse;
leading the horse and pushing the cart will not make it advance;
but replacing the driver, holding the reins and the whip,
then the horses will all gallop forward.
Therefore, the key lies in hammering and forging to make things level and smooth,
and using boards and frames to correct and straighten.
Otherwise,
failure lies in Nào Chǐ using the state of Qí to slaughter King Mǐn,
and Lǐ Duì using the state of Zhào to starve Lord Father (Zhǔ Fù).
Canon Five: 〓#
Following the natural principles of things
results in achievement without labor.

The trouble lies in Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ's tax officials requesting light and heavy taxes;

Explanation 1: 〓#
Zào Fù drove four horses,
galloping, circling,
and indulging the horses' desires.
Indulging the horses' desires
means monopolizing control of the reins and whip.
Yet when the horses were startled by a escaping pig,
Zào Fù was unable to restrain them,
not because the severity of the reins and whip was insufficient,
but because his authority was diluted by the escaping pig.
Wángzǐ Yúqī, serving as a secondary driver,
did not use reins and whip,
but satisfied the horses' desires,
monopolizing the benefits of fodder and water.
Yet when the horses passed by a garden pond
and the secondary driving failed,
it was not because the benefits of fodder and water were insufficient,
but because his virtue was diluted by the garden pond.
Therefore, Wáng Liáng and Zào Fù
were the best drivers in the world.
However, if Wáng Liáng held the left rein and shouted at them,
and Zào Fù held the right rein and whipped them,
the horses would not be able to travel ten *lǐ*,
because of divided purpose.
Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào
were the best in the world at playing the zither.
However, Tián Lián played the upper registers,
and Chéng Qiào the lower registers,
yet they could not create a melody,
and that too was for a reason.
Now, even with the skill of Wáng Liáng and Zào Fù,
if they shared the reins, they could not control the horses.
How then can a ruler
share power with his ministers to govern?
With the skill of Tián Lián and Chéng Qiào,
they could not produce a melody by playing the zither together.
How then can a ruler
share authority with his ministers to achieve success?

Argument Two:
King Zhāo of Qín was ill,
The common people in the lì (里) bought oxen

Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) went out and saw this,

and praying for the king!"
The king sent someone to inquire about it,
and it was indeed the case.
The king said:
"Fine each of those people two jiǎ (甲).
To presumptuously pray without an order
is to love me.
If they love me,
and I were to change the law
so that my heart followed theirs,
then the law would not stand;
if the law does not stand,
it is the path to chaos and ruin.
It is better to fine each person two jiǎ (甲)
and then continue to govern them."

Even though I am fond of fish,

This clarifies that relying on others is not as good as relying on oneself,
and that relying on others to act on one's behalf
is not as good as acting on one's own behalf.
The third persuasive argument:
"When you, Zǐ, were the prime minister of Yān,
you were esteemed, and you were in charge of decisions."
Sū Dài was the envoy of Qí to Yān,
and the King asked him,
"“Qí Wáng (齊王), what kind of ruler is he?”
He replied,
“He certainly will not achieve hegemony.”
Yān Wáng (燕王) said,
“Why?”
He replied,
“In the past, when Duke Huán (桓公) achieved hegemony,
internal affairs were entrusted to Bào Shū (鮑叔),
and external affairs were entrusted to Guǎn Zhòng (管仲).
Duke Huán let his hair down and attended to women,
and spent his days playing in the marketplace.
Now, the Qí Wáng (齊王) does not trust his great ministers.”
Thereupon, Yān Wáng (燕王) increasingly trusted Zǐ Zhī (子之).
Zǐ Zhī (子之), upon hearing this,
sent someone to give Sū Dài (蘇代) one hundred *yì* of gold,
and listened to his instructions.
One account says:
Sū Dài (蘇代) was sent by Qí (齊) as an envoy to Yān (燕).
Realizing that it was beneficial to Zǐ Zhī (子之),
otherwise he would not be able to accomplish his mission and would have to return,
and the tribute would not be given,
therefore, he met with Yān Wáng (燕王),
and praised the Qí Wáng (齊王).
Yān Wáng (燕王) said,
“How is it that the Qí Wáng (齊王) is so virtuous?
Then will he surely become king?”
Sū Dài said, "
There's no time to save the state from ruin;
how can there be a king?"
The King of Yān said, "
What do you mean?"
He said, "
He doesn't distribute responsibilities equally among those he favors."
The King of Yān said, "
How do you know it will fall?"
He said, "
In the past, Qí Huán Gōng loved Guǎn Zhòng,
placed him in the position of 'Second Father,'
had him manage internal affairs,
and make decisions on external affairs.
He entrusted the entire state to him,
therefore he rectified the world once
and united the various lords nine times.
Now, the Qí sovereign does not distribute responsibilities equally among those he favors,
and that is why I know it will fall."
The King of Yān said, "
Now, I will entrust Zǐ Zhī;
the world has not heard of this yet, has it?"
Thereupon, the next day he held court
and listened to Zǐ Zhī.
Pān Shòu said to the King of Yān,
"Your Majesty would do well to yield the kingdom to Zǐzhī.
The reason people call Yáo wise
is because he yielded the empire to Xǔ Yóu.
Xǔ Yóu certainly would not accept it,
thus Yáo had the reputation of yielding to Xǔ Yóu,
but in reality, he did not lose the empire.
Now, Your Majesty yields the kingdom to Zǐzhī,
Zǐzhī certainly will not accept it,
thus Your Majesty has the reputation of yielding to Zǐzhī,
and is acting in the same way as Yáo."
Thereupon, the King of Yān entrusted the entire kingdom to
Zǐzhī, making Zǐzhī greatly esteemed.
Another account states:
Pān Shòu
was a recluse.
Yān sent someone to engage him.
Pān Shòu met with the King of Yān and said,
"Your servant fears Zǐzhī will be like Yì."
The king said,
"How so with Yì?"
He replied,
"In ancient times, when Yǔ died,
he was going to pass the empire to Yì.
The people of Qǐ then joined together to attack Yì and establish Qǐ.
Now, the king deeply trusts and loves Zǐzhī 子之,
and intends to pass the kingdom to him.
All the followers of the crown prince harbor resentment,
while not a single follower of Zǐzhī 子之
is in the court.
If the king unfortunately abandons his officials,
then Zǐzhī 子之 will only gain."
The king then collected the official seals,
and all officials above 300 *shí* 石 submitted them to Zǐzhī 子之,
making Zǐzhī 子之 greatly powerful.
The means by which a ruler reflects on himself are
the retainers of the feudal lords;
now, the retainers of the feudal lords
are all partisans of private households.
The means by which a ruler avoids shallowness and disgrace are
the hermits
and reclusive scholars;
now, the hermits and reclusive scholars
are all personal attendants of private households.
Why is this so?
Because the power to reward and punish lies with Zǐzhī 子之.
Therefore, Wú Zhāng 吳章 said:
"A ruler should not feign love or hate towards people.
If you feign love for someone,
you cannot hate them again;
if you feign hate for someone,
bù dé fù ài yě."
One says:
The King of Yān wanted to pass the state to Zǐ Zhī,
and asked Pān Shòu about it.
He replied,
"Yǔ loved Yì and entrusted the world to Yì,
but then he employed Qǐ's men as officials.
When he grew old,
he thought Qǐ was not worthy to be entrusted with the world,
so he nominally passed the world to Yì,
but the power was entirely in Qǐ's hands.
Later, Qǐ and his allies attacked Yì and seized the world from him.
Thus, Yǔ nominally passed the world to Yì,
but in reality, he was letting Qǐ take it for himself.
This shows that Yǔ was not as wise as Yáo and
Shùn.
Now, Your Majesty wants to pass the state to Zǐ Zhī,
but all the officials are men of the Heir Apparent.
This is nominally passing it to him, but in reality, letting the Heir Apparent take it for himself."
The King of Yān then collected the seals and
all those with salaries of three hundred shí or more turned them over to Zǐ Zhī,
and Zǐ Zhī became powerful.
Fāng Wú Zǐ said:
"I have heard of an ancient custom:
one should not ride in the same carriage with someone wearing the same clothing,
“One does not share a household with those not of one's own clan,
how much less should a ruler
borrow power and estrange himself from his own influence!"
Wú Zhāng 吳章 said to King Xuān of Hán 韓宣王:
"A ruler should not feign love for others,
and then suddenly hate them;
nor should he feign hatred for others,
and then suddenly love them.
Therefore, if the signs of feigned hatred and feigned love are revealed,
flatterers will seize upon this to praise and slander accordingly.
Even a wise ruler
cannot regain control,
much less one who sincerely lends out his authority!"
The King of Zhào 趙王 was strolling in a park.
His attendants brought a hare and a tiger to a halt,
glaring around with their eyes.
The King said:
"How hateful,
the tiger's eyes!"
His attendants said:
"The eyes of Lord Píngyáng 平陽君 are even more hateful than this.
Seeing this causes no harm,
but if one sees Lord Píngyáng's 平陽君 eyes like this,
then one is sure to die."
The next day,
Lord Píngyáng 平陽君 heard of this
and sent someone to kill the speaker,
and the King did not punish him.
The ruler of Wèi 衛君 entered the court of Zhōu 周.
The Zhōu 周 official asked his title,
He replied,
"A vassal named Qiáng."
The Zhōu official rejected him, saying,
"Vassals are not allowed to have the same name as the Son of Heaven."
The ruler of Wèi then changed his name himself, saying,
"A vassal named Huǐ."
Only then was he allowed to enter.
Zhòng Ní heard of it and said,
"How far-reaching is the prohibition and constraint!
Empty names are not lent to others,
how much more so actual affairs?"
Persuasion Four:
One who shakes a tree,
if he picks each leaf individually,
it will be laborious and incomplete.
If he strikes the base of the tree from left and right,
then all the leaves will shake.
If one shakes a tree by a deep pool,
the birds will be startled and fly high,
and the fish will be frightened and dive down.
One who is good at spreading nets pulls the main rope.
If he were to pick each of the ten thousand meshes one by one before catching anything,
that would be laborious and difficult;
Pulling the main rope of the net,
and the fish are already in the bag.
Therefore, officials
are the basis of the people,
and the main rope.
Therefore, the sage governs officials, not the people.
In rescuing a fire,
ordering officials to carry pots and jars and run to the fire
is the use of one person's strength;
wielding a whip and pointing and directing to urge people,
is controlling ten thousand men.
Therefore, the sage does not personally deal with trivial matters of the common people,
and the enlightened ruler does not personally engage in small tasks.
Zào Fù was once weeding when
a father and son passed by in a carriage.
The horse was startled and would not move.
The son got out of the carriage to pull the horse,
and the father and son pushed the carriage.
They asked Zào Fù to help them push the carriage.
Zào Fù then put away his tools,
He stopped and had them load it onto the cart.
He helped his son onto the cart.
Then he began to check the reins and hold the whip,
but did not use them.
Yet the horses all bolted.
If he were to employ Zào Fù 造父 but he couldn't control them,
even if he exhausted his strength and toiled
to help him push the cart,
the horses still wouldn't move.
Now, if he makes himself comfortable
and also loads the cart,
and has virtue toward the people,
then he has the skill to control them.
Therefore, the state
is the ruler's chariot;
power
is the ruler's horses.
Without the skill to control them,
even if he toils,
he still cannot avoid chaos.
With the skill to control them,
he lives in a place of ease and joy,
and also achieves the accomplishments of an emperor or king.
The hammer and anvil
Therefore, it is to level what is uneven;
the plank and frame
are used to correct what is not straight.
The law-making of the sage
is to level what is uneven
and correct what is not straight.
When Nào Chǐ was employed in Qí,
he pulled out the tendons of King Mǐn;
when Lǐ Duì was employed in Zhào,
he starved the Zhǔfù to death.
These two rulers
both failed to employ their hammers and anvils, planks and frames,
and therefore died under execution
and were laughed at by the world.
It is said:
entering Qí,
one only hears of Nào Chǐ and not of the King of Qí;
entering Zhào,
one only hears of Lǐ Duì and not of the King of Zhào.
Therefore, it is said:
if the ruler of men does not grasp the art,
then his authority will be light
and his ministers will usurp his fame.
It is said:
King Wǔlíng of Zhào had King Huìwén oversee the government,
Lǐ Duì 李兌 was the prime minister.
King Wǔlíng 武靈王 did not personally manage the power of life and death,
therefore he was held hostage by Lǐ Duì 李兌.
It is said:
Tián Yīng 田嬰 was the prime minister of Qí 齊.
Someone persuaded the king, saying:
"For the plans of the whole year,
if the king does not take a few days to listen to them himself,
then he will have no way to know the deceitful or inept actions of the officials."
The king said:
"Good."
Tián Yīng 田嬰 heard this,
and immediately requested the king to listen to his plans.
The king was about to listen to them,
so Tián Yīng 田嬰 ordered the officials to prepare the records of contracts, measures of capacity (斗 dǒu) and weight (石 dàn), and standards of measurement (參升 cān shēng).
The king personally listened to the accounts,
but he could not keep up with listening to them.
After stopping for a meal,
he sat down again,
not even stopping for supper.
Tián Yīng 田嬰 then said:
"These are matters that your ministers dare not neglect day and night throughout the year.
If the king listens to them in one evening,
then your ministers will be encouraged to work hard."
The king said:
"Yes."
Soon after, the king was already asleep.
The officials all drew their knives and scraped away the calculations of the signed contracts and measuring stones.
Wáng himself listened to it,
and chaos then began to arise.
Argument Five:
Now, Zī Zhèngzi pulls a handcart up a high ridge but cannot support it.
Zī Zhèng sits on the shaft and sings,
those in front stop,
those behind rush forward,
and the handcart then goes up.
If Zī Zhèng did not have the method to induce people,
then even if his body exhausted its strength to death,
the handcart still would not go up.
Now, that his body does not reach the point of toil and hardship
and the handcart still goes up,
is because he has the method to induce people.
Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ sent out tax collectors,
and the officials requested leniency or severity.
Jiǎnzhǔ said:
"Neither lenient nor severe.
If it is severe,
then the profit enters the ruler,
if it is lenient,
then the profit returns to the people.
"If the officials have no selfish interests, they will be upright."
Bó Yí (薄疑) said to Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ (趙簡主):
"Your lord's country is sated."
Jiǎnzhǔ (簡主) was delighted and asked with joy:
"How is that so?"
He replied:
"The treasuries are empty above,
the common people are poor and hungry below,
yet the corrupt officials are rich."
Duke Huán of Qí (齊桓公) traveled among the people's homes in disguise.
There was a man who was old and supported himself.
Duke Huán (桓公) asked him the reason.
He replied:
"I have three sons,
my family is poor and I have no means to provide them with wives,
the hired labor has not been returned."
Duke Huán (桓公) returned
and told Guǎn Zhòng (管仲).
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) said:
"If stored goods have decaying and discarded wealth,
then people will be hungry;
if there are resentful women in the palace,
then the people will have no wives."
Duke Huán (桓公) said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he discussed finding husbands for the women in the palace and marrying them off.
He issued an order to the people, saying:
"Men should marry at the age of twenty,
women should marry at the age of fifteen."
It is said:
Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) traveled incognito among the people.
There was one Lùmén Jì (鹿門稷),
who was seventy years old and had no wife.
Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) asked Guǎn Zhòng (管仲), saying:
"Are there people who are old and without wives?"
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) said:
"There is Lùmén Jì (鹿門稷),
who is seventy years old and still has no wife."
Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) said:
"What should be done to ensure he has a wife?"
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) said:
"I have heard that:
If those above accumulate wealth,
then the people and subjects below will surely be in poverty;
if there are resentful women in the palace,
then there will be old men without wives."
Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) said:
"Good."
He ordered in the palace,
"The women who have not yet been favored should be married off."
Thereupon, he ordered that men should marry at the age of twenty,
and women should marry at the age of fifteen.
Then there would be no resentful spinsters within,
and no single men without.
Yánlíng Zhuōzǐ rode a carriage adorned with blue dragons and embroidered patterns.
Hooks and ornaments were in the front,
and inlaid spurs were in the back.
When the horse wanted to advance, the hooks and ornaments restrained it;
when it wanted to retreat, the inlaid spurs pierced it.
The horse consequently went sideways.
Zàofù passed by and wept for it,
saying:
"The way people are governed in ancient times is also like this.
Rewards are meant to encourage them, yet destruction lies within them;
punishments are meant to restrain them, yet praise is added to them.
The people stand in the middle, not knowing where to go,
this is also what causes the sages to weep."
Another version says:
Yánlíng Zhuōzǐ rode a carriage adorned with blue dragons and pheasant-feather patterns.
In front there were inlaid ornaments,
and in back there were sharp spurs.
When it advanced, he pulled it back;
when it retreated, he whipped it.
The horse could not advance forward,
nor could it retreat backward,
so it avoided and ran away,
Consequently, he drew his knife and cut off his foot.
Zào Fù saw this,
and wept.
He said:
"Yánlíng Zhuōzǐ rides a blue dragon, as does Dí Wén’s carriage.
In front, there are ornate decorations;
behind, there are sharp chisel-like points.
When advancing, they are pulled;
when retreating, they are whipped.
The horse could not advance forward,
nor could it retreat backward,
so it evaded and fled,
and consequently drew its knife and cut off its foot."
Zào Fù saw this and wept,
not eating for the entire day.
Then he looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"The whip [cè] is
for advancing;
ornate decorations are in front.
The reins [yǐn] are
for retreating;
sharp chisel-like points are behind.
Now, the rulers advance people because of their purity,
and dismiss them because they don't suit those on the left and right.
They praise them for their impartiality, 〓#
Because he did not obey him, he deposed him.
The people were fearful,
remained neutral and did not know what to follow,
this is why the sage wept."
Difficulty One, Thirty-Sixth
Duke Wén of Jìn was about to fight with the people of Chǔ,
summoned Jiù Fàn and asked him,
saying:
"I am about to fight with the people of Chǔ,
they are many and we are few,
what should be done?"
Jiù Fàn said:
"Your servant has heard:
a gentleman of elaborate etiquette
is never tired of loyalty and trustworthiness;
in the midst of battles,
one is never tired of deception and trickery.
Your lord should just deceive them."
Duke Wén dismissed Jiù Fàn,
and then summoned Yōng Jì and asked him,
saying:
"I am about to fight with the people of Chǔ,
they are many and we are few,
what should be done?"
Yōng Jì replied:
"To burn the forest for hunting,
to stealthily take many beasts,
afterwards there will surely be no beasts;
to treat the people with deception,
to stealthily take for a time,
"It is fitting that Duke Wén became a hegemon!
Fitting indeed!
He understood both the expedient measures of the moment
and the long-term benefits for generations to come."
Some say:
Yōng Jì's reply
was not appropriate to Duke Wén's question.
All replies to questions
are given in accordance with the importance, magnitude, urgency of the question.
If the question is lofty and grand,
but the reply is low and narrow,
then an enlightened ruler will not accept it.
Now, Duke Wén asked
"how to encounter a large force with a small one,"
but the reply was,
"there must be no recurrence in the future."
This is not a suitable response.
Moreover, Duke Wén did not understand the expedient measures of the moment,
nor did he understand the long-term benefits for generations to come.
If he fought and won,
then the state would be secure and his position stable,
his army would be strong and his prestige established.
Even if there were recurrences in the future,
nothing would be greater than this.
What worry would there be that the benefits for generations to come
would not arrive?
To fight and not win
, then the state will be ruined and the army weakened
, one's body will die and one's name cease to exist
. Even brushing away today's death is unattainable
, how can one have leisure to wait for the benefits of ten thousand generations?
Waiting for the benefits of ten thousand generations
lies in today's victory
; today's victory
lies in deceiving the enemy
; deceiving the enemy
is simply the benefit of ten thousand generations.
Therefore, it is said:
Yōng Jì's 雍季 answer
was not appropriate to Duke Wén's 文公 question.
Moreover, Duke Wén 文公 did not understand what Jiù Fàn 舅犯 said.
What Jiù Fàn 舅犯 meant by
"never being tired of deception and falsehood"
was
not to deceive his own people
, but to deceive his enemies.
The enemy
is the state to be attacked
; even if there is no recovery afterward
, what harm is there?
As for why Duke Wén [Wén Gōng] prioritized Yōng Jì [雍季],
was it because of his merit?
Then, regarding the victory over Chǔ [楚] and the defeat of its army,
it was Jiù Fàn's [舅犯] strategy.
Was it because of his skillful words?
Then Yōng Jì [雍季] only spoke of
"later without repeating,"
and this cannot be considered skillful speech.
This is not skillful speech.
Jiù Fàn [舅犯] possessed both of these qualities.
Jiù Fàn [舅犯] said,
"A gentleman of elaborate rituals
does not tire of loyalty and trustworthiness,"
loyalty
is the way to love one's subordinates;
trustworthiness
is the way to not deceive one's people.
is the way to not deceive one's people.
Since he both loved and did not deceive,
what speech is better than this?
Yet if one must say it "arose from deceit and falsehood,"
it was a military strategy.
Jiù Fàn [舅犯] had skillful words beforehand
and victory in battle afterward.
Thus Jiù Fàn [舅犯] had two merits and was assessed later,
while Yōng Jì [雍季] did nothing and was rewarded first.
"Wasn't it fitting that Duke Wén became a hegemon?"
Zhòng Ní (Confucius) didn't understand proper rewards.
The farmers of Mount Lì were encroaching on boundaries.
Shùn went and farmed there.
After a year,
the ditches and fields were straightened.
The fishermen on the riverbank were fighting over the sandbars.
Shùn went and fished there.
After a year, they yielded to their elders.
The potters of the Eastern 夷 (Yí) made utensils that were poorly made.
Shùn went and made pottery there.
After a year, the utensils were sturdy.
Zhòng Ní sighed and said,
"Farming,
fishing, and pottery
were not Shùn's official duties,
but the reason Shùn went to do them
was to remedy the failures.
Shùn was truly trustworthy in benevolence!
He personally began to cultivate and dwell in hardship,
and the people followed him.
Therefore it is said:
The virtue of a sage transforms people!"
Someone asked a Confucian scholar,
"At this very time,
where is Yáo?"
The man said,
"Yáo is the Son of Heaven."
"If that is so,
how does Zhòngní's (Confucius) sagacity compare to that of Yáo?
A sage with clear discernment in a high position
will ensure that there is no treachery in the world.
Now, if farmers and fishermen do not quarrel,
and pottery is not flawed,
what virtue does Shùn possess that transformed them?
Shùn's rescuing of failures
means that Yáo had shortcomings.
If you praise Shùn,
then you diminish Yáo's clear discernment;
if you praise Sage Yáo,
then you diminish Shùn's virtuous transformation;
you cannot have both.
There was a man of Chǔ who was selling shields and spears.
He praised them, saying:
'My shields are so sturdy
that nothing can pierce them.'
He also praised his spears, saying:
'My spears are so sharp
that there is nothing they cannot pierce.'
Someone asked:
"Using your spear to pierce your shield,
what would happen?"
That person was unable to answer.
A shield that cannot be pierced
and a spear that can pierce anything
cannot exist in the same era.
Today, Yáo
and Shùn cannot both be praised equally;
this is the "spear and shield" argument.
Moreover, Shùn rescuing defeats,
one year already passed once,
and three years already passed three times.
Shùn's abilities are finite,
his lifespan is finite,
but the world's problems are endless;
using the finite to chase the endless,
those who cease are few.
Rewards and punishments should make the world certainly follow them.
Issue an order, saying:
"Those who meet the standard will be rewarded,
those who do not meet the standard will be punished."
If the order changes from morning to evening,
and from evening to morning,
the entire country would be finished in ten days.
Why wait for a year?
Shùn still didn't use this argument to persuade Yáo to follow him.
Instead, he personally labored.
Isn't this lacking in skill?
Moreover, for one to personally endure hardship
and then transform the people,
this is what Yáo and Shùn found difficult.
To use one's position to correct those below,
this is what mediocre rulers find easy.
If one intends to govern the world,
but abandons what mediocre rulers find easy,
and follows what Yáo
and Shùn found difficult,
then one cannot be entrusted with governance."
Guǎn Zhòng fell ill.
Duke Huán went to inquire about his health,
and said:
"If Zhòngfù's illness
unfortunately leads to his demise,
what advice will you give to me?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Even without your words,
I was about to request this.
I hope Your Lordship will dismiss Shù Diāo,
eliminate Yì Yá,
and keep distant from Wèi's Gōngzǐ Kāifāng.
Yì Yá 以為 the ruler's taste,
the ruler had only never tasted human flesh.
Yì Yá steamed his son's head and presented it.
Of all human feelings, none do not love their children;
now he doesn't love his child,
how can he love the ruler?
The ruler was jealous and fond of the inner palace,
shù Diāo castrated himself to manage the inner palace.
Of all human feelings, none do not love their own body;
he doesn't even love his own body,
how can he love the ruler?
Kāi Fāng served the ruler for fifteen years.
The distance between Qí and Wèi was not more than a few days' journey,
he abandoned his mother,
and served as an official for a long time without returning home.
He doesn't love his mother,
how can he love the ruler?
Your servant has heard it said:
"Pretentious falsehoods do not last long;
indeed, emptiness does not endure for long."
I wish the ruler would remove these three men."
Guǎn Zhòng died in the end,
Duke Huán did not act on it.
When Duke Huán died,
worms came out of the door, and he was not buried.
Someone may say:
Guǎn Zhòng's 管仲 advice to Duke Huán 桓公
was not the speech of a person with measured judgment.
The reason he wanted to get rid of Shù Diāo 豎刁
and Yì Yá 易牙
was because they didn't cherish their own bodies
in order to satisfy the ruler's desires.
He said,
"If they don't cherish their own bodies,
how can they cherish the ruler?"
In that case, would Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 not employ a subject
who exerts all their strength and effort for their lord?
He would say,
"If they don't value their own lives,
how can they cherish the ruler?"
This is wanting the ruler to get rid of loyal ministers.
Furthermore, to assume that someone does not cherish their ruler
because they do not cherish their own body,
is like judging that Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 would not die for Duke Huán 桓公
based on his failure to die for Gōngzǐ Jiū 公子糾.
In that case, Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 would also be among those to be dismissed.
The way of a wise ruler is not like this.
He establishes what the people desire in order to attain their service,
therefore he establishes titles and stipends to encourage them.
He establishes what the people hate in order to prevent their transgressions,
therefore he establishes punishments to deter them.
If rewards are trustworthy and punishments are certain,
then the ruler ascribes achievements to his ministers,
and treachery cannot be employed against the superior.
Even if there is Shù Diāo,
what can he do to the ruler?
Moreover, ministers exert their utmost strength
to barter with the ruler,
and the ruler bestows rank and emolument
to barter with his ministers.
The relationship between ruler and minister
is not the intimacy of father and son,
but arises from calculation.
If the ruler has the Dao,
then the ministers exert their strength and treachery does not arise;
if he lacks the Dao,
then the ministers above block the ruler's discernment
and below form private cliques.
If Guǎn Zhòng did not make this standard clear
to Duke Huán,
merely removing Shù Diāo
would only lead to another Shù Diāo appearing;
it is not the way to eliminate treachery.
Moreover, the reason Duke Huán died
and maggots flowed out the door unburied
is that his ministers were powerful.
Chén Zhòng's power,
is usurping the ruler's authority.
If there is a minister who usurps the ruler's authority,
then the ruler's commands will not reach the lowest levels,
and the minister's feelings will not be communicated upwards.
The power of one person can separate the ruler and his ministers,
causing success and failure to be unheard of,
and fortune and misfortune to be uncommunicated,
therefore there is the danger of not being buried (of losing the state).
The way of an enlightened ruler:
one person does not hold multiple offices,
one office does not handle multiple affairs;
the lowly and humble do not wait for the honored and noble to advance,
great ministers are not seen through the attendants;
all officials are properly connected,
all ministers converge like spokes of a wheel;
when there are rewards, the ruler sees their merit,
when there are punishments, the ruler knows their crime.
Seeing and knowing are not contrary to the past,
and rewards and punishments are not corrupted in the future,
how can there be the danger of not being buried?
Guǎn Zhòng did not make this clear to Duke Huán,
causing him to dismiss the three men,
therefore it is said:
Guǎn Zhòng lacked proper measure.
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 was besieged in Jìnyáng 晉陽.
When he broke out of the siege,
he rewarded five men who had rendered meritorious service.
Gāo Hè 高赫 was ranked first among those rewarded.
Zhāng Mèngtán 張孟談 said,
"In the matter of Jìnyáng 晉陽,
Hè 赫 had no great merit.
Now he is ranked first among those rewarded,
why is that?"
Xiāngzǐ 襄子 said,
"In the matter of Jìnyáng 晉陽,
my state was in danger,
and the altars of the state were imperiled.
None of my ministers did not have thoughts of arrogance and disrespect,
only Hèzi 赫子 did not lose the proper etiquette between ruler and subject,
therefore I put him first."
Zhòngní 仲尼 heard of this and said,
"What a good reward,
Xiāngzǐ 襄子!
By rewarding one person, those who are ministers in the world will not dare to lose their sense of propriety."
Someone said,
"Zhòngní 仲尼 does not understand good rewards.
Those who are good at rewards and punishments
ensure that the officials do not overstep their duties,
and that the ministers do not lose their sense of propriety.
The ruler establishes the laws,
and those below have no deceitful hearts.
If it is like this,
then it can be said that rewards and punishments are well-administered.
When you sent Xiāng Zǐ to Jìnyáng,
orders were not carried out,
prohibitions were not stopped,
it was as if Xiāng Zǐ had no state,
and Jìnyáng had no ruler.
Then with whom would they defend it?
Now, when Xiāng Zǐ is in Jìnyáng,
the Zhī clan flooded it,
turtles grew in the mortar and stove,
yet the people had no rebellious thoughts,
this is because the ruler and his subjects are close.
Xiāng Zǐ possessed the grace of closeness between ruler and subjects,
wielded the law of commands being carried out and prohibitions being enforced,
and yet still had arrogant and disrespectful ministers,
this is because Xiāng Zǐ's punishments were flawed.
For ministers,
if they achieve merit by undertaking tasks, then they should be rewarded.
Now, Hè barely avoided being arrogant and disrespectful,
and yet Xiāng Zǐ rewarded him,
this is a flawed reward.
An enlightened ruler does not bestow rewards on those without merit,
and punishments are not applied to those without guilt.
Now Xiāngzǐ does not punish arrogant and disrespectful ministers,
but rewards those who have no merit with great honors.
Where is Xiāngzǐ's goodness in rewarding?
Therefore, it is said
"Zhòng Ní does not know good rewards."
Duke Píng of Jìn was drinking with his ministers.
When the drinking was at its height,
he sighed and said,
"Nothing is more joyful than being a ruler,
because whatever I say, no one dares to disobey."
Shī Kuàng was attending him, sitting in front,
and he took his qín and struck him with it.
The duke pulled back his robe and avoided the blow,
and the qín broke against the wall.
The duke said,
"Grand Music Master, whom did you strike?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"Just now, there was a petty man speaking by your side,
so I struck him."
The duke said,
"It was I."
Shī Kuàng said,
"Ah!
These are not the words of a man who should be a ruler."
The attendants on the left and right requested that he be removed.
The Duke said,
"Release him,
and let it be a warning to me."
Someone said,
"Píng Gōng 平公 has lost the way of a ruler,
and Shī Kuàng 師曠 has failed in the propriety of a minister.
To punish one's person for something other than their actions,
that is how a ruler treats his ministers.
If it is not their action,
then they present their words.
If good advice is not heeded,
then those who distance themselves,
that is how a minister treats his ruler.
Now, Shī Kuàng 師曠 criticizes the actions of Píng Gōng 平公,
does not offer the counsel of a minister,
but carries out the punishment of a ruler,
raising his qin and striking his person directly.
This reverses the positions of superior and inferior,
and violates the propriety of a minister.
As for being a minister,
when the ruler has faults, he should be advised.
If the advice is not heeded,
then one should regard rank and salary lightly and wait for the ruler to change.
This is the propriety of a minister.
Now, Shī Kuàng 師曠 does not point out Píng Gōng's 平公 faults,
To hold a qín (琴) and caress its body,
even a stern father would not do this to his son.
Yet Shī Kuàng (師曠) did it to his ruler.
This is a technique of great disobedience.
The subject performing great disobedience,
Duke Píng (平公) happily listened to it,
this is losing the way of a ruler.
Therefore, Duke Píng's (平公) actions cannot be clearly praised,
lest it cause rulers to excessively listen
without realizing their errors.
Shī Kuàng's (師曠) actions also cannot be clearly praised,
lest treacherous ministers imitate extreme remonstrance
and embellish the path to assassinating the ruler.
One cannot call both "clear,"
as this constitutes two faults.
Therefore, it is said:
Duke Píng (平公) lost the way of a ruler,
Shī Kuàng (師曠) also lost the proper conduct of a subject.
During the time of Duke Huán of Qí (齊桓公),
there was a recluse called Xiǎochén Jì (小臣稷).
Duke Huán (桓公) went to see him three times but failed to meet him.
Duke Huán (桓公) said:
"I have heard that a commoner,
who does not lightly value rank and emolument,
cannot be easily exchanged for a ruler of ten thousand chariots.
"A ruler of ten thousand chariots,
if he does not favor benevolence and righteousness,
will not be able to associate with even humble commoners."
Therefore, it took five visits to finally be granted an audience.
Someone said:
"Duke Huán does not understand benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness consist of
worrying about the harm to the whole world,
rushing to the troubles of one's country,
not avoiding lowliness and humiliation;
this is called benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, Yī Yǐn, because the central states were in disarray
and losing their way,
became the cook and advisor to Tāng;
Bǎi Lǐxī, because Qín was in disarray
and losing its way,
became a captive and advisor to Duke Mù of Qín.
Both worried about the harm to the whole world,
rushed to the troubles of their countries,
and did not refuse lowliness and humiliation;
therefore, they are called benevolent and righteous.
Now, Duke Huán, with the power of ten thousand chariots,
condescends to commoners,
intending to worry about the state of Qí,
yet this petty subject does not comply.
This shows that this petty subject forgets the people.
To disregard the people cannot be called benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence and righteousness are
not losing the propriety of a minister toward his ruler,
and not undermining the positions of ruler and minister.
Therefore, within the boundaries of the state,
those who hold birds to offer as tribute are called subjects,
and the subordinate officials who are assigned duties and receive tasks are called the common people (méng).
Now, this petty minister, being among the common people,
goes against the desires of his ruler,
therefore he cannot be called benevolent and righteous.
Benevolence and righteousness are not present in him,
yet Duke Huán still proceeds to treat him with ceremony.
If this petty minister has intelligence and evades Duke Huán,
this is a form of reclusion,
and he deserves punishment.
If he has no intelligence
and falsely and arrogantly insults Duke Huán,
this is a form of deceit,
and he deserves execution.
This petty minister's actions
deserve either punishment or execution.
Duke Huán is unable to grasp the principles of ruler and subject,
yet he treats someone deserving punishment or execution with ceremony.
This is Duke Huán teaching the custom of disrespecting superiors and insulting the ruler to the state of Qí,
which is not the way to govern.
Thus it is said:
Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) did not understand benevolence and righteousness.
During the Mí Jī (Mí Jī) campaign,
Hán Xiànzǐ (韓獻子) was about to execute a man.
Xì Xiànzǐ (郄獻子) heard of it
and drove his chariot to go and save him.
By the time he arrived,
the man had already been executed.
Xìzǐ (郄子) then said:
"Why not parade him?"
His servant said:
"Weren't you going to save him earlier?"
Xìzǐ (郄子) said:
"How dare I not share the blame?"
Someone said:
Xìzǐ's (郄子) words
must be carefully examined;
it was not about sharing the blame.
If the one whom Hànzǐ (韓子) executed
was indeed a criminal,
then he should not have been saved.
Saving a criminal
is how the law is ruined;
when the law is ruined, the state is in chaos.
If he was not a criminal,
Otherwise, one should not encourage it with *xùn*.
To encourage it with *xùn*
is to double the injustice.
Doubling the injustice
is what causes the people to harbor resentment.
When the people resent, the state is endangered.
The words of Xì Zǐ
are either "danger" or "chaos",
one cannot but examine them carefully.
Moreover, if what Hán Zǐ beheaded were criminals,
what share does Xì Zǐ have in it?
If what was beheaded were not criminals,
then they have already been beheaded.
Yet Xì Zǐ arrives only now,
this means Hán Zǐ's slander has already been established,
and Xì Zǐ is arriving late.
Furthermore, Xì Zǐ says
"to be buried alive (*xùn*)
is not enough to share in the slander of beheading people,
but rather it gives rise to the slander of live burial (*xùn*).
Is this what you call sharing the slander?
In the past, Zhòu created the burning pillar punishment,
Chóng Hóu
and È Lái also said
"cut off the shins of those who wade across."
How does that share in the slander of Zhòu?
Moreover, the people's expectations of their superiors are extremely high.
If Hán Zǐ cannot obtain something,
they will expect Qiè Zǐ to obtain it.
Now, if Qiè Zǐ also cannot obtain it,
then the people will lose all hope in their superiors.
Therefore, it is said:
Qiè Zǐ's words do not divide the blame,
but increase it.
Furthermore, Qiè Zǐ went to rescue him from his crime,
because he considered Hán Zǐ to be wrong.
However, he did not explain why he was wrong,
but instead urged him
"to commit suicide,"
which is to make Hán Zǐ unaware of his mistakes.
If superiors cause the people to lose all hope in them,
and also cause Hán Zǐ to be unaware of his faults,
I have not understood how Qiè Zǐ divides the blame.
Duke Huán released Guǎn Zhòng from his bonds and appointed him as his prime minister.
Guǎn Zhòng said,
"Your servant is favored,
but I am lowly."
The Duke said,
"I will make you stand above Gāo
and the state."
Guǎn Zhòng said,
"Your servant is honored,
"However, I, your servant, am poor."
The Duke said,
"I will grant you a household with triple the income."
Guǎn Zhòng said,
"I am rich now,
however, I, your servant, am distant."
Thereupon, he was established as Zhòngfǔ (Second Father).
Xiāo Lüè said,
"Guǎn Zhòng considered that one who is of low status cannot govern those of high status,
therefore, he requested being above Gāo
and Guó;
considering that one who is poor cannot govern the rich,
therefore, he requested a triple income;
considering that one who is distant cannot govern relatives,
therefore, he assumed the position of Zhòngfǔ.
Guǎn Zhòng was not greedy,
but seeking to facilitate governance."
Someone said,
"Now, if a servant is ordered to deliver the ruler's commands and decrees to the ministers and counselors,
none would dare disobey,
it is not that the ministers and counselors are inferior and the servant is superior,
but the ruler's command is imposed,
and none would dare not follow.
Now, if Guǎn Zhòng's governance
did not rely on Duke Huán,
It is the same as having no ruler.
If a state has no ruler,
it cannot be governed.
If one relies on the authority of Duke Huán (Huán Gōng),
and issues orders in the name of Duke Huán (Huán Gōng),
then even a servant or slave can be believed.
Why wait for the honor of Gāo,
Guó, or the paternal uncle Zhòngfù (仲父)
before acting?
Those who carry out affairs in the current era,
and the officials who collect taxes and issue commands,
do not avoid the honored and noble,
nor do they yield to the lowly and base.
Therefore, if laws are executed lawfully,
even a commoner in the lanes will trust the ministers;
if laws are executed unlawfully,
even high officials will be defeated by the common people.
Now, Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) did not focus on honoring the ruler and clarifying the laws,
but instead devoted himself to increasing favor and adding ranks.
If this is not because Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) was greedy for wealth and honor,
it must be because he was ignorant and did not understand strategy.
Therefore it is said:
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) had faulty conduct,
and Xiāo Lüè (霄略) was excessively praised.
King Xuān (宣王) of Hán (韓) asked Jiū Liú (樛留):
"I wish to employ both Gōngzhòng and
Gōngshū;
is that acceptable?"
Jiūliú replied,
"In the past, Wèi employed both Lóu and
Dí,
and lost Xīhé.
Chǔ employed both Zhāo and
Jǐng,
and lost Yān and
Yǐng.
Now, if you, my lord, employ both Gōngzhòng and
Gōngshū,
they will surely compete for affairs and seek external influence,
then the state will surely be troubled."
Someone said:
"In the past, Qí's Huán Gōng employed both Guǎn Zhòng and
Bào Shū;
Chéng Tāng employed both Yī Yǐn and
Zhòng Huī.
If employing two ministers is a source of worry for the state,
then Huán Gōng would not have become a hegemon,
and Chéng Tāng would not have become a king.
Mǐn Wáng solely employed Nào Chǐ
and died in the Eastern Temple;
Zhǔ Fù solely employed Lǐ Duì,
reduced his food, and died.
When a ruler possesses *shù* (skill/method),
employing two (officials/methods) does not cause trouble;
lacking *shù*,
employing two then leads to disputes over matters and external bidding,
while employing one leads to autocratic control
and usurpation.
Now, advising the ruler, lacking *shù*,
to eliminate two (officials/methods) and employ one,
if it does not lead to the worries of Xī Hé (西河),
Yān (鄢), and Yǐng (郢),
then it will certainly lead to the misfortune of death and reduced sustenance.
Thus, Jiū Liú (樛留) has not used wisdom to understand language well.
Difficulty Two, Section Thirty-Seven
Jǐng Gōng (景公) visited Àn Zǐ (晏子) and
said:
"Your house is small,
near the market.
I request to move your family to the Yùzhāng (豫章) gardens."
Àn Zǐ (晏子) bowed twice and declined, saying:
"Moreover, my family is poor,
relying on the market for food,
and I must hasten there morning and evening;
I cannot be far away."
Jǐng Gōng (景公) laughed and said:
"Since your family is accustomed to the market,
"Can you distinguish between the noble and the lowly?"
At that time, Jǐng Gōng was excessive in his punishments.
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"The price of *yǒng* (綁腿，leg wrappings) is high, while the price of *jù* (麻鞋，hemp shoes) is low."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"Because there are many punishments."
Jǐng Gōng suddenly changed color and said:
"Am I being tyrannical!"
Thereupon, he reduced the number of punishments by five.
Someone said:
Yàn Zǐ's valuing of *yǒng*
was not sincere;
he merely wanted to use a convenient excuse
to stop the excessive punishments.
This is a problem of not understanding governance.
Punishments should not be too many,
but should not be too few either.
Not addressing what is inappropriate,
but arguing only about the quantity being too great,
is the problem of lacking skill.
Punishing defeated armies by the hundreds or thousands,
yet their retreat does not stop.
If punishments for governing chaos
If you fear you cannot overcome the evil,
and the wrongdoing still isn't completely eradicated,
now, Yàn Zǐ 晏子 doesn't examine whether it's appropriate or not,
but uses "too much" as his argument,
isn't that absurd?
For cherishing weeds diminishes the grain's harvest,
and favoring thieves injures good people.
Now, easing punishments
and practicing leniency
is benefiting the wicked and harming the good;
this is not the way to govern.
Duke Huán of Qí 齊桓公, drunk with wine,
lost his hat,
and was ashamed of it,
so he did not hold court for three days.
Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 said,
"This is a disgrace to the state,
why doesn't Your Grace wipe it away with good governance?"
The Duke said,
"That's a good idea!"
So he opened the granaries,
bestowed gifts on the poor,
reviewed the prisoners,
and released those with minor offenses.
After three days, the people sang a song saying,
"Gōng hú bù fù yí guān hū!"
Someone said:
Guǎn Zhòng snowed the shame of Duke Huán upon petty men,
and produced the shame of Duke Huán upon gentlemen.
If Duke Huán had opened granaries
and bestowed gifts upon the poor,
examined prisons
and released those with minor offenses,
if it were not righteous,
it would not be able to wash away the shame;
if causing him to do so was righteous,
and Duke Huán harbored righteousness,
waiting to lose his cap before carrying it out,
then Duke Huán was acting righteously,
not because of losing his cap?
This, although washing away the shame of losing the cap among petty men,
would also produce the shame of abandoning righteousness among gentlemen.
Moreover, opening granaries and bestowing gifts upon the poor,
is rewarding those without merit;
examining prisons and releasing those with minor offenses,
is not punishing transgressions.
Rewarding those without merit,
then the people will greedily hope for favor from above;
not punishing transgressions,
then the people will not be deterred and will easily commit wrongdoings.
This is the root of disorder.
How can one wipe away shame in this way?
In the past, King Wén Wáng attacked Méng,
conquered Jǔ,
and captured Fēng.
After these three undertakings, Zhòu resented him.
King Wén Wáng then became fearful
and offered to cede land west of the Luò River,
a state with red soil,
a thousand *lǐ* square,
to request the abolishment of the *páo luò* torture.
Everyone in the world was pleased.
Zhòng Ní heard of this
and said,
"How benevolent,
King Wén Wáng!
He valued lightly a thousand *lǐ* of land
to request the abolishment of the *páo luò* torture.
How wise,
King Wén Wáng!
He gave up a thousand *lǐ* of land
and won the hearts of the world."
Someone said:
Is it not an overstatement that Zhòng Ní considers Wén Wáng wise?
Now, the wise
are those who recognize dangerous and troublesome places and avoid them,
thereby keeping themselves from harm.
If the reason King Wén Wáng was disliked by Zhòu
was because he did not have the people's support,
then even seeking the people's support
to dispel the dislike would be acceptable.
But Zhòu disliked him because he greatly had the people's support,
and he had already lightened the land
to gather the people's hearts.
This is doubling his suspicion,
which is why he was shackled and imprisoned in Yǒulǐ.
A senior official of Zhèng once said:
"To embody the Dao
is to be without action and without appearance."
This is most suitable for King Wén Wáng,
so as not to cause people to suspect him.
Zhòng Ní (Confucius) considered Wén Wáng wise,
but he did not reach this conclusion.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shū Xiàng,
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí united the feudal lords nine times
and rectified the world.
I don't know if it was due to the power of his ministers
or the power of the ruler?"
Shū Xiàng replied,
"Guǎn Zhòng was good at cutting and dividing,
Bīn Xūwú was skilled at cutting seams,
Xí Péng was skilled at edging hems.
Once the garment was complete,
the ruler would lift it and wear it.
"This is also due to the efforts of your ministers;
what effort have you, the ruler, exerted?"
Shī Kuàng leaned over his qín (zither) and laughed at this.
The duke said,
"Grand Master, why do you laugh?"
Shī Kuàng replied,
"I laugh at Shū Xiàng's response to you, my lord.
Generally, those who serve as ministers
are like cooks who prepare and blend the five flavors and present them to the ruler.
If the ruler does not eat them,
who would dare to force him?
Allow me to use an analogy:
the ruler
is the soil;
the ministers
are the grass and trees.
Only if the soil is fertile
can the grass and trees grow large.
This is also due to the ruler's strength;
what strength have the ministers exerted?"
Some say:
Shū Xiàng,
and Shī Kuàng's replies
were both biased statements.
To rectify the world once,
and unite the lords nine times,
is the greatest of achievements,
but it is not solely the power of the ruler,
nor is it solely the power of the minister.
In the past, Gōng Zhīqí was in Yú,
and Xī Fùjī was in Cáo.
With the wisdom of these two ministers,
their words hit the mark,
and their actions produced results,
yet Yú and Cáo both perished.
Why?
This is because they had their ministers but lacked their rulers.
Furthermore, Jiǎn Shū, when he was in Gān, Gān perished,
but when he was in Qín, Qín became dominant.
It was not that Jiǎn Shū was more foolish in Gān
and more intelligent in Qín;
it was a matter of having a ruler versus not having a ruler.
Shū Xiàng said
"It was the minister's power,"
but that is not so.
In the past, Duke Huán had two markets inside his palace,
He had two hundred women's quarters,
and let the women wear their hair down and manage the women.
Having gotten Guǎn Zhòng,
he became the leader of the Five Hegemons;
losing Guǎn Zhòng,
and getting Shù Diāo,
he died,
and maggots flowed out of the door, and he was not buried.
To think that it was not the minister's power,
and not to regard Guǎn Zhòng as a hegemon;
to think that it was the ruler's power,
and not to regard Shù Diāo as a source of chaos.
In the past,
Duke Wén of Jìn was enamored with a daughter of Qí
and forgot to return home.
Jiù Fàn vehemently remonstrated,
therefore causing him to return to the state of Jìn.
Therefore, Duke Huán succeeded with Guǎn Zhòng,
and Duke Wén achieved hegemony with Jiù Fàn.
But Shī Kuàng said
"It is the ruler's power,"
which is again not so.
All of the Five Hegemons were able to achieve fame and success in the world
because both ruler and minister had power.
Therefore, it is said:
The responses of Shū Xiàng [叔向] and
Shī Kuàng [師曠] were both one-sided arguments.
During the time of Duke Huán of Qí [齊桓公],
a guest from Jìn [晉] arrived,
and the officials requested instructions on etiquette.
Duke Huán
said "Inform Zhòngfù [仲父]"
three times.
And a jester laughed and said:
"How easy it is
to be a ruler!
One says Zhòngfù,
two says Zhòngfù."
Duke Huán
said: "I have heard
'A ruler is burdened by seeking men,
but rests easy in employing men.'
It was already difficult for me to obtain Zhòngfù,
after obtaining Zhòngfù,
why would it not be easy?"
Someone said:
What Duke Huán said to the jester
is not the language of a ruler.
Duke Huán considered ruling to be burdened by seeking men,
Why seek to trouble people with labor?
Yī Yǐn 伊尹 considered himself a kitchen manager for Tāng 湯,
and Bǎi Lǐxī 百里奚 considered himself a captive manager for Duke Mù of Qín 秦穆公.
"Captive" is a term of humiliation;
"kitchen manager" is a term of shame.
To endure shame and humiliation in order to serve one's lord,
this is the urgency with which the wise are concerned about the world.
Therefore, the ruler of men must not oppose the wise,
seeking out the wise is not difficult for a ruler.
Furthermore, offices and positions
are the means by which to employ the worthy;
titles and emoluments
are the means by which to reward merit.
Establish offices and positions,
display titles and emoluments,
and scholars will naturally come;
why should the ruler of men labor?
Employing people is also not effortless.
Even when the ruler employs people,
he must measure them by standards,
and compare them using punishments and titles;
if matters align with the law, then proceed;
if they do not align with the law, then stop;
if merit matches their words, then reward;
if it does not match, then punish.
To employ officials based on penal law,
and to judge subordinates with fixed standards,
these are things that cannot be relinquished.
