Unimportant people use high ranks and generous salaries to entice them.
If the ranks and salaries of wicked people are high,
their followers will become even more numerous,
and if they also have wicked intentions,
then the wicked minister will turn around and persuade them,
saying:
"The so-called sage rulers and enlightened kings of ancient times
did not come to power through seniority, hereditary succession, or following the proper order.
[They did it] by forming factions,
gathering their clans,
coercing and assassinating the ruler
to seek their own advantage."
They say:
"How do you know this is the case?"
Then he says:
"Shùn *bī* Yáo,
Yǔ *bī* Shùn,
Tāng *fàng* Jié,
Wǔwáng *fá* Zhòu.
These four kings,
were ministers who murdered their lords,
yet the world praised them.
Examining the motives of the four kings,
it was a desire for selfish gain;
judging their actions,
they were armies of violent rebellion.
However, the four kings sought to expand themselves,
and the world called them great;
they sought to make their names known,
and the world called them enlightened.
So, their power was enough to oversee the world,
their benefit was enough to cover the age,
and the world followed them."
It is further said:
"According to what we hear in the present day,
Tián Chéngzǐ seized Qi,
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn seized Song,
Tàizǎi Xīn seized Zheng,
the Dān clan seized Zhou,
Yìyá seized Wei,
and the three sons of Han, Wei, and Zhao divided Jin.
These eight people
are those ministers who murdered their lords."
When treacherous ministers hear this,
they prick up their ears and think it is right.
Therefore, they inwardly form cliques and factions,
and outwardly extend their influence to clans and families in the lanes.
They observe the times and launch their schemes,
seizing the state in one fell swoop.
Moreover, they inwardly use cliques and factions to coerce and murder their lords,
and outwardly use the power of the feudal lords
to fraudulently change their state.
They obscure the correct path,
uphold selfish and crooked principles,
restrain their superiors (the rulers),
and disrupt those who govern below.
They are too numerous to count.
Why is this so?
It is because they are not discerning in selecting ministers.
The records say:
"Since King Xuān of Zhōu (周宣王),
dozens of states have been destroyed,
and there have been many ministers who murdered their lords and seized their states."
Thus, the disasters that arise from within are equal to those that originate from external actors.
Those who are able to fully exhaust the strength of their people,
To be able to fully utilize the strength of one's people,
and yet lose the state and one's life,
these are still wise rulers.
As for changing one's position and easily changing place,
preserving the multitude and passing down the state,
this is the worst of ailments.
For a ruler,
if he is truly clear about what his ministers say,
then even if he hunts with nets and hawks,
strikes bells and dances with women,
the state will still survive;
if he is not clear about what his ministers say,
even if he is frugal and diligent,
wears plain clothes and eats poorly,
the state will still perish.
The late ruler of Zhào, Jìng Hóu,
did not cultivate virtue and conduct,
but instead indulged in desires,
catering to the comfort of his body,
and the pleasure of his ears and eyes.
In winter he hunted with nets and hawks,
in summer he floated and indulged,
making long nights,
for days on end he did not put down the goblet,
those who could not drink were forced to drink through bamboo tubes,
those whose deportment was not respectful,
Those who respond disrespectfully will be executed on the spot.
Therefore, his living and diet were so immoderate,
his punishments and killings were so excessive,
yet Marquis Jìng (敬侯) enjoyed the state for several decades.
His troops were not blunted against enemy states,
his territory was not diminished by neighboring states,
there was no rebellion among the officials within the court,
and no troubles from neighboring states without.
This was due to his clarity in how to employ his ministers.
The lord of Yān, Zǐ Kuài (子噲),
was a descendant of Shào Gōng Shì (邵公奭).
His territory spanned several thousand *lǐ*,
and he commanded hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
He did not indulge in the pleasures of his children,
nor did he listen to the sounds of bells and chimes.
He did not have ponds or terraces built in the palace,
nor did he engage in netting birds or hunting in the fields.
He even personally handled the plow and hoe to cultivate the fields.
Zǐ Kuài's (子噲) hardship and concern for the people
were so extreme that
even the so-called sage kings and enlightened rulers of ancient times
were not more diligent and concerned about the world
than he was.
Yet Zǐ Kuài (子噲) died and his state was destroyed,
seized by Zǐ Zhī (子之),
and the world laughs at him.
What is the reason for this?
He is not clear about how to employ his ministers.
Therefore it is said:
A minister has five kinds of treachery,
which the ruler does not know.
Those who serve as ministers,
some extravagantly use wealth and bribes
to gain praise;
some are keen on lavish celebrations, rewards, and bestowals
to sway the masses;
some are keen on forming cliques and pursuing wise and respected scholars
to indulge themselves;
some are keen on granting pardons and releasing prisoners
to enhance their authority;
some are keen on flattering inferiors with dishonest arguments,
strange words,
extravagant clothing,
and grandiose titles
to dazzle the people's ears and eyes.
These five things
are what a wise ruler should suspect,
and what a sage ruler should prohibit.
If these five things are removed,
then clamorous and deceitful people will not dare to stand in court and talk;
Those who are eloquent but
do little in practice,
and whose conduct is not worthy of emulation,
dare not falsely represent the situation with idle talk.
Therefore, when at home, the ministers cultivate themselves,
and when active, they exert their strength.
Without the ruler's command,
they dare not arbitrarily speak harshly or fabricate matters.
This is how the sage-kings govern their subjects.
Those sagacious rulers and enlightened monarchs
do not resort to suspicious devices to spy on their ministers.
If one sees a suspicious device and does not rebel,
such a person is rare in the world.
Therefore, it is said:
When a concubine bears a son who rivals the legitimate heir,
a concubine rivals the wife,
a minister in court rivals the prime minister,
a minister possesses favor that rivals the ruler,
these four situations are perilous to the state.
Therefore, it is said:
"When inner favor parallels the empress,
outer favor rivals the government,
a branch son rivals the heir apparent,
and a great minister rivals the ruler,
it is the way to chaos."
Therefore, the *Zhōu Jì* (周記) says:
"Do not honor concubines and demean the wife,
do not favor illegitimate sons over the proper heir,
do not honor favored ministers and make them equal to high ministers,
do not honor great ministers to rival their lord."
If these four rivalries are broken,
then the ruler will have no suspicion,
and the subjects will have no grievances.
If the four rivalries are not broken,
then one will ruin oneself and destroy the state.
*Guǐ Shǐ* (詭使) Forty-Fifth
The ways in which a sage governs are three:
The first is profit (lì),
the second is authority (wēi),
and the third is reputation (míng).
Now, profit
is the means by which the people are won;
authority
is the means by which orders are carried out;
reputation
is the path upon which superiors and subordinates agree.
Without these three,
one would be in dire straits.
Now, it is not as if profit does not exist,
yet the people are not transformed by their superiors;
it is not as if authority does not exist,
Yet inferiors do not listen and obey;
officials are not without laws,
yet governance does not correspond to the title.
These three things are not nonexistent,
yet the world is sometimes orderly and sometimes chaotic.
Why is this?
The things valued by superiors
are contrary to the means by which they govern.
Establishing names and titles
is the way to establish honor;
yet now those who despise titles and disregard reality
are considered "high-minded" by the world.
Establishing ranks and positions
is the way to create a foundation for lowliness and nobility;
yet those who are disdainful of superiors and do not seek audience
are considered "worthy" by the world.
Authority and benefit
are the means to enforce commands;
yet those who have no interest in benefit and make light of authority
are considered "important" by the world.
Laws and ordinances
are the means to govern;
yet those who do not follow laws and ordinances but act out of private benevolence
are considered "loyal" by the world.
The world calls them loyal.
Official positions and ranks
are what are used to encourage the people.
But those who love fame and righteousness and do not advance to officialdom
the world calls them heroes (lièshì).
Punishments
are what are used to establish authority.
But those who disregard the law and do not avoid the punishments of execution and death,
the world calls them brave men (yǒngfū).
The people's eagerness for fame
is greater than their pursuit of profit.
Because of this,
how can scholars who are hungry and destitute
not live in caves and subject themselves to hardship
in order to contend for fame throughout the world?
Therefore, the reason why the world is not well-governed
is not the fault of those below,
but because those above have lost their way.
They constantly value that which causes disorder,
and despise that which brings about order.
Therefore, what those below desire
constantly contradicts what those above consider to be good governance.
Now, if those below listen to those above,
this is what those above urgently desire.
As for being honest and trustworthy,
being conscientious and hesitant in speech,
then they are called narrow-minded (jù).
If they uphold the law rigidly,
and heed orders carefully,
then they are called foolish (yú).
If they respect superiors and fear punishment,
then they are called timid (qiè).
If they speak according to the times,
and act moderately,
then they are called unworthy (bùxiào).
If they have no ulterior motives and study privately,
and listen to officials and follow their teachings,
then they are called ignorant (lòu).
If they are difficult to influence (zhì),
they are called upright (zhèng).
If they are difficult to give to (yǔ),
they are called incorruptible (lián).
If they are difficult to restrain (jìn),
they are called uniform (qí).
If they do not obey orders,
they are called brave.
If they bring no benefit to the ruler,
they are called simple-minded (yuàn).
If they have few desires,
are generous and kind,
and practice virtue,
they are called benevolent (rén).
If they are dignified and self-respecting,
they are called elders (zhǎngzhě).
If they study privately and form groups,
Therefore, those above cannot overcome those below.
Six Reversals, Number Forty-Six
Fearing death and avoiding difficulty are
people who surrender and submit to the north,
yet the world esteems them and calls them "shì who value life" (Guìshēng zhī shì).
Studying the Way to establish positions are
people who deviate from the law,
yet the world esteems them and calls them "literary shì" (Wénxué zhī shì).
Indulging in leisure and seeking lavish support are
people who seek profit through food,
yet the world esteems them and calls them "capable shì" (Yǒunéng zhī shì).
Speaking deviously to gain knowledge are
people who are false and deceitful,
yet the world esteems them and calls them
"eloquent and wise shì" (Biànzhì zhī shì).
Wielding swords to attack and kill are
people who are violent and aggressive,
yet the world esteems them and calls them
"courageous shì" (Lián yǒng zhī shì).
Harboring thieves and concealing adulterers are
people who deserve to die,
yet the world esteems them and calls them "reputable shì" (Rènyù zhī shì).
These six types of people
are those praised by the world.
Rushing into danger and sacrificing oneself for sincerity are
people who die for their principles,
Yet the world scorns them, calling them "
shījì zhī mín" (people who miscalculate)."
Those who hear little and obey orders
and completely follow the law are called "
pǔlòu zhī mín" (simple and uncultured people),"
and the world scorns them.
Those who labor diligently to eat
and produce profit are called "
guǎnéng zhī mín" (people of little ability),"
and the world scorns them.
Those who are admirably generous, pure,
and honest are called "
yúzhuàng zhī mín" (foolish and naive people),"
and the world scorns them.
Those who value life, fear trouble, and respect their superiors are called "
qièshè zhī mín" (timid and fearful people)," and the world scorns them.
Those who thwart bandits and suppress treachery
and clarify matters for their superiors are called "
chǎnchán zhī mín" (flattering and slanderous people),"
and the world scorns them.
These six kinds of people
are those whom the world vilifies.
The six kinds of treacherous, false, and useless people
are praised by the world as such;
the six kinds of people who are beneficial to agriculture and war
are vilified by the world in this way.
This is called the six reversals.
Commoners pursue private gain and praise him;
the ruler of the age listens to empty praise and treats him with ceremony.
Wherever ceremony is bestowed, profit is sure to be added.
The common people pursue private harm and criticize him;
the ruler of the age is obstructed by common custom and despises him.
Wherever contempt is directed, harm is sure to be added.
Therefore, if fame and rewards are given to people who are privately wicked and deserving of punishment,
while disgrace and harm are given to officers who are publicly virtuous and deserving of reward,
to seek the wealth and strength of the state
will be impossible.
There is an ancient proverb that says:
"Governing is like bathing;
even if there is discarded hair, it must be dealt with."
To begrudge the expense of discarding hair and forget the benefit of long hair
is to not understand the principle of weighing (benefits).
Moreover, removing carbuncles is painful,
and drinking medicine is bitter.
If, because of the bitterness and weariness,
one does not remove carbuncles or drink medicine,
then one's body will not live, and the illness will not cease.
Now, in the interaction between superiors and inferiors,
there is no kindness of father and son,
and if one wishes to use righteous conduct to restrain inferiors,
then their interaction will surely have discord.
Moreover, the relationship between parents and children is such that
if a son is born, they congratulate each other,
but if a daughter is born, they kill her.
Both come from the bosom of their parents,
yet the reason a son is congratulated and a daughter is killed is
because they consider what is beneficial later and calculate what is of long-term advantage.
Therefore, the way parents treat their children
is with a calculating mind
towards each other,
how much more so when there is no bond of parent and child?
Now, when scholars advise rulers,
they all discard the pursuit of self-interest
and speak of the way of mutual love.
This is demanding the ruler to be closer than parents,
which is not being versed in discussing benevolence,
it is deceitful and false.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not accept it.
The way of governing of a sage
is to be thorough in laws and prohibitions.
When laws and prohibitions are clearly stated,
the officials govern well;
it relies on rewards and punishments.
When rewards and punishments are impartial,
the people are useful.
When the people are useful and the officials govern well,
Zé guó fù,
if the state is rich
then the army will be strong,
and the enterprise of a hegemon or king will be accomplished.
Hegemons and kings
are the great benefit for the ruler.
When the ruler holds great benefit in order to listen to government,
therefore those he appoints as officials should be capable,
and his rewards and punishments should be without bias.
If he makes it clear to the gentry and commoners,
that exerting their strength to the point of death
will allow meritorious service to be established and titles and stipends to be obtained,
then once titles and stipends are obtained, the enterprise of wealth and nobility will be accomplished.
Wealth and nobility are the great benefit for the subject.
When a subject holds great benefit in order to engage in affairs,
therefore he will act in danger even unto death,
and he will exhaust his strength without expectation.
This is to say that if the ruler is not benevolent,
and the subject is not loyal,
then hegemony or kingship can be achieved.
Now, if treachery is certainly known, then there is preparation;
if it is certainly punished, then it ceases;
if it is not known, then it is unrestrained;
if it is not punished, then it proceeds.
Now, if light goods are displayed in secret places,
even Zēng (Zēng Shēn 曾參) and Shǐ (historian) can be suspected;
If one hangs a hundred *jin* of gold in the marketplace,
even a great thief would not take it.
If it is unknown,
then Zēng (Zēng Shēn) and Shǐ (Shǐ Yú) may be suspected of secret wrongdoing;
but if it is certainly known,
then a great thief would not take the hung gold in the marketplace.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler's governing of the state
is to make heavy their guard and heavy their punishment,
causing the people to be restrained by law
and not stopped by integrity.
A mother's love for her son is twice that of the father,
but the father's orders are ten times more effective with his son than the mother's;
the official has no love for the people,
but his orders are ten thousand times more effective with the people than a father's.
A mother accumulates love but her orders fail,
an official uses awe and severity and the people obey,
so the strategy of severity versus love can be decided.
Moreover, what parents seek from their son
in his actions
is his peace and benefit,
in his conduct
is that he stays far from crime.
The lord above, in relation to the people,
uses their lives in times of difficulty,
and exhausts their strength in times of peace
Then they exhaust their strength.
If a parent uses deep affection to secure the child's comfort and profit
but is not listened to,
and a ruler uses unloving profit
to demand that the people exert themselves to the death, yet his commands are carried out,
an enlightened ruler understands this.
Therefore, he does not foster feelings of kindness and affection,
but increases the power of his majesty and authority.
Thus, where a mother's love is excessive,
her son often fails;
this is due to excessive love.
Where a father's love is restrained and he disciplines with the rod,
his son often becomes good;
this is due to the use of strictness.
Now, concerning the management of a family's property,
if they endure hunger and cold together,
and force each other to work hard,
even if they encounter the difficulties of military campaigns
and the suffering of famine,
those with warm clothes and delicious food
will certainly be from this family.
If they sympathize with each other through clothing and food,
and bestow ease and pleasure upon each other,
when there is a famine and the years are barren,
those who marry off their wives and sell their children
It must be the [correct] way for a state.
Therefore, the way of law
is initially painful but yields long-term benefit;
the way of benevolence
brings temporary pleasure but ultimately leads to ruin.
The sage weighs their relative importance,
and chooses the greater benefit.
Therefore, he adopts the mutual restraint of law
and abandons the mutual compassion of benevolent people.
The words of scholars all say
"lighten punishments,"
this is the art of disorder and ruin.
In all cases, the certainty of rewards and punishments
is encouragement and prohibition.
If rewards are generous, then what is desired is quickly obtained;
if punishments are severe, then what is disliked is quickly prevented.
Now, those who desire benefit must hate harm;
harm
is the opposite of benefit.
[If something] is contrary to what is desired,
how can one not hate it?
Those who desire order must hate disorder;
disorder
is the opposite of order.
Therefore, those who greatly desire order,
其 shǎng bì hòu yǐ; [His] rewards will certainly be generous;
其 è luàn shèn zhě, [Those] whose wickedness and disorder are severe,
其 fá bì zhòng yǐ. [Their] punishments will certainly be heavy.
Jīn qǔ yú qīng xíng zhě, Now, considering those who receive light punishments,
其 è luàn bù shèn yě, Their wickedness and disorder are not severe,
其 yù zhì yòu bù shèn yě. Their desire for order is also not strong.
Cǐ fēi tè wú shù yě, This is not merely a lack of skill,
Yòu nǎi wú xíng. It is also a lack of moral conduct.
Shì gù jué xián, bù xiào, Therefore, the means to distinguish between the worthy and unworthy,
Yú, zhī zhī cè, the foolish and the wise,
Zài shǎng fá zhī qīng zhòng. lies in the lightness or heaviness of rewards and punishments.
Qiě fú zhòng xíng zhě, Moreover, heavy punishments,
Fēi wèi zuì rén yě. are not for punishing criminals.
Míng zhǔ zhī fǎ, kuí yě. The laws of an enlightened ruler are a standard [of measurement].
Zhì zéi, Governing robbers,
Fēi zhì suǒ zhì yě, is not governing those who have already been governed;
Zhì suǒ zhì yě zhě, Governing those who have already been governed,
Shì zhì sǐ rén yě. is governing the dead.
Xíng dào, Punishing thieves,
Fēi zhì suǒ xíng yě; is not governing those who have already been punished;
Zhì suǒ xíng yě zhě, Governing those who have already been punished,
Shì zhì xū mí yě. is governing the corvée laborers.
Gù yuē: Therefore, it is said:
Zhòng yī jiān zhī zuì "Heavily punish one act of wickedness
Ér zhǐ jìng nèi zhī xié, and stop the evil within the borders,"
Cǐ suǒ yǐ wéi zhì yě. this is what it means to govern.
Zhòng fá zhě, Those who are heavily punished,
Those who are thieves and robbers
are feared and detested by
the good people.
Why should those who desire order hesitate to use severe punishments!
As for generous rewards,
they are not only for rewarding merit,
but also for encouraging the whole state.
Those who receive rewards appreciate the benefit,
and those who have not yet been rewarded admire the work,
thus rewarding the merit of one person
encourages the masses within the territory.
Why should those who desire order hesitate to use generous rewards!
Nowadays, those who do not understand governance all say:
"Severe punishments harm the people;
light punishments can stop wrongdoing.
Why necessarily use severe ones?"
These are people who do not understand governance.
For that which is stopped by severity
is not necessarily stopped by leniency;
but that which is stopped by leniency
is certainly stopped by severity.
Therefore, when those above establish severe punishments,
wrongdoing is completely stopped.
When wrongdoing is completely stopped,
then how does this harm the people?
What is meant by "heavy punishments" is that
the benefit that comes from transgressions is small,
while the penalty the ruler imposes is great.
The people will not exchange a small gain for a great punishment,
therefore, transgressions will necessarily cease.
What is meant by "light punishments" is that
the benefit that comes from transgressions is great,
while the penalty the ruler imposes is small.
The people admire the benefit and disregard the punishment,
therefore, transgressions will not cease.
Therefore, the ancient sages had a proverb that said:
"One does not stumble on a mountain, but stumbles on an anthill."
The mountain is large,
therefore, people are careful when approaching it;
the anthill is small and insignificant,
therefore, people disregard it.
Now, if punishments are light,
the people will certainly disregard them.
To transgress and not be punished
is to drive the state and abandon it;
to transgress and be punished
is to set a trap for the people.
Therefore, light punishments are
the anthill of the people.
Thus, that light punishments should be the way for the people,
if it is not to ruin the state,
To establish [a system] that entraps the people
can be said to harm the people.
Now, scholars all recite the laudatory words from books and bamboo slips,
not examining the real events of the present age,
saying:
"If the ruler does not love the people,
and taxes are always heavy,
then resources will be insufficient
and the people will resent the ruler,
therefore, the world will be in great chaos."
This is to believe that being able to satisfy their wealth and resources is to add love,
and even if punishments are light,
[the state] can be governed.
This statement is not correct.
Generally, people commit crimes warranting heavy punishment precisely
after their needs have been met.
Even if wealth and resources are sufficient
and then abundant love is given,
if punishments are still lenient,
it will still result in chaos.
Consider wealthy families who love their sons,
their wealth and goods are sufficient for use.
If wealth and goods are sufficient for use,
then they are used carelessly.
If [they are] used carelessly,
Then they become extravagant and excessive.
If parents love their children,
they cannot bear to punish them.
If they cannot bear to punish them,
then they become arrogant and unrestrained.
Extravagance and excess
lead to poverty in the family.
Arrogance and unrestraint
lead to violent behavior.
This, even if wealth is sufficient and love is deep,
is the danger of lenient punishments.
Generally, in the life of people,
if wealth is sufficient, they become lax in exerting effort,
and if the superiors are weak,
they indulge in wrongdoing.
One who has sufficient wealth and still exerts effort is
Shén Nóng 神農;
one who lives under a weak government and still practices self-cultivation is
Zēng Zǐ 曾子 and Shǐ Yú 史魚.
That the people are not up to Shén Nóng 神農, Zēng Zǐ 曾子, and Shǐ Yú 史魚
is also quite clear.
Lǎo Dān 老聃 had a saying:
"Knowing sufficiency avoids disgrace,
knowing when to stop avoids danger."
To avoid the cause of danger and disgrace
and not seek beyond sufficiency,
Lǎo Dān yě.
Now, if it is thought that making the people content
is sufficient for governing,
it is because the people are all thought to be like Lǎo Dān.
Therefore, Jié valued being the Son of Heaven
yet was not satisfied with honor,
possessed the wealth within the four seas
yet was not satisfied with treasure.
Though a ruler makes the people content,
he cannot make them content enough to become the Son of Heaven,
and Jié may not have considered being the Son of Heaven sufficient,
so even if the people are content,
how can that be considered governing?
Therefore, the enlightened ruler's governing of the state
consists of suiting actions to the times to procure wealth and goods,
discussing tax levies to equalize wealth and poverty,
increasing ranks and stipends to fully employ the worthy and capable,
emphasizing punishments to prohibit villainy and evil,
causing the people to gain wealth through effort,
attain honor through achievement,
receive punishment for transgressions,
and attain rewards for merit,
without dwelling on gifts of kindness and grace.
This is the policy of emperors and kings.
If everyone is asleep,
Then the blind person does not know.
If all are silent,
then the mute person does not know.
Awaken them and make them see;
question them and make them answer;
then the mute and blind are exposed.
If you do not listen to their words,
then those without skill do not know;
if you do not employ their person,
then the unworthy do not know.
Listen to their words and seek what is appropriate;
employ their person and demand achievement;
then those without skill and the unworthy are exposed.
If one desires to obtain a strong man
and listens to his own claims,
then even an ordinary person and Wū Huò
cannot be distinguished;
give them a cauldron and sacrificial vessels,
then strength and weakness become apparent.
Therefore, official positions
are the cauldron and sacrificial vessels of capable people;
entrust them with affairs, and foolishness and wisdom are distinguished.
Therefore, those without skill benefit from not being employed,
the unworthy benefit from not being entrusted.
They embellish their words when not employed, thinking themselves eloquent;
they adorn themselves when not entrusted, thinking themselves noble.
the ruler of the world is deluded by his eloquence,
excessively praises his loftiness, and honors him.
This is like determining clarity without needing to see,
and determining eloquence without waiting for a response.
One who is incompetent but adorns himself to appear lofty,
The deaf and blind cannot do this.
An enlightened ruler listens to his words
and must demand their usefulness,
observes his actions
and must seek their effectiveness.
Then, empty, outdated learning will not be discussed,
and boastful, deceitful conduct will not be adorned.
Chapter Forty-Seven: Eight Sayings
Acting privately for an old friend
is called "not abandoning";
distributing public wealth as charity
is called "benevolent";
valuing one's person more than emolument
is called a "gentleman";
bending the law to favor relatives
is called "virtuous conduct";
abandoning office to favor friends
is called "chivalrous";
separating oneself from the world and avoiding superiors
is called "lofty and arrogant";
To wrangle and defy orders
is called "gāng cái" (rigid talent);
to bestow favor and win the masses
is called "dé mín" (gaining the people).
Not abandoning (criminals)
means the officials are corrupt;
being benevolent
means public funds are diminished;
being a "jūnzǐ" (gentleman)
means the people are difficult to employ;
acting virtuously
means laws and regulations are destroyed;
being chivalrous
means official duties are neglected;
being haughty
means the people do not serve;
being "gāng cái" (rigid talent)
means orders are not carried out;
"dé mín" (gaining the people)
means the ruler is isolated.
These eight,
are the private praises of common men,
and the great defeats of the ruler.
To oppose these eight,
are the private detractions of common men,
and the public benefits to the ruler.
If the ruler does not examine the benefits and detriments to the state [shè jì],
but instead employs people based on the private reputations conferred by commoners [pǐ fū],
it will be impossible
to expect the state to be free from danger and chaos.
Entrusting people with responsibilities
is the crux of survival, destruction, order, and chaos.
If there is no method for entrusting people,
there will be nothing entrusted that does not end in failure.
Those whom the ruler employs
are either those with keen intellect or those with refined integrity.
To employ someone
is to grant them power.
Those with keen intellect are not necessarily trustworthy,
because their extensive knowledge
can obscure their trustworthiness.
If, relying on the plans of a man of keen intellect,
one places him in a position of power
and he pursues his private interests with urgency,
then the ruler will surely be deceived.
Because those with keen intellect are not to be trusted,
one employs those with refined integrity
to judge affairs.
But those with refined integrity are not necessarily wise,
because their purity of self
obscures their wisdom.
Using the bewilderment of fools
to fill positions of governing affairs
and validating their actions
, affairs will certainly be in chaos.
Therefore, without methods for employing people,
relying on intelligence, the ruler is deceived;
relying on cultivation (morality), the ruler's affairs are thrown into chaos.
This is the trouble with having no methods.
The way of an enlightened ruler is to
allow those of low status to discuss those of high status,
those below must observe those above,
decide truthfully by consulting widely,
and listen without favoritism.
Therefore, the wise cannot commit deception.
Calculating merit and then granting rewards,
measuring ability and then assigning tasks,
observing beginnings and watching for shortcomings:
those who err are punished,
those who are capable are rewarded.
Therefore, fools are not entrusted with tasks.
The wise dare not deceive,
fools are not allowed to decide,
and then affairs will have no mistakes.
Observing officers, then one can know them,
but this cannot be made an order,
for the people are not all discerning.
Recommending the worthy, then one can act (in accordance with it),
but this cannot be made a law,
for the people are not all worthy.
Yáng Zhū,
Mò Dí,
are what the world considers discerning,
(yet) they interfered with the world's chaos but ultimately could not resolve it.
Although discerning,
(their methods) cannot be used as decrees for official duties.
Bào Jiāo
and Huá Jiǎo
are what the world considers virtuous.
Bào Jiāo embraced a withered tree,
Huá Jiǎo jumped into the river.
Although virtuous,
(their actions) cannot be used as examples for soldiers in farming and war.
Therefore, what the ruler examines,
clever scholars will exhaust their arguments on;
what the ruler honors,
capable individuals will exhaust their actions on.
If the rulers of today examine useless debates
and honor actions of distant merit,
seeking the wealth and strength of the state
will be unattainable.
Those who broadly study and are intelligent in debate, like Kǒngzi
Mò,
Kǒng,
Mò and Kǒng did not engage in farming,
then what benefit did the state derive from them?
Practicing filial piety and frugality like Zēng
Zēng and Shǐ did not engage in warfare,
then what benefit did the state derive from them?
A commoner has private advantages,
but the ruler has public benefits.
To have sufficient sustenance without working,
and to have a prominent reputation without serving in office,
these are private advantages;
to suppress literary pursuits and clarify laws and regulations,
to block private advantages and unify meritorious service,
these are public benefits.
Establishing laws to guide the people,
and yet also valuing literary pursuits,
then the people's model for imitation becomes uncertain;
rewarding merit to encourage the people,
and yet also respecting virtuous conduct,
then the people's production of benefits becomes lazy.
To value literary pursuits to cast doubt on the law,
to respect virtuous conduct to divide meritorious service,
to seek the wealth and strength of the state,
is unattainable.
Holding court tablets and battle axes,
they are not suitable for having sharp iron weapons.
Ascending and descending, turning and circling,
they cannot match performing hundreds of acts by midday.
The "Líshǒu" (狸首) arrows for shooting at targets
are not as effective as crossbows firing quickly.
Using shields and walls to resist enemy attacks
is not as effective as blocking tunnels and setting ambushes with bellows.
The ancients valued virtue,
the middle ages pursued wisdom,
and the present age contends for power.
In ancient times, there were few affairs and preparations were simple,
they were unadorned and did not exhaust resources,
therefore, there were those who used clam shells to push carts.
but used pushcarts.
In ancient times, people were few and close to each other,
goods were plentiful and lightly valued, and it was easy to yield them,
therefore, there were those who yielded the world through courteous resignation.
Thus, practicing courteous resignation,
valuing kindness and generosity,
and advocating benevolence and sincerity
are all forms of political advancement.
To live in a time of many affairs
using tools suitable for a time of few affairs
is not the preparation of a wise person;
In an age of great contention,
to follow the path of yielding and deference
is not the way a sage governs.
Therefore, the wise do not ride in pushcarts,
and the sage does not practice push-over governance.
Law is that by which affairs are controlled,
and affairs are that by which merit is named.
Law has its establishment and its difficulties.
Weigh its difficulties and if the affair succeeds,
then establish it.
If the affair succeeds and has harm,
weigh its harm and if the merit is greater,
then do it.
Law without difficulty,
merit without harm,
such things do not exist in the world.
Therefore, to capture a city wall of a thousand *zhàng*,
defeat a multitude of a hundred thousand,
with the dead and wounded filling the army's transport,
armor and weapons broken and damaged,
soldiers killed and wounded,
and yet celebrate the victory and the acquisition of land,
is to take the small harm into account while calculating the great benefit.
Now, those who bathe discard hair,
and those who excise injure blood and flesh.
To see something as difficult
and therefore abandon the task,
is to be an unskilled person.
The ancient sages had a saying:
"A compass has imperfections,
and water has waves.
I wish to correct them,
but what can I do?"
This is a saying about adapting to circumstances.
Therefore, some theories must be established
but are far from reality,
some words are clumsily phrased
but urgently needed.
Thus, the sage does not seek harmless words,
but focuses on tasks that are not easily done wrong.
The reason people do not use scales and weights
is not because they are upright and avoid profit,
but because scales cannot add or subtract from what people have,
and weights cannot make things lighter or heavier for people.
If one seeks something and cannot obtain it,
then people will not pursue it.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
officials dare not bend the law,
and subordinates dare not pursue personal gain.
Bribes are not accepted.
This means that affairs within the territory
are completely as accurate as a balance and weight.
Therefore, if his ministers have deceitful intentions, he will certainly know,
and those he knows he will certainly punish.
Therefore, a ruler with the Way
does not seek officials who are pure and uncorrupted,
but strives for methods to know them for sure.
A loving mother towards her weak child,
her love cannot be surpassed.
However, if the weak child has wayward behavior,
she sends him to follow a teacher;
if he has a serious illness,
she sends him to be treated by a doctor.
If he does not follow a teacher, he will fall into punishment;
if he does not seek a doctor, he will be in danger of death.
Although the loving mother loves him,
it is of no use in avoiding punishment or saving him from death;
therefore, what preserves the child is not love.
The nature of mother and child
is love;
the power of minister and ruler
is strategy.
If a mother cannot preserve her family with love,
how can a ruler maintain the state with love?
An enlightened ruler, by understanding the path to wealth and power,
then desires can be achieved.
Therefore, being careful in listening to governance
is the way to wealth and power.
Make its laws and prohibitions clear,
and examine its plans and strategies.
If the laws are clear, then there will be no internal troubles;
if the plans are successful, then there will be no external disasters from dead enemies.
Therefore, those who preserve a state
do not rely on benevolence and righteousness.
The benevolent are
kind and generous and regard wealth lightly;
the violent are
resolute in mind and prone to punish.
Kindness and generosity
lead to lack of fortitude,
and regarding wealth lightly
leads to a fondness for giving.
Resolute minds
cause hatred to be seen by subordinates,
and being prone to punish
causes indiscriminate killing to be inflicted on people.
Lack of fortitude
results in punishments often being pardoned,
and a fondness for giving
results in rewards often being given without merit.
When hatred is seen
subordinates resent their superiors,
and indiscriminate killing causes the people to rebel.
Therefore, when benevolent people are in positions of power,
subordinates will act wantonly
and lightly violate the laws and prohibitions.
hoping to get lucky and looking to those above;
when cruel people are in positions of power,
then laws and decrees are arbitrary, and ministers and rulers are at odds,
the people resent, and rebellious thoughts arise.
Therefore it is said:
Benevolent and cruel people
are all destroyers of states.
Not being able to prepare delicious food and urging hungry people to eat
is not considered being able to save the hungry;
not being able to clear away weeds to produce grain
and urging loans, gifts, and rewards
is not considered being able to enrich the people.
Now, the words of scholars
do not focus on the fundamental tasks but love trivial matters,
knowing the ways of false sages
to persuade the people;
this is the talk of urging people to eat.
The talk of urging people to eat
the enlightened ruler does not accept.
When documents are brief, disciples dispute;
when laws are simple, the people's lawsuits are easily brought.
Therefore, the writings of a sage must include arguments;
the laws of an enlightened ruler must be detailed in matters.
To exhaustively contemplate,
to assess gains and losses,
is difficult for the wise.
To be without thought or consideration,
to take previous words and demand later accomplishments,
is easy for the foolish.
An enlightened ruler considers what is easy for the foolish,
and does not demand what is difficult for the wise.
Therefore, wise thought and laborious effort are not needed,
and the state is governed.
If sour, sweet, salty, and bland
are not judged by the mouth
but decided by the steward,
then the cook will regard the ruler lightly
and value the steward more.
If high and low pitches,
clear and muddy tones, are not judged by the ear
but decided by the music master,
then the blind musicians will regard the ruler lightly
and value the music master more.
If right and wrong in governing the state
If decisions are not made based on principles
but are determined by favored individuals,
then ministers will hold the ruler in light regard
and place importance on favored individuals.
If the ruler does not personally observe and listen,
and the power to decide rests with subordinates,
then it is akin to relying on those who are supported by the state for sustenance.
If people do not suffer from lack of clothing or food
and are neither hungry nor cold,
and they also do not fear death,
then they will have no intention of serving their superiors.
If their will is not controlled by the ruler,
then they cannot be employed.
If the power of life and death
lies with the high officials,
and yet the ruler's commands can be carried out,
such a case has never occurred.
It is certain that tigers and leopards cannot abandon their claws and teeth
and share the same authority as shrews. The wealthy family of ten thousand gold pieces cannot abandon its riches
and have the same resources as a gatekeeper.
If a ruler with territory
cannot benefit those he favors,
and cannot harm those he dislikes,
yet seeks to have people fear and respect him,
it is unattainable.
When a subject freely expresses their desires, it is called "xiá" (俠, chivalry);
when a ruler freely expresses their desires, it is called "luàn" (亂, chaos).
When a subject disrespects their superior, it is called "jiāo" (驕, arrogance);
when a ruler disrespects their subordinates, it is called "bào" (暴, tyranny).
If actions are effectively the same,
the subordinate receives praise,
while the superior receives blame.
When a subject gains greatly,
the ruler loses greatly.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
there are "guì chén" (貴臣, honored officials),
but no "zhòng chén" (重臣, powerful officials).
"Guì chén" (貴臣, honored officials) are those
whose ranks are high and offices are great;
"zhòng chén" (重臣, powerful officials) are those
whose words are heeded and whose power is extensive.
In the state of an enlightened ruler,
promotions are based on merit and ranks are inherited,
offices and titles are received based on accomplishments,
therefore there are "guì chén" (貴臣, honored officials).
If words do not match deeds and there is falsehood,
punishment is certain,
therefore there are no "zhòng chén" (重臣, powerful officials).
Chapter Forty-eight of the Eight Canons
48.1 Following Human Nature
In general, to govern the world,
one must accord with human nature.
Human nature
has likes and dislikes,
therefore rewards and punishments can be used;
if rewards and punishments can be used,
then prohibitions can be established,
and the methods of governance are complete.
The ruler holds the power and occupies a position of authority,
therefore orders are carried out and prohibitions are enforced.
Power is the control over life and death;
authority is the resource for overcoming the masses.
Unrestrained appointments and dismissals corrupt authority;
when rewards and punishments are shared with subordinates, authority is divided.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not listen with affection,
nor does he decide based on retained arguments.
Therefore, if listening to words is not impartial,
then power is divided among the treacherous;
if wisdom and strength are not used,
then the ruler is at the mercy of his ministers.
Therefore, the actions and regulations of an enlightened ruler are like Heaven,
his employment of people is like ghosts.
Heaven is never wrong,
ghosts are never stumped.
When authority is exercised and teaching is strict,
there is opposition but no disobedience,
praise and blame proceed in unison without dissent.
Therefore, rewarding the worthy and punishing the violent
is the ultimate in promoting goodness;
rewarding the violent and punishing the worthy
is the ultimate in promoting evil:
this is called rewarding the same and punishing the different.
There is no reward like generosity,
making the people benefit from it;
there is no praise like commendation,
making the people feel honored by it;
there is no punishment like severity,
making the people fear it;
there is no blame like censure,
making the people feel ashamed by it.
Then, the laws are enforced uniformly,
prohibiting private punishment within families,
so that meritorious service and transgressions are not obscured.
Rewards and punishments must be known,
and when they are known,
the Way is exhausted.
48.2 The Way of the Ruler
Strength cannot overcome numbers,
wisdom cannot comprehend all things.
Rather than employing a single person,
it is better to employ an entire nation.
Therefore, intellectual strength rivals,
but the multitude of things prevails.
If a guess hits the mark, it is private merit;
if it misses the mark, one bears the blame.
An inferior ruler exhausts his own abilities,
a mediocre ruler exhausts the strength of others,
a superior ruler exhausts the wisdom of others.
Therefore, when matters arise, wisdom is gathered,
and decisions are made collectively and impartially.
If opinions are not unified,
later actions will contradict earlier ones.
If later actions contradict earlier ones,
then the foolish and the wise are indistinguishable.
If there is no impartial consensus,
there will be hesitation and indecision.
If there is indecision, then affairs will be delayed.
If one makes decisions alone,
then one will not suffer the burden of falling into a pit.
Therefore, one should have them admonish,
and after the admonishment is settled, then show anger.
Therefore, on the day words are presented,
there must be written records.
Those who gather wisdom, when events unfold, their wisdom is proven.
Those who gather ability,
The merit of the work is seen, and the success or failure of the plan is determined.
Success or failure has evidence,
and rewards and punishments follow accordingly.
If the matter succeeds, the ruler takes the credit;
if the plan fails, the minister takes the blame.
A ruler does not personally verify even tallied documents (hé fú),
how much less should he rely on physical strength?
Even with wisdom, he does not act personally,
how much less should he rely on guesswork?
Therefore, in employing people, he does not seek uniformity;
if there is uniformity, the ruler will be angered.
Making people use each other makes the ruler like a spirit;
if the ruler is like a spirit, then his subordinates will exert themselves to the utmost.
If subordinates exert themselves to the utmost,
then the ministers will not rely on the ruler,
and the way of the ruler is complete.
48.3 Causing Disorder
The one who understands the different interests of the ruler and the minister will become a king;
the one who thinks they are the same will be threatened;
the one who shares affairs with others will be killed.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler carefully examines the distinction between public and private,
and carefully examines the grounds of benefit and harm,
then treachery will have no opportunity to take advantage.
There are six sources of disorder:
The principal mother,
the secondary consorts,
the members of the ruling clan,
brothers,
great ministers,
and exhibiting the worthy.
Appoint officials and hold ministers responsible,
the principal mother does not interfere;
rites are bestowed according to different ranks,
the secondary consorts do not harbor doubts;
power is divided without ambiguity,
legitimate and illegitimate sons do not contend;
authority and records are not lost,
brothers do not encroach upon each other;
inferiors do not form exclusive cliques,
great ministers do not gather support;
prohibitions and rewards are certainly carried out,
exhibiting the worthy is not disorderly.
Ministers have two causes [for disorder],
which are called external and internal.
External is called fear,
internal is called love.
If what is feared is obtained through seeking,
and what is loved is listened to when spoken,
this is what causes ministers to create disorder.
As for appointing officials from other states,
punish those who form cliques, execute close associates, and heavily tax them,
then external influence will not take root;
ranks and emoluments follow merit,
and those who seek favors are all punished,
then internal influence will not become a cause [for disorder].
If external influences are not relied upon,
and internal connections are not relied upon,
then treachery and villainy will be blocked.
Official positions are advanced sequentially according to one's integrity,
until reaching a major responsibility,
this is wisdom.
Those whose positions are high and responsibilities are great,
are controlled by three constraints:
they are called *zhì* (質),
they are called *zhèn* (鎮),
they are called *gù* (固).
Having relatives, wives, and children,
is *zhì* (質);
thick and assured ranks and emoluments,
are *zhèn* (鎮);
collective responsibility with mutual oversight and shared blame,
is *gù* (固).
The worthy stop at *zhì* (質),
the greedy and gluttonous are transformed by *zhèn* (鎮),
the treacherous and evil are driven to their end by *gù* (固).
If forbearance is not controlled, the lower will overreach the upper;
If small evils are not eliminated, great punishments will follow.
When names and realities correspond, follow the correct path.
To be alive causes harm to affairs;
to die damages reputation.
In such cases, administer food and drink (i.e., provide for them).
If not,
and instead give it to their enemies,
this is called eliminating hidden treachery.
Obscurity is called guǐ (詭, deceit).
Guǐ (詭, deceit) arises from yì (易, carelessness/laxity).
When merit is seen, reward it;
when crime is seen, punish it;
then guǐ (詭, deceit) will cease.
If right and wrong are not made public,
and persuasive advice is not heeded,
then yì (易, carelessness/laxity) will not be eliminated.
Letting worthy fathers and elder brothers be cast aside is called "wandering calamity" (yóu huò 游禍).
The trouble with this is that it provides neighboring enemies with more resources.
Allowing disgraced and humiliated people to become close associates is called "befriending thieves" (xiá zéi 狎賊).
The trouble
is that it gives rise to feelings of anger and suspicion over their disgrace.
Hiding anger and holding onto accusations without expressing them is called "increasing chaos" (zēng luàn 增亂).
The trouble lies in allowing those who seek fortune through reckless actions to rise.
If the high ministers hold the scales of power equally without bias,
it is called "avoiding disaster."
The trouble lies in the prosperity of families,
which leads to the difficulty of usurpation and assassination arising.
If changes are made lightly without careful consideration,
it is called "weakening authority."
The trouble lies in treacherous men, which leads to the rise of poisonous and chaotic plots.
These five troubles arise
because the ruler does not understand them,
and then there are matters of usurpation and assassination.
Matters of dismissal and appointment,
if originating within the state, lead to order;
if originating outside the state, lead to chaos.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler judges merit within the state based on achievements [gōng],
and uses profits to benefit those outside the state.
Thus, his state is orderly while his enemies are in chaos.
The way to chaos is this:
If the ministers are resentful,
chaos arises externally like dizziness;
if the ministers are loving,
chaos arises internally like a harmful drug.
48.4 Establishing the Way [Lì Dào]
The method of comparison and verification:
Conduct investigations by consulting with many;
assess groups of five to assign responsibility for failures.
Investigations must be disruptive;
assessments must provoke anger.
If not disruptive, one will be disrespectful to superiors;
if not provoking anger, there will be mutual collusion.
The indications of disruption
are sufficient to know the quantity;
the indications of anger precede reaching the masses.
The method of observation and listening,
its indications lie in forming factions
while rewarding the different,
punishing without reporting
while the crimes are the same.
To gather many viewpoints,
one must measure them against the earth,
deliberate upon them with heaven,
verify them with objects,
and compare them with people.
When these four indicators align,
then one can observe.
Compare statements to know their sincerity,
easily change one's appearance to alter their countenance,
hold firmly to one's views to obtain the extraordinary.
Employ one person to focus on those close by,
Chóng yán yǐ jù yuǎn shǐ. (Use repeated statements to intimidate distant envoys.)
Jǔ wǎng yǐ xī qí qián, (Raise past events to fully understand their past,)
jí ěr yǐ zhī qí nèi, (get close to learn their inner workings,)
shū zhì yǐ zhī qí wài. (treat them distantly to know their external affairs.)
Wò míng yǐ wèn suǒ àn, (Grasp the clear to ask about the obscure,)
guǐ shǐ yǐ jué dú xiè. (use deceptive envoys to cut off pestering leaks.)
Dǎo yán yǐ cháng suǒ yí, (Use inverted language to test suspected matters,)
lùn fǎn yǐ dé yīn jiān. (discuss the opposite to discover secret treachery.)
Shè jiàn yǐ gāng dú wéi, (Establish remonstrance to control individual actions,)
jǔ cuò yǐ guān jiān dòng. (observe actions and movements to see treacherous activities.)
Míng shuō yǐ yòu bì guò, (Clearly explain to entice the avoidance of faults,)
bēi shì yǐ guān zhí chǎn. (act humbly to observe straightforward flattery.)
Xuān wén yǐ tōng wèi jiàn, (Publicly announce what is heard to understand what is unseen,)
zuò dòu yǐ sàn péng dǎng. (create conflict to disperse factions and parties.)
Shēn yī yǐ jǐng zhòng xīn, (Deeply unite to warn the hearts of the masses,)
xiè yì yǐ yì qí lǜ. (reveal differences to change their considerations.)
Sì lèi zé hé qí cān, (If they seem similar, then unite their support,)
chén guò zé míng qí gù. (point out past mistakes to clarify their entrenchment.)
Zhī zuì bì zuì yǐ zhǐ wēi, (Know the crimes and punish the crimes to stop the abuse of power,)
yīn shǐ shí xún
yǐ shěng
zhōng, (secretly send people to periodically patrol, to examine their true intentions,)
jiàn gēng yǐ lí tōng bǐ. (gradually change things to separate those who communicate and collude.)
Xià yuē yǐ qīn qí shàng, (Have those below make agreements to encroach upon those above,)
xiàng shì
He constrains his court officials,
the court officials
constrain their subordinates,
military officers
constrain their soldiers,
envoys
constrain their travelling attendants,
the county magistrate
constrains his appointed officials,
the courtier
constrains his attendants,
the queen
constrains her palace women.
This is called the way of ordered communication;
if words leak out and affairs are divulged,
then stratagems will not succeed.
48.5 Speaking to
an enlightened ruler,
his duty lies in thoroughness and secrecy;
therefore, if joy is shown, then virtue is repaid,
zé dé cháng,
if anger is shown, then authority is divided.
Therefore, the words of an enlightened ruler
are blocked and do not flow through,
thoroughly sealed and not visible.
Therefore, the way to gain ten from one
is the way of the inferior;
the way to gain one from ten
is the way of the superior.
An enlightened ruler practices both the upper and lower ways,
so that no wrongdoing can be concealed.
Make *wǔ* (伍), *lǘ* (閭),
*lián* (連), and *xiàn* (縣) neighbors,
reward those who report transgressions,
and punish those who commit transgressions.
The same applies to the relationship between superiors and inferiors,
and inferiors and superiors.
Therefore, superiors and inferiors, nobles and commoners, mutually fear each other because of the law,
and mutually advise each other for benefit.
The nature of the people
is that there are the realities of life
and the reputations of life.
The role of the ruler
is that there is the reputation of wisdom and knowledge,
and the reality of rewards and punishments.
When reputation and reality both arrive,
then the blessing of goodness will surely be heard.
48.6 Listening to the Law
If listening is not verified,
then there is no way to hold subordinates accountable;
if words are not examined for their use,
Then, deviant doctrines will prevail.
The nature of speech is such that it gains credence through numbers.
If something is not true,
ten people will say they doubt it,
and a hundred will question it!
With a thousand, it becomes impossible to unravel.
The words of a stammerer are doubted,
while the words of an eloquent speaker are believed.
When the wicked are in positions of power,
they draw support from the masses,
gain credibility through eloquence,
and use sophistry to adorn their selfish motives.
If the ruler is not satisfied with just anger and awaits collective consultation,
the situation will inevitably benefit those below.
A ruler who follows the Way, when listening to speech,
supervises its application,
assesses its merit,
and when merit is assessed, rewards and punishments arise.
Therefore, useless arguments do not remain in the court.
If those in office know they are inadequate to govern their positions,
then their offices will be taken away.
If speeches are grand and boastful, then their flaws will be exposed,
and the wicked will be angered.
Baseless and improper accusations are called slander.
Slander then incriminates the ministers.
Words must have consequences,
and speech must be held accountable for its usefulness;
therefore, the words of factions will not reach the ears of the ruler.
The way of listening is this:
loyal ministers present arguments to expose villainy,
and broad discussions bring about internal unity.
If the ruler is not wise,
then villainy will find support.
The way of an enlightened ruler is to
seek out the reasons behind what pleases him when he is happy;

upon entering service, should they not act as the sovereign's subject,
and upon retiring, should they not act as a father's son?
The reason why a father desires to have a virtuous son
is so that if the family is poor, he will enrich it;
and if the father suffers, he will bring him joy.
The reason why a ruler desires to have a virtuous minister
is so that if the state is in disorder, he will bring order to it;
and if the ruler is humbled, he will elevate him.
Now, if there is a virtuous son who does not act for the benefit of his father,
then the father's life at home will be one of suffering;
if there is a virtuous minister who does not act for the benefit of his ruler,
then the ruler's position will be precarious.
In that case, a father having a virtuous son,
and a ruler having a virtuous minister,
are only enough to bring harm,
how could they gain any benefit from it?
The so-called loyal minister
does not endanger his ruler;
the filial son does not criticize his parents.
Now, Shùn 舜, because of his virtue, took the sovereign's state,
and Tāng 湯 and Wǔ 武, on account of righteousness, exiled and murdered their rulers.
These were all cases of using virtue to endanger the ruler,
yet the world considers them virtuous.
The heroic men of old
upon entering service, did not serve the ruler,
and upon retiring, did not care for their families.
This means that when entering service, they went against their ruler,
and when retiring, they went against their parents.
Moreover, upon entering service, they did not serve the ruler,
to retreat without providing for one's family,
is a path to chaos and the extinction of one's lineage.
Therefore, to praise Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ
and glorify martyrs [liè shì]
is a method of creating chaos in the world.
Gǔsǒu was Shùn's father, yet Shùn banished him;
Xiàng was Shùn's brother, yet Shùn killed him.
Banishing his father and killing his brother cannot be called benevolent;
marrying the two daughters of the emperor and seizing the world
cannot be called righteous.
Without benevolence and righteousness,
one cannot be called enlightened.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Under all of vast heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's;
Within the borders of all the earth,
there is no person who is not the king's subject."
If one believes in the words of the *Book of Poetry*,
then Shùn, when outside, was a subject of his ruler,
and when inside, was a subject of his father,
making his mother a concubine, and marrying the daughter of his lord.
Gù lièshì nèi bù wéi jiā,
and in chaotic times cuts off their lineage;
outwardly they are devoted to their ruler,
letting their decaying bones and rotten flesh
be spread on the land,
flow into the streams and valleys,
not hesitating to tread through water and fire.
To make the world follow and emulate this,
is to make the world die universally
and willingly suffer premature death.
All this is to abandon the world
and not govern it.
Those whom the world calls zealous people
separate from the masses and act alone,
seeking to be different from others,
pursuing the learning of tranquility and detachment
and discoursing on vague and indistinct words.
Your servant believes that tranquility and detachment
are useless teachings;
vagueness and indistinctness
are lawless words.
Words that come from lawlessness,
teachings that come from uselessness,
the world calls discerning.
Your servant believes that in life
One must serve one's lord and nourish one's parents;
serving one's lord and nourishing one's parents
cannot be done with ease and indifference.
Governing the people
must be done with words, trustworthiness, and laws;
words, trustworthiness, and laws
cannot be done vaguely.
Vague words
and a philosophy of ease and indifference
are arts of confusing the world.
A filial son's service to his father
is not competing to seize his father's estate;
a loyal minister's service to his lord
is not competing to seize his lord's state.
If a person, as a son,
constantly praises the parents of others, saying,
"The parents of that person
sleep late and rise early,
and exert strength to produce wealth
to nourish their descendants, servants, and concubines,"
he is slandering his own parents.
If a person, as a minister, constantly praises the great virtue of former kings
and desires it,
he is slandering his own lord.
Those who are not his relatives know to call him unfilial,
but those who are not his lord
When everyone in the world is considered virtuous,
this is the cause of disorder.
Therefore, ministers should not praise the virtue of Yáo or Shùn,
nor should they commend Tāng and Wǔ's military campaigns,
nor should they speak of the loftiness of martyrs.
Those who exhaust their strength in upholding the law
and are single-minded in serving their lord are loyal ministers.
In ancient times, the common people were simple, ignorant, and foolish,
therefore, they could be acquired with empty fame.
Now the people are clever, inquisitive, and wise,
wanting to use their own judgment,
and not listening to their superiors.
Superiors must encourage them with rewards
before they will advance,
and also intimidate them with punishments
before they will not retreat.
But the world all says:
"Xǔ Yóu declined the world,
so rewards were not enough to encourage him;
Zhí Dào violated the law and rushed into danger,
so punishments were not enough to restrain him."
Your servant says:
One who has not yet acquired the world
but treats the world as nothing to him is Xǔ Yóu;
Xǔ Yóu is one such example.
Those who already possessed the world but did nothing with it were
Yáo and Shùn.
Those who would destroy their integrity for wealth,
commit crimes for profit,
and forget the possibility of their own death were
Dào Zhí.
These two types of people
are dangerous elements.
The way to govern a state and employ the people
should not be measured by these two types.
Governing means
governing the constant;
the Way means following the constant.
Dangerous elements and clever words
are harmful to governance.
The highest type of men in the world
cannot be encouraged by rewards;
the lowest type of men in the world
cannot be restrained by punishments.
However, if rewards are not established for the highest type of men,
and punishments are not established for the lowest type of men,
then the way to govern a state and employ the people will be lost.
Therefore, many people in the world do not speak of the laws of the state
but speak of alliances.
The feudal lords who advocate alliances say:
"If alliances succeed, one will surely become a hegemon."
And those who advocate counter-alliances say:
"If counter-alliances succeed, one will surely become a king."
The discussions of alliances and counter-alliances in the region east of the mountains
have never ceased for a single day.
